The authors compare networks of different depths under attack in both intrusion detection and computer vision.

In intrusion detection, extra layers did not improve performance and could significantly weaken robustness against adversarial attacks. In computer vision, by contrast, depth changed robustness only modestly. The contrast suggests the network security domain behaves differently from image tasks where most attack research is done. Designers of intrusion detection systems, the authors argue, should not assume deeper is safer.
arxiv-2510-19961:
Michael Kinyon and J. D. Phillips study loops, algebraic structures weaker than groups, in which every square lies in at least two of the loop's nuclei, the parts that associate with everything. One nuclear condition alone says little, but two together impose surprising order. Several known families, including C loops and extra loops, fall in this class.

For loops with left and middle nuclear squares, the intersection of those nuclei is a normal subloop. Such a loop is therefore simple exactly when it is a group or a simple unipotent loop. Loops where squaring is also a centralizing endomorphism have even more structure: they are power-associative. A torsion loop of that kind splits as a direct product, of a loop of two-elements and a loop of elements of odd order. Mild associativity assumptions, the results show, tame nonassociative structures.
arxiv-2510-20061:
Wm. Matthew Kennedy and twelve co-authors propose a public approach to red teaming artificial intelligence systems. Expert testing has found bias, hate speech, and false claims, but current evaluation methods are falling behind as systems enter schools, hospitals, and intelligence work. The authors argue that this gap leaves risks poorly understood and security flaws unaddressed.

Their model is a cooperative public exercise where a broad group probes a system together under a shared design. They review an early exercise held with CAMLIS 2024, a pilot run by the National Institute of Standards and Technology, and a similar exercise in Singapore. They conclude the approach gives useful results and can scale across countries.
arxiv-2510-20161:
Ahmed Alanazi, Duy Ho, and Yugyung Lee build a transformer that plans how a robot arm should move. The model must make paths that are exact, fit the task, and stay in bounds. Their design stores each move on a grid with three parts: where, what, and when. Masked steps force each move to step to a next cell and stay in the work zone.

The model trains on more than 53,000 paths. It matches the true path step by step in most cases. Near all paths are legal by build. Sent to a real xArm Lite 6 arm with a depth camera twin, it picks up test items at high rates. On 60 spoken tasks in clutter, it ends well in most runs.
arxiv-2510-20361:
Nick Fischer and Vasileios Nakos show how to regain the best sparse form of a long vector from a short sketch. The sketch is a fixed linear mix with few rows and thin columns. Their time is less than the best past sketch by a log factor. For a broad set of case sizes, no way can do much less, so the gain is near as good as it gets.

The steps rest on a new trick the pair call weighted hypergraph peeling. It grows the peel steps known from Bloom-type tools to graphs whose edges and nodes hold weights. Those weights may link to each other. The pair call their steps plain and apt for real use in sparse regain work.
arxiv-2510-20461:
Fabio Martinelli, Assaf Shapira, and Cristina Toninelli sum up long-time acts of the one-facilitated kinetically constrained model and its kin. Such models pair plain rules with glass-like slow acts. A move can fire just when a near site is on, and that gate makes the whole set act in a rich way. The models are named KCMs and date to the past century.

Much has been won on the still-state acts of KCMs in the past ten years. But when on-sites are rare, key asks on the live path stay open. The piece lays out those asks, with part new results and guesses. It spans the one-facilitated model, its kin, and a slanted branch-and-kill flow as well.
arxiv-2510-20561:
A. Galan and thirteen co-authors model the strong lens and dust maps of the host galaxy of supernova H0pe. The burst star sits far off, found by the Webb scope in a field where a rich cluster makes three views of it. Such split views are rare shots to read both the lens and the far host in fine grain. Their first model rests on spots of split views of back galaxies.

The team then adds the full glow shape of the host, which adds many more checks near the burst spot. Mean doubt on mass traits falls by more than ten times. Dust in the arc is mapped, and loss at the burst spot is gauged against three free SED-fit ways. The marks match at the one-sigma line.
arxiv-2510-21061:
Subhajit Sarkar leads three co-authors on a critical perspective examining the spinterface mechanism proposed to explain the chiral induced spin selectivity effect, where chiral molecules pass one electron spin preferentially. The effect appears across transport, photoemission, and chemistry platforms, yet no full theory commands agreement.

The spinterface model posits a feedback interaction at the molecule surface contact that aligns spins. The authors weigh its explanatory reach against the full experimental record, marking where it unifies and where it strains. A clear verdict on this candidate mechanism helps focus the search for the true origin of a much debated phenomenon.
arxiv-2510-21261:
Andrew T. Powis and forty co-authors report a community benchmark for plasma simulation codes, part of a series called Landmark. Seventeen codes from nineteen institutions modeled the same partly magnetized discharge, a hard test case chosen because large rotating structures appear inside it.

In that discharge, the rotating structures, called spokes, span a huge range of time scales, which makes them hard to simulate well. The codes agreed closely on how fast the spoke rotates and on average ion density, electric potential, and electron temperature. The authors share lessons from running the comparison, covering code design, hardware, and run times, to guide future benchmarking efforts and the next round of plasma software development.
arxiv-2510-21361:
Jaesik Yoon, Hyeonseo Cho, and Sungjin Ahn extend a planning method that pairs diffusion models with tree search to lay out action sequences step by step. The original method can only plan as far as its training paths reach, and stitching short plans together still leaves each search blind to the whole route.

Their compositional version plans over whole assemblies of partial plans instead of single paths. Three parts cooperate: an online composer searches across full plan assemblies with global context, a distributed composer cuts search cost by exploring in parallel from many starting points. A preplan composer speeds up answers by reusing stored plan graphs. Together they aim at long tasks that no single training-length plan could cover.
arxiv-2510-21461:
Ming Xie and four co-authors repair damaged video, filling masked regions so the result stays stable across time. Recent methods borrow strength from image-to-video generators, yet picture quality still degrades inside each chunk of frames, and weak alignment between frames lets content wobble within and across chunks.

Their framework, VidPivot, splits the job in two: first paint several frames consistently as still images, then spread motion into the masked areas. Clues from the spacing between frames guide the painting, and a propagation module carries content from a reference frame into later ones by splicing. A context controller feeds those aligned clues into the video generator as a soft constraint that suppresses distortion. Evaluations across benchmarks place VidPivot among the leading methods, with good transfer to new inpainting situations.
arxiv-2510-21761:
Jesse Atuhurra and three co-authors release J-ORA, a data set that teaches robots to understand Japanese conversation about the objects in front of them. Robot perception benchmarks skew heavily English, while real service robots in Japan must identify objects, resolve what a speaker means by a description. Predict the next action, all in Japanese dialogue.

Each scene is annotated through a rich attribute template: category, color, shape, size, material, and spatial relations between objects. Tested vision-language models, both proprietary and open, perform markedly better with those attributes supplied than without them, though a gap between the two model classes persists. An affordance analysis, asking what each object can be used for, shows uneven understanding across models, underscoring how much context-rich annotation matters for robots in dynamic settings.
arxiv-2510-21961:
Iskander Azangulov, Teodora Pandeva, Niranjani Prasad, Javier Zazo, and Sushrut Karmalkar make masked diffusion language models faster without making them sloppier. Unlike ordinary models that write one word at a time, these models can reveal many words at once. Only words that do not depend on each other can safely be revealed together.

The tension is that the most confident guesses tend to cluster and lean on each other. Their sampler, PUNT, works with any such model: it tests which candidate words are roughly independent, drops the less confident members of tangled groups, and unmasks the rest in parallel. Experiments show a better balance of accuracy against computing cost than rival samplers. The method offers a practical route to the speed that parallel generation promised.
arxiv-2510-22161:
Shuhong Liu, Lin Gu, Ziteng Cui, Xuangeng Chu, and Tatsuya Harada rebuild three-dimensional scenes from photographs taken through murky media, where water, haze, or darkness bends the rules of light. Neural radiance fields, the usual tool for such reconstruction, sample points in an object-centered way that distorts distances and struggles once the medium itself starts glowing, absorbing, and scattering.

Their system, I2-NeRF, samples space in a reverse-stratified pattern that stays nearly uniform, preserving true scale. Folds the medium into the rendering through a general radiative model grounded in the Beer-Lambert attenuation law. Direct light and light scattered by the medium are composed together, and the treatment stays even-handed between vertical and horizontal directions. The framework can even estimate properties of the medium itself, such as water depth.
arxiv-2510-22261:
Shireen Kudukkil Manchingal's thesis builds machine learning models that can say they do not know. Ordinary deep networks speak with the same confidence in and out of their depth, which blocks them from safety-critical work. The thesis separates epistemic uncertainty, the kind born of limited, biased, or incomplete training data, from the randomness no model can remove, and aims squarely at the first kind.

Its central construction is the Random-Set Neural Network, which borrows random set theory to carry a richer description of ignorance through the network than a single probability can. The goal throughout is practical humility: a model that recognizes out-of-distribution inputs, resists adversarial nudges, and holds back from overconfident decisions when its knowledge runs out. The work advances the broader program its author calls epistemic artificial intelligence.
arxiv-2510-22361:
El-Mehdi Mehiri introduces a parity constrained version of the four peg Tower of Hanoi puzzle. Two pegs stay neutral, while the other two are reserved for even labelled and odd labelled discs. Starting from the classical tower, he studies four goals covering the full tower and its even and odd sub towers.

Recursive methods split discs by parity and use classical three peg moves between steps. Move counts obey linked recurrences that simplify into closed formulas with a repeating pattern, growing slower than the classical puzzle. Whether these methods are truly optimal stays open, much like the famous four peg conjecture.
arxiv-2510-22461:
Josue Abreu and two co-authors ask whether BBR should become the default congestion control method for TCP, the rules that set how fast data flows. They compare newer BBR versions against older methods such as Reno and Cubic, plus data centre and satellite schemes. Settings range from home internet and campus networks to wireless and satellite links, using experiments and past studies.

BBR gave high throughput across settings and shared fairly when flows were alike or paths were fast. Home tests against major websites also favoured BBR, and it coexisted well with Cubic flows. The authors weigh these gains against latency traits seen on campus links.
arxiv-2510-22761:
Black holes in a modified gravity theory may orbit in odd ways. Tehreem Zahra leads a team with five co-authors. In 2025 they study a black hole with nonlinear Maxwell and Yukawa terms. They track orbits and rapid brightness flickers near it. Those flickers are called quasi-periodic oscillations.

The team derives motion equations from a Hamiltonian. They find the innermost stable and bound orbits. Periodic orbits are sorted by frequency ratios. Gravitational wave output from those orbits is computed. Several flicker models are compared with data. Data cover stellar, middle weight, and supermassive black holes. A sampling method then bounds mass and Yukawa values.
arxiv-2510-22961:
Jing-Xuan Zhang and five co-authors build one system that can read speech from sound alone, lips alone, or both together. Speech foundation models excel with audio, yet they are rarely adapted to use visual cues. Adding sight could help when noise drowns out sound or a speaker cannot be heard.

Their UASR-LLM injects visual features into many layers of a frozen speech model, then links it to a large language model that writes the transcript. Training runs in two stages, first aligning sight, then fine-tuning recognition. The unified design aims to handle all three input modes in one framework.
arxiv-2510-23161:
Wilhelmina Maryann Joseph, Beate Stelzer, Salvatore Orlando, and Moritz Klawin present a new way to measure how much of a star corona each region type covers. Stellar coronae cannot be resolved in X-rays, so structure must be inferred from spectra alone. Earlier Sun-as-a-star methods were indirect and heavy to run.

Their implementation turns solar emission measure distributions for distinct coronal regions into spectral components in XSPEC. Tests ask whether broad-band X-ray spectra alone can recover the filling factors of those regions. Success would let astronomers read coronal structure on distant stars using the Sun as a calibrated template.
arxiv-2510-23261:
Felix Chavelli, Paul Boniol, and Michael Thomazo seek evaluation measures for time series segmentation that humans can interpret. Segmentation finds the borders where a series changes behavior, in activity data, energy use, and more. Existing scores focus on change-point accuracy or point-based indices that ignore segment quality and the nature of errors.

Their work addresses those shortcomings with measures that reflect what a segmentation gets right and wrong in readable terms. Interpretable scoring helps practitioners choose methods and explain results. Better evaluation should steer the many segmentation methods now competing in applied fields.
arxiv-2510-23361:
Fleur Seuren, Santiago A Triana, Jeremy Rekier, Veronique Dehant, and Tim Van Hoolst study how a stably stratified layer at the top of Earth outer core affects hydromagnetic waves there. Evidence for such a layer from seismology, mineral physics, and geomagnetism is inconclusive, yet a stable layer could strongly shape waves below the core-mantle boundary.

Those waves probe the outermost core through their interaction with the geomagnetic field and mantle rotation. The authors numerically compute wave behavior and the electromagnetic torques the waves exert. Their results help interpret geomagnetic signals that might reveal the hidden layer.
arxiv-2510-23561:
Konstantin Schmidt and Thomas Richter improve a low-bandwidth way of sending talking-head video, where only a few facial keypoints cross the network. The First Order Motion Model rebuilds a face by warping a still source image, which keeps bitrates tiny and computing needs modest. Its weak spot is strong head movement, since the warping math cannot recreate real rotations well.

Focusing on head rotations, the authors replace the model's local Jacobian warps with one global rotation step. On clips with rotating heads, the change improves picture quality while cutting the data sent for predicted frames by forty to eighty percent. They also add modern normalization tricks to the training critic, which steadies the adversarial training. Scores from the LPIPS and DISTS quality measures confirm the gains.
arxiv-2510-23661:
Cook Hyun Kim and three co-authors study the Ashkin-Teller model, a spin system that couples two Ising-like layers through pairwise and four-spin interactions. They place it on random scale-free networks, where a few hub nodes hold many links, and work in the less explored regime where the four-spin coupling is antiferromagnetic. There, strong order in one layer suppresses order in the other.

Mean-field analysis reveals a phase diagram with four phases, from a disordered paramagnetic state to an antiferromagnetic one, with transitions between them. The clash between layers leaves the two order parameters asymmetric, one strong where the other is weak. One result concerns robustness: the degree exponent for hub-driven order stretches far past the value seen in ferromagnetic systems. The authors connect the tug-of-war to social settings, where consensus on one issue can block consensus on another.
arxiv-2510-23761:
Kevin Han and five co-authors present TDFlow, a workflow that aims coding agents at human-written tests and asks them to make the tests pass. Test-driven development frames repository-scale repair as a test-resolution task: the tests define success, and the agent must find the patch. Rather than one agent doing everything, TDFlow splits the work among four constrained sub-agents.

Sub-agents propose patches, debug them, revise them, and optionally write tests, so no single agent drowns in long context. Each part can then be improved on its own. Given human-written tests, TDFlow passed 88.8 percent of SWE-Bench Lite tasks, beating the next best system by nearly twenty-eight points, and 94.3 percent on SWE-Bench Verified. Hand checks of eight hundred runs found only seven cases of test hacking, counted as failures. The authors argue the remaining bottleneck is writing good reproduction tests.
arxiv-2510-24361:
M. Rumo and twelve co-authors track how dimer stripes in iridium ditelluride form and dissolve after a flash of light. This layered material undergoes phase transitions below room temperature with lattice shifts as large as twenty percent of a bond length. Strong electron phonon coupling creates local dimers that line up into one dimensional stripes.

Using time resolved X-ray photoemission at a free electron laser, the team follows the dimer population after infrared excitation. Dissolution of the dimers is driven by energy transfer from the electronic system to the lattice. The ultrafast measurements reveal the recovery dynamics of the stripe order, informing broader work on light controlled phase transitions.
arxiv-2510-24461:
Korneel Van den Berghe and three co-authors tackle training spiking neural networks for sequential reinforcement learning in energy constrained robots. Spiking networks promise large efficiency gains on neuromorphic hardware and process time naturally. Two obstacles stand out: spiking neurons are not differentiable, so surrogate gradients with unclear properties must be used, and their stateful dynamics require training on sequences.

In reinforcement learning, early training offers only short sequences, so the network cannot bridge its warm up period. The authors propose adaptive surrogate gradients tailored to sequential learning, aiming to stabilize optimization and lengthen effective training horizons. The work targets capable control policies that run within tight energy budgets.
arxiv-2510-24761:
Anirudh Ganesh and Nitin Sood review the Open Data Protocol, a shared way to build and use web data services with rich ask tools. For all its strength, the protocol is used most in big firm setups, in the worlds of two large software firms. Their work asks what holds back wider use of it.

They then bring in ODataX, a new form of the protocol that keeps the old form's fit with past tools. New traits add a more plain ask syntax, guards that gauge ask cost first, and stronger cache steps. The aim is to keep firm grade rules but meet the plain style that new web work wants.
arxiv-2510-24861:
Nanyi Zheng, William A Sands, Daniel Hayes, Andrew J Christlieb, and Jing-Mei Qiu stretch a rank lean code for plasma flow to work in up to six dimensions. The Vlasov task tracks how a gas of charged parts spreads, and its cost blows up with each added dimension. Their past code kept the rank lean in a plain grid form.

The new form works with high order blocks that nest in a tree, not flat grids. A third order build fills point reads at the foot of each path with lean cost. A fast wave solver in the same tree form keeps the Poisson step cheap. Big time steps stay stable, with no split by dimension.
arxiv-2510-24961:
Christian Klein, Iryna Petrenko, Svetlana Roudenko, and Nikola Stoilov study how waves act in a one line rule with a fourth order spread term. That rule, a bi harmonic form of a known wave law, has a drive term plus a self term set by a power. They build ground state waves by code and test how those waves hold up when poked.

Ground states come in two twigs, one firm and one not, which steer long run acts. Pokes on the loose twig can fade out or jump to the firm twig. Past a key power, waves can blow up in finite time. The team maps the blow up rate and shape, and weighs how a low spread term shifts it.
arxiv-2510-25061:
Chengyu Wu and Jiaqing Yang show that the traits of a stuff that guide light and magnet waves can be read off at its edge, from local data alone. Their case is the Maxwell rules for such waves. A hid block inside the stuff does not block the read, they show.

The traits are set to a count with no end, at the edge, from a local map that links in and out waves there. In fact, just the local data of one base wave form is used. The proof leans on a close study of odd forms of the Maxwell rules near set points. Their way trims and grows past work on this read task.
arxiv-2510-25161:
Keidai Iiyama and Grace Gao design short and mid term flight notes for moon orbit craft in a planned moon nav web. Such notes, called almanac and ephemeris forms, must pack a craft's path in few bits while it stays true. Moon pull and third body tugs bend those paths in hard ways.

For the near notes, a mix of curve fits and wave sums packs long arcs tight, more true than past fits. For the far notes, a low order mix spans a mid term arc of more than two weeks. Tests on four moon path types show sub metre place fits in the bit cap set by the shared spec. Speed fits came in far more tight.
arxiv-2511-00261:
Neha Balamurugan, Sarah Wu, Adam Chun, Gabe Gaw, Cristobal Eyzaguirre, and Tobias Gerstenberg test whether vision-language models can read social cues. People infer hidden facts from gaze, pose, and body direction with ease. The benchmark, Spot The Ball, removes the ball from sports photos in soccer, basketball, and volleyball, then asks where it was.

Humans beat four leading models by a wide margin, scoring two to three times higher. Models lean on shallow habits, such as guessing near the center or near players. Humans instead follow eyes and body orientation. The gap suggests future models need built-in ways to encode behavior cues, not just raw pattern matching.
arxiv-2511-00361:
Kayua Oleques Paim and four co-authors present MalDataGen, an open-source framework that creates synthetic tabular data for malware detection. Good training data is scarce in security work, which caps machine learning performance. MalDataGen uses modular deep learning generators, including adversarial and quantized autoencoder models, that can be swapped and combined as needed.

The team validates the output both ways: training on synthetic data and testing on real data, and the reverse. Seven classifiers and utility metrics judge the results. MalDataGen beat benchmarks such as SDV while keeping the data useful for real detection tasks. Its modular design drops into existing pipelines, giving security teams a practical way to expand scarce datasets.
arxiv-2511-00561:
Vladimir Toussaint shows how to protect a Majorana qubit by reshaping the noise around it. Majorana qubits, built in superconducting wires, gain protection from a tiny energy splitting, but that same smallness leaves them open to low-frequency noise that scrambles their phase. Starting from a microscopic local interaction, Toussaint derives how strongly the qubit's parity couples to a surrounding bosonic field.

The coupling itself scales with the small splitting, and the dephasing rate follows the environmental noise power at that low frequency. Engineer the surroundings so their density of states is suppressed near zero frequency, and the rate falls off with extra powers of the splitting. Longer wires then yield exponentially better coherence, an inverse Purcell effect that works with topological protection rather than against it. Spectral shaping becomes a concrete design rule.
arxiv-2511-00661:
Farideh Mazoochi and sixteen co-authors map the energy balance around Sagittarius A Star, the black hole at the Milky Way's center. The surrounding circumnuclear region, a few parsecs across, mixes hot plasma, magnetic fields, cosmic rays, and molecular gas. Using MeerKAT radio data and ALMA recombination line emission from the ACES survey, the team separates thermal free-free glow from nonthermal synchrotron light at fine resolution.

Only about thirteen percent of the radio emission is thermal. Magnetic, cosmic ray, and molecular gas pressures balance each other south of the central disk, while turbulent nonthermal pressure nearly matches them and dwarfs thermal pressure a hundredfold. Molecular gas thins inside the central cavity, likely blown by feedback from the black hole itself. The region looks magnetically subcritical overall, so fields can hold clouds against collapse.
arxiv-2511-00861:
Vinay Badewale and colleagues redesign the mouldboard plough, the curved blade that lifts and turns soil in farming. Good soil inversion improves aeration and weed control, so the shape of the blade matters for yield and for how fast the tool wears out.

Using the discrete element method, which simulates soil as many interacting grains, they test a modified cylindroid blade profile against an earlier design. The new profile raised the soil inversion index by up to about thirty three percent at some speeds and cut wear by up to about twenty four percent. Stresses rose slightly but stayed well within safe limits for the material. The authors note the study is simulation only, with field trials planned next.
arxiv-2511-01061:
Przemyslaw Spyra and Witold Dzwinel benchmark forward only learning algorithms, which train neural networks without backpropagation. Backpropagation must store every activation and wait for a global backward sweep, so replacements promise big energy savings. The authors note those promises usually rest on operation counts, not on measurements from real hardware.

Across almost a thousand runs on four vision benchmarks, they read energy, power, and memory directly from a modern GPU. Most forward only methods used several times more energy than tuned backpropagation. One, Mono-Forward, was the exception. On the largest networks tested it used less energy and memory at similar speed. Trained to convergence, it beat backpropagation on CIFAR accuracy, though it needed more passes.
arxiv-2511-01261:
Jiatong Shi and colleagues build a framework for judging speech role play, where a voice model must act a character, not just say words. Prosody, emotion, and delivery all count, and current evaluation pipelines lean on audio language models as zero shot judges, which miss those cues and squeeze many qualities into one coarse score.

Speech-DRAME contributes a bilingual, human annotated evaluation benchmark, with protocols for training speech evaluation models. It also adds a fine tuned judge. That judge agrees with human ratings much better than zero shot or few shot judges. A companion role play benchmark uses that judge to compare speech foundation models. Two strategies are distinguished: archetype evaluation, checking adherence to broad role types, and realism evaluation, grounded in real human speech.
arxiv-2511-01361:
Egor Podlesnyi and Foteini Oikonomou hunt for neutrinos from flaring blazars, jets of active galaxies pointed at Earth, allowing for the possibility that the neutrinos arrive late. A delay could arise because protons lose energy slowly in collisions with photons, or because accelerating them takes time.

They cross match high energy neutrinos from the public IceCat-1 alert catalog against active galaxies from two source samples, using gamma ray light curves from the Fermi telescope's public repository. Scanning a wide range of jet frame delays, they find a weak correlation, about two sigma before accounting for the scan, at a delay near a thousand days. After trial correction the result is consistent with the null hypothesis, so no claim of association survives.
arxiv-2511-01561:
Xiaobao Liu, Wentao Liu, Si-Han Shang, and Shu-Min Wu ask whether the direction of quantum steering matters near a black hole. Steering is a strong form of quantum correlation. In it, one party's measurements can sway another's state. Here four parties share a Gaussian state in Schwarzschild spacetime. Hawking radiation eats away at the correlations.

The team finds three distinct behaviors depending on direction. Steering from ordinary observers toward gravitational ones dies suddenly at maximal asymmetry, marking a crossover from two-way to one-way steerability. Steering the other way fades smoothly, vanishing only for an extreme black hole. A third arrangement, from mixed partitions toward an ordinary mode, survives at a finite level set by the initial squeezing. Even the inaccessible steering created by the Hawking effect is intrinsically lopsided.
arxiv-2511-01961:
Kyle Bystrom and Timothy C. Berkelbach present a new way to compute electron correlation energies, a key ingredient in quantum chemistry. Their method sits inside density functional theory, the workhorse framework for predicting molecular behavior from electron density. It builds on the adiabatic connection, a device that links a simple reference system to the real one.

The method, called OSMI, builds correlation energy matrices for the weak and strong correlation limits in the space of occupied orbitals, then interpolates between them. The design stays size-consistent and orbital-invariant, dodging flaws of earlier attempts. It matches the uniform electron gas correlation energy across a wide range of densities. On parts of the GMTKN55 set it beat MP2 and standard functionals on average, with barrier height errors under two kilocalories per mole. It also balanced spin and charge errors on bond breaking curves better than density functional theory and MP2 did.
arxiv-2511-02061:
David Hollenbach, Antonio Parravano, and Christopher McKee model how giant molecular clouds, the cold gas clouds where stars form, are destroyed by the hot bubbles blown around young massive stars. These HII regions evaporate ionised gas and push out neutral gas as they expand. Depending on the ultraviolet output of the star cluster, the expansion can stall inside the cloud, break out as a blister flow, or reshape the cloud into a comet-like form.

The authors compute accumulated and final mass loss across wide ranges of cloud mass, surface density, cluster brightness, and cluster position. Strong enough clusters destroy at least seventy percent of a cloud, and a critical cloud mass exists above which clouds never turn cometary. Low-mass clouds lose most of their mass by ejection of neutral gas.
arxiv-2511-02361:
Ayako Itaba, Masaki Matsuno, and Yu Saito complete a corner of the classification of a family of noncommutative algebras. Three-dimensional cubic AS-regular algebras are a noncommutative analogue of polynomial rings, A classical theorem represents each one geometrically, through a curve called its point scheme with an automorphism. This paper handles the cases where the point scheme is not integral, in three shapes. One is a conic with two lines forming a triangle, one a conic with two lines meeting in one point, and one a quadrangle.

For each configuration the authors list all the defining relations of the algebras and classify them up to graded isomorphism and graded Morita equivalence. They also write down explicit twisted superpotentials whose derived algebras realise the examples, checking regularity directly. Combined with earlier classifications of the other types, the work finishes the non-integral point scheme case.
arxiv-2511-02461:
Yu-Hui Song, Huan-Cheng Yang, Kai Liu, and Zhong-Yi Lu simulate, atom by atom in time, what a laser pulse does to the magnetism of a single layer of iron chloride. Ultrafast demagnetisation, where a magnet loses its order within femtoseconds of a flash, still lacks an explanation. The earliest stage is dominated by electrons thrown out of equilibrium. The team used time-dependent density functional theory, with a self-consistent correction for on-site repulsion, to follow the process.

The pulses drive magnetic moment from the iron atoms onto the chlorine atoms. Orbital analysis attributes the transfer to charge pathways within and between atoms, driven by the non-thermal electrons. The iron's demagnetisation peaks when the laser colour hits resonance, and the material's band gap shrinks by up to forty-one percent within tens of femtoseconds. This suggests routes to optically engineering magnetism in two-dimensional materials.
arxiv-2511-03361:
Gabriel Pirlogeanu, Alexandru-Lucian Georgescu, and Horia Cucu release an open speech recognizer for Romanian that sets new accuracy marks. Built on a fast conformer design tried here for Romanian for the first time, the model learned from more than two thousand six hundred hours of speech, much of it loosely transcribed.

A hybrid decoder lets the team test several reading strategies, from quick greedy picks to beam search guided by a word model. Word errors fell by up to about a quarter versus the best older systems, across read, casual, and specialist speech alike. Releasing the system openly gives Romanian speakers and builders a strong base that closed tools have rarely offered for their language.
arxiv-2511-03761:
Umut Calikyilmaz, Nitin Nayak, Jinghua Groppe, and Sven Groppe propose OptiMA, a transaction-based framework for very complex multi-agent systems. As agent systems grow past a hundred agents, the authors warn, two risks grow with them: faults spread more easily, and work slows at bottlenecks.

Transactions are used to guard against faults, while transaction scheduling is added to protect speed. The built system ran with more than a hundred agents, and scheduling improved performance by more than sixteen percent in their tests. A theoretical analysis of the scheduling problem is included as well. The work gives builders of large agent systems practical tools for later research.
arxiv-2511-04061:
Denuwan Vithanage, Skyler Wright, Edith Luveina-Joseph, Christopher Larson, and Edward Carlo Samson simulate fast transport of a trapped Bose-Einstein condensate using shortcuts to adiabaticity through counterdiabatic driving. Moving ultracold atoms quickly without heating them is a practical need, and painted potentials model both trap and auxiliary control fields.

Two-dimensional Gross-Pitaevskii simulations used experimentally feasible trap depths and atom numbers. Counterdiabatic transport was compared with a constant-acceleration scheme across varied times, depths, and distances. Every simulation showed a minimum time needed for fast transport, matching earlier quantum speed limit findings. The result bounds how aggressively shortcuts can move a condensate before control breaks down.
arxiv-2511-04161:
Suranjan Goswami is the lead author among eight authors on detecting document orientation before optical character recognition. Scanned and photographed pages often arrive rotated, usually from camera handling, and character recognition fails badly on sideways text, making rotation correction a critical real-world preprocessing step.

A new benchmark covers rotated English documents and a multilingual set spanning eleven Indic languages with limited resources. Their fast classifier, built on a vision encoder with dynamic cropping and fine-tuned for four rotation classes, reached near-perfect accuracy on both sets, in the mid-ninety and low-ninety percent ranges. Placed before recognition, the module substantially boosted downstream OCR performance in the reported tests.
arxiv-2511-04261:
Ming Liu, writing alone, presents a parallel, region-adaptive framework for private image pixelization, where grid noise gives formal privacy guarantees for visual data. High-resolution sensing plus foundation models raise re-identification risk, while classic pixelization struggles with fidelity, scale, and real-time speed at once.

Grid sizes and noise scales adapt to regional detail, and graphics chip parallelism speeds the process well beyond the classic baseline. Only key noisy stats are stored, cutting space sharply. Formal analysis uses the Laplace mechanism and parallel composition. Tests on three video datasets showed favourable privacy-utility trade-offs, and a face re-identification attack test on a celebrity set confirmed protection in practice.
arxiv-2511-04361:
Dennis Thumm, writing alone, introduces augmented time series structural causal models for energy markets. Prices there form through weather, generation mix, and demand, and regimes shift continuously rather than at clean break points. Existing price models rarely support explicit causal reading or counterfactual questions, limiting what analysts can ask of them.

Interpretable factors for weather, generation, and demand join grid dynamics and market observables in one model. Neural causal discovery learns time-varying causal graphs without needing a known ground-truth graph. Applied to real electricity price data, the framework answers counterfactual queries such as how prices would move under different renewable generation scenarios, a capability plain forecasting cannot offer.
arxiv-2511-04561:
Mattia Morbello, writing alone, compactifies a moduli space of connections on the Riemann sphere. The connections have rank two, with one double pole and two simple poles. Such irregular connections appear in the study of differential equations with wild behavior.

Morbello links one class of them to rational irregular curves plus one extra complex number. He first compactifies the curve space using a method inspired by Kapranov. Boundary points are then described by irregular stable nodal curves, in the spirit of Deligne and Mumford. Tracking the extra parameter completes the compact space, adding the missing limit points cleanly.
arxiv-2511-04961:
Ruijian Gou and co-authors ask why climate models keep missing how fast Arctic sea ice is lost. The ice is shrinking as the world warms, and new data hint the loss may be faster than models project.

The authors point to coarse model grids as a main cause. Wide grid cells blur small eddies, floe contacts, and sharp weather events that help drive melt. They argue that finer grids are needed to catch these small-scale acts. With them, forecasts of future ice loss should rest on much firmer ground for planners and coastal towns alike.
arxiv-2511-05261:
Pedro Zanineli and co-authors weigh accuracy against clarity in models that predict quantum wave probability maps, a core need in chemistry and materials work. They compare a plain neural network with a fuzzy neural system on data for a hydrogen molecular ion made by a physics-based net.

The plain network scored higher on fit, but used more than fifty times as many parameters. The fuzzy system, with Gaussian membership rules, stayed close in score and stays far easier to read. The trade-off matters when a model's reasons must be checked, not just its numbers.
arxiv-2511-05461:
Olivier Dietrich and co-authors test whether Copernicus satellite images can map building damage after a disaster, to guide aid. Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 give medium-resolution views, coarser than the sharp images aid teams prefer, but they are free and frequent.

The team built xBD-S12, a set of more than ten thousand before-and-after image pairs from both satellites, aligned with the known xBD benchmark. Tests show damage can be spotted and mapped rather well in many events. That reach could speed first damage maps when sharp images are late or very scarce.
arxiv-2511-05661:
Hayden Zammit and co-authors study what happens when a quantum channel is used again and again without being reset. Quantum networks need to move quantum states between distant nodes, for tasks like key distribution and shared computing. Most theory resets the channel after each use, which costs time and resources, so channels are treated as memoryless.

Working with a class of symmetric channels, the team derives a general formula for transfer quality on the nth use. They apply it to a perfect transfer channel with slightly mistimed readouts. Even small timing errors create memory effects, they show, and those effects badly damage later transfers. Reuse, in short, is not free.
arxiv-2511-05961:
Julian Gurs and co-authors test light sensors for a future set of wave detectors that would use lasers of longer wavelength. Squeezed light can sharpen such detectors, but only if the sensors catch near all the light, by a strict score that counts their dark noise. Lasers near two micrometers promise gains, if sensors can keep up.

The team measured a store-bought sensor of extended InGaAs across a range of cold and warm states, in the low tone band the detectors use. Cooling cut the dark noise as hoped. Sadly, it also cut how much light the sensor caught. At room heat the dark noise already drags the strict score down hard. The authors say this sensor class will not do, and a new design is needed.
arxiv-2511-06161:
Ibna Kowsar, Kazi Akhter, and Manar Samad address a stubborn gap in transfer learning: tables from different fields rarely share the same columns. Large language models hold broad knowledge that could help, but plain text prompts and in-context learning stall on mixed table data. Their method, called LATTLE, moves knowledge through the model's attention weights instead.

The attention transplant lets learning cross between tables with no shared features, no prompt crafting, and no huge pretrained model. Tests used ten pairs of unrelated source and target datasets against twelve baseline methods. LATTLE beat traditional models and leading deep table architectures, even ones trained on far larger collections of tables.
arxiv-2511-06261:
Ghosh, Harikumar, and Rana redefine what it means for two images to be neighbors. Nearest-neighbour retrieval usually depends on hand-tuned feature layers and distance measures. Their method, TMM-NN, instead asks how easily a sample can be nudged into a chosen region of the model's feature space.

A small patch is added to the query image, and the network is lightly steered so patched inputs drift toward a dummy class. Images truly similar to the query need only a slight push and land there confidently, while unrelated ones resist. Ranking by that confidence retrieves the most meaningful neighbors, and tests showed the ranking stays robust under noise.
arxiv-2511-06361:
Qi Shi and Pavel Naumov study how to write the leanest possible laws for systems of interacting agents. A law is a set of behavior constraints meant to prevent bad outcomes. Useful laws block those outcomes entirely, while gap-free laws only guarantee that someone can be blamed whenever one occurs.

For both law types, the authors ask for the law that imposes the fewest restrictions while doing its job. They prove that finding such a minimum law is NP-hard, even for simple one-shot interactions where all agents act at once. A hypergraph vertex cover approximation method can, however, efficiently produce near-minimum laws in both settings.
arxiv-2511-06661:
Tapti Palit, Seyedhamed Ghavamnia, and Michalis Polychronakis sharpen the call graphs that security tools depend on. A call graph maps which functions can invoke which others, and static pointer analysis draws it blurry because it ignores how each program is actually structured. Split-phase programs, with separate setup and working phases, offer an opening.

PhaseSeed runs the setup phase and harvests the pointer relationships formed at runtime, which stay fixed across runs under one configuration. Seeding those facts into static analysis of the working phase sharpens the graph considerably. Applied to control flow integrity, debloating, and system call filtering, it improved precision sharply and blocked nine extra dangerous system calls in generated profiles.
arxiv-2511-06961:
Erel Naor and Ofir Lindenbaum tackle the weakness of neural networks on tabular data when labeled examples are scarce. Networks favor smooth patterns and are distracted by irrelevant columns, while tabular signals are often sharp and localized. Self-supervised learning could help, but tables lack the natural augmentations that images enjoy. Their hybrid autoencoder creates the missing augmentation from the model itself.

Two structurally different encoders, a neural network and an oblivious soft decision tree, each view the data through its own learned feature-selection gates, producing complementary views. Trained with a shared decoder and a cross-reconstruction loss, the tree encoder guides the neural one toward tabular-friendly representations. At inference only the neural encoder runs. The method gained consistently on low-label classification and regression across diverse data sets, beating deep and tree baselines.
arxiv-2511-07061:
Xinran Li, Yu Liu, Jiaqi Qiao, and Xiujuan Xu ask whether large language models can truly perceive emotion in conversation, and build a training system to make them better at it. Emotion recognition in conversation matters for natural human-computer interaction, but models often miss the link between emotions stated outright and those only implied. Their system, PRC-Emo, combines prompt engineering, demonstration retrieval, and curriculum learning.

Emotion-sensitive prompts draw on both explicit and implicit cues to frame each speaker's psychological state. A purpose-built retrieval repository supplies demonstration dialogues, mixing benchmark training samples with model-generated, human-verified examples. During LoRA fine-tuning, dialogues are ordered from easy to hard using weighted emotional shifts between speakers. The result was new state-of-the-art performance on the IEMOCAP and MELD benchmarks.
arxiv-2511-07261:
Kasper Bågmark and Filip Rydin benchmark two deep learning filters for tracking hidden states of noisy dynamical systems in high dimensions. The filtering density is modeled through the Fokker-Planck equation with Bayesian updates at observation times, and both candidate filters rest on Feynman-Kac formulas, Euler-Maruyama discretization, and neural networks. Logarithmic formulations keep the approximations positive and robust as dimension grows.

Against a bootstrap particle filter and an ensemble Kalman filter, the deep methods win where it is hardest. In low dimensions the particle filters do fine, but on a partially observed one-hundred-dimensional Lorenz-96 model the particle methods fail while the logarithmic deep backward filter prevails. The deep filters also cut inference time by roughly two to five orders of magnitude, changing what real-time filtering is feasible.
arxiv-2511-07361:
Antoine Amarilli, Mikaël Monet, and Rémi De Pretto settle the complexity of testing whether a regular language is local. Local languages form a classic subclass of the regular languages with many equivalent characterizations, useful in areas from pattern matching to linguistics. Given a nondeterministic finite automaton, deciding whether the language it accepts is local turns out to be PSPACE-complete, as this short note establishes.

The result draws a sharp line against the deterministic case: for deterministic automata the same question is solvable in polynomial time. Nondeterminism, which usually costs nothing in expressiveness for finite automata, here costs a great deal in testing effort. The completeness proof places locality testing for nondeterministic automata among the canonical hard problems of automata theory, closing a natural complexity question about a well-studied language class.
arxiv-2511-07461:
Akshat Singh Jaswal presents DuTerm, a two-stage system for translation that must respect fixed terminology. Specialized texts need the same approved term every time, yet forcing terms rigidly can hurt fluency. DuTerm pairs a tuned neural translation model with a language model editor.

The first stage drafts a translation using synthetic training data rich in terminology. The second stage revises the draft, fixing terms with context in mind. Tests cover English into German, Spanish, and Russian on a shared task corpus. Flexible, context-aware handling beat strict enforcement. The findings cast language models as skilled revisers rather than sole translators.
arxiv-2511-07561:
Lazzoni and colleagues take the sharpest look yet at the dusty ring around star HD 92945. Debris disks are leftover rubble from planet building, and gaps or lopsided shapes can betray unseen planets. Webb coronagraph images in two infrared filters reveal the disk around this nearby Sun-like star.

Modeling and subtracting the disk leaves residuals that are checked for companion planets. Contrast curves and detection maps show what sizes of planet could hide there. The disk appears broad, tilted, and split by a gap, matching earlier radio and scattered light views. Agreement across wavelengths strengthens the case that sculpting forces shape the ring.
arxiv-2511-07861:
Changseok Kim and Jong-Hak Woo model the winds blowing out of active black holes more realistically. Ionized gas streams away in twin cones, but the host galaxy rotating disk also shapes the observed motions. Ignoring rotation can bias estimates of how fast the wind launches.

Adding a rotating disk to the standard biconical model changes the fit: local type two active nuclei need launch speeds up to about fifteen hundred kilometers per second. Monte Carlo runs over roughly thirty nine thousand objects pin down launch speed and cone opening. A notable minority launch far faster. Wind speeds decide how strongly black holes push back on their galaxies.
arxiv-2511-08361:
Helena Monke, Benjamin Sae-Chew, Benjamin Fresz, and Marco Huber present ProtoScore, a framework for evaluating prototype based explanations of neural networks. Prototype methods explain a decision by showing representative examples, which suits high stakes fields like health care, finance, and law. No standard benchmark exists to compare such methods fairly, especially for time series data, leaving evaluations subjective and progress hard to measure.

ProtoScore builds on the Co-12 property set from earlier explainability research to score methods across data types, with a time series focus. Practitioners can compare prototype methods against each other and against other explanation styles without costly user studies. All code is released publicly for reuse.
arxiv-2511-08661:
Ahmed Farag Ali develops a link between two ideas about limits in physics. One is the generalized uncertainty principle, which deforms quantum brackets. The other is the Bekenstein bound, which caps the information a region can hold. The whole setup works with expectation values rather than operators.

In Ali's account, the entropy bound feeds back into the deformed bracket, and at saturation the leftover uncertainty in a sector cancels. He argues this allows conjugate quantities to be known together in practice, easing the classic EPR tension without hidden variables. A single self-check then fixes confinement scales, matching the hydrogen Bohr radius and the proton charge radius. The framework also predicts a short-distance regime where spacetime looks complex before settling into ordinary Lorentzian form.
arxiv-2511-08761:
Benjamin Fregoso computes how the average electron density inside a crystal responds to a weak, uniform magnetic field. The crystal can be any three-dimensional multiband material, metal or insulator, of any symmetry, and the calculation runs to first and second order in the field strength.

At first order, insulators follow the well-known Streda formula, while metals gain an extra term from orbital magnetic moments at the Fermi surface. At second order several microscopic processes enter, and the quantum metric tensor plays a starring role by generating a pseudo-magnetic moment as Bloch wave functions rotate. Fregoso also works out what the results imply for volume and pressure. The method is gauge invariant and treats intraband and interband processes on equal footing.
arxiv-2511-10061:
Xiang Guo, Xiaojun Zhang, Yong Li, and Zhihai Wang design a way to tell left-handed from right-handed molecules inside a cavity quantum electrodynamics setup. The two mirror forms of a chiral molecule, called enantiomers, behave identically in most measurements, so detecting their excess is hard. Their scheme uses three-level cyclic molecules whose two forms carry an intrinsic phase difference that can be turned into interference.

By watching the steady-state photon number inside the cavity, constructive and destructive pathways reveal the enantiomeric excess directly, with error below five percent. To handle finite ensembles without brute-force simulation, they use a generalized discrete truncated Wigner approximation suited to many-molecule systems. The results aim at realistic quantum-optical enantiodetection beyond the single-molecule idealization.
arxiv-2511-10161:
J. Javier Alonso-Ramos, Ignacio Aguilera-Martos, Francisco Herrera, and Andrés Herrera-Poyatos present DenoGrad, a data cleaning approach that uses a trained neural network to fix its own training data. Many noise-cleaning methods assume rigid rules or demand a clean reference set, which real data sets rarely offer. DenoGrad keeps the pre-trained model frozen and iteratively corrects the inputs themselves by gradient-based optimization.

The approach handles tabular regression and time-series forecasting, adding a consensus plan so corrections in sequences stay temporally coherent. Across ten real-world data sets, cleaned data consistently improved downstream predictive performance while preserving the data's spread and correlation structure. DenoGrad even helped on nominally clean data sets, acting as a data set-level smoother. Code is available publicly.
arxiv-2511-10261:
Lucas Rudelt, Fabian Mikulasch, Viola Priesemann, and André Ferreira Castro review representation learning inside cerebellum-like brain circuits, the vertebrate cerebellum and the insect mushroom body. Both structures expand sensory inputs into a much larger layer, improving pattern separation so animals can learn distinct associations quickly. Classical models treated that expansion layer as fixed wiring, with learning only at the output synapses.

New evidence instead shows plasticity inside that layer itself matters. Comparing granule layer and mushroom body calyx data, the authors find strikingly similar interneuron circuits, dendritic shapes, and change mechanisms, hinting at general principles. The overlap with recent theory is strong, though how stimulus-driven and reward-driven change interact there remains not well understood.
arxiv-2511-10361:
Rodrigo Mesquita and Bernardo Toninho study linear types, a system that tracks whether a program uses each resource exactly once. In lazy languages like Haskell, a resource can appear in the code yet never be used when the program runs. Haskell's optimizing compiler also rewrites programs in ways that break the syntactic count while keeping behavior correct.

Their system, Linear Core, accepts the lazy meaning of linearity directly and targets the Core language inside the Glasgow Haskell Compiler. They prove the system sound, so linear use is still guaranteed where it matters. Several compiler transformations preserve linearity in Linear Core while failing in plain Core. A working compiler plugin also checks the system against real linear libraries.
arxiv-2511-10461:
Simon Donike, Cesar Aybar, Julio Contreras, and Luis Gómez-Chova release OpenSR-SRGAN, an open software framework for sharpening satellite images with adversarial networks. Super-resolution promises finer detail from multispectral Earth observation data such as Sentinel-2, but research code is often hard to adapt. Their package unifies SRGAN-style models behind simple configuration files instead of code edits.

Users can swap generators, discriminators, loss functions, and training schedules, and change scale factors or band setups, all through settings. Ready-made configurations cover common remote sensing cases, with sensible defaults and built-in logging, validation, and large-scene inference. The authors present it as a practical, reproducible benchmark tool that lowers the barrier for researchers and practitioners, not as a record-setting model.
arxiv-2511-10561:
Benjamin Yu, Vincenzo Lordi, and Daniel Schwalbe-Koda address a cost problem in atomistic machine learning. Potentials trained on quantum calculations are only as good as their datasets, but big diverse datasets are expensive to produce and train on, while small ones risk dropping rare atomic environments.

The authors build an information-theoretic measure of compression efficiency and an algorithm that maximizes it, framing the task as a minimum set cover problem over atom-centered environments. Their method keeps the smallest set of structures that still carries the original information. On benchmark datasets including GAP-20 and TM23, plus 64 varied datasets from ColabFit, it preserved outliers and diversity even at high compression. Models trained on the compressed data handled out-of-distribution cases better. The code ships in the open-source QUESTS package.
arxiv-2511-10661:
Saatvik Kher, Shang Wu, Rachel Longjohn, Catarina Belém, and Padhraic Smyth develop a statistical framework for evaluating language model systems honestly. Benchmark scores usually come from a single run, yet the same prompt can score differently on repeated runs, so a single number hides real uncertainty.

Their Bayesian approach models that stochasticity directly and quantifies uncertainty in the evaluation metric itself. It also enables sequential evaluation: the model decides which benchmark prompts to run next, spending the evaluation budget where it teaches the most. Four case studies demonstrate the method, covering dialogue preferences, refusal rates on adversarial inputs, embodied agent reasoning, and web-search question answering. The authors argue black-box systems need this kind of uncertainty reporting.
arxiv-2511-11061:
Jan Vorberger, Gabriel Smith, and their colleagues compare math recipes for electron behavior in hydrogen under extreme heat and pressure. Such warm dense hydrogen sits between molecule and metal states, and lab work needs a recipe that handles both ends well. The recipes differ in how they treat electron exchange and weak van der Waals attraction.

The team checks basic facts such as bond length and the energy needed to split the molecule. One recipe matched those facts best, while recipes with the weak-force fix did no better than a standard one. They also compare structure and energy spread in the changeover region to guide future choices.
arxiv-2511-11161:
Yuzhen Zhao, Yating Liu, and Marc Hoffmann use neural networks to estimate the drift of a diffusion process from discrete snapshots along many independent paths. Drift, the local pull on a random motion, must be inferred without a preset formula shape in this nonparametric setup. High-frequency samples from separate runs supply the evidence.

Their network estimator comes with a proven error rate split into training, approximation, and diffusion parts. For drift built by layered composition, they give an explicit rate. In tests with a wiggly layered drift, the rate did not worsen with dimension, and the network beat spline methods at capturing local features, especially in higher dimensions.
arxiv-2511-11261:
Wanda Duss, Askar Iliasov, and Tomáš Bzdušek derive the full energy spectrum of decorated Cayley trees, branching structures that mirror certain flat two-dimensional lattices such as Lieb, kagome, and star lattices. Those lattices are known for flat energy bands, where particles stall in compact localized states. The question is whether tree versions keep such bands and what they mean there.

The trees do show flat or near-flat bands at matching energies, but with a new reading: they act as edge states pinned to the inner or outer boundary of the branches. An exact mapping links one tree to chains with topological edge states, giving its flat band topological stability. Like mappings cover the other decorations.
arxiv-2511-11961:
Shuning Zhang and five co-authors show an attack that uses conversation itself as the weapon. A language model profiles its user in real time. It adapts its style to coax out private facts. All the while, it sounds perfectly innocent. Guardrails watch for forbidden questions. They are not built for polite manipulation spread across a chat.

The frame picks a communication strategy predicted to loosen disclosure. It then rewrites its messages to stay stealthy. A study with eighty-four users tested the attack. Three models and three scenarios were used. Targeted attacks raised elicitation sharply. Defenses against social engineering by AI are the clear need.
arxiv-2511-12161:
Jonas Pleyer argues, in a short opinion piece, that agent-based models in cell biology are not flexible enough for the systems they claim to describe. Such models treat cells as agents and are widely used to study biological processes. Many tools have appeared, each built for a narrow research question.

Pleyer draws out broad principles from widely used software in several fields and compares them with current cell biology models. The comparison, he concludes, shows a clear flexibility gap. That gap, in his view, holds back progress in the whole field, because models cannot easily grow to match the true complexity of living systems.
arxiv-2511-12761:
Hanna Furmańczyk, Didem Gözüpek, and Sibel Özkan study packing coloring. It is a way of labeling a graph's vertices so that vertices sharing a label must sit far apart, with higher labels demanding larger distances. The rule mirrors frequency assignment in wireless networks. The packing chromatic number is the fewest labels that suffice. Earlier work bounded this number for paths and cycles; this paper pushes into graph families built around long paths, which are harder to control.

The authors define path-aligned graph products and prove the number stays bounded by a constant for several such families. They then turn to caterpillar graphs, tree-like graphs with a central path, where the known bound was seven colors. They fully characterize which caterpillars need at most three. It tells engineers and mathematicians which path-like networks keep channel demands modest.
arxiv-2511-12961:
Pritam P. Karmokar and William J. Beksi estimate motion from event cameras by borrowing a cue from biology: inertia. Event cameras report pixel changes rather than frames, giving dense timing but sparse spatial data. A leading method, contrast maximization, warps events until they align, but the optimization is badly non-convex and easily lands in wrong minima. The authors add orientation maps computed from the camera's three-dimensional velocity, which act as priors telling the optimizer which directions of motion are plausible at each point.

Guided this way, the same optimization becomes more robust and converges better. On the MVSEC, DSEC, and ECD benchmark datasets, the hybrid method beat the state of the art in flow accuracy. Event cameras are attractive for drones and fast robots because they handle motion blur and darkness well. Reliable flow from a cheap inertial prior brings that hardware closer to dependable navigation.
arxiv-2511-13061:
Vladimír Macko and Vladimír Boža make pruned language models actually run faster. Sparse matrix-vector multiplication is the core operation when a sparse model generates text, but existing methods handle the low, messy sparsity of pruned models, thirty to ninety percent, badly. That failure meant pruning saved little memory and less time. Their MACKO design pairs a new storage format with a matching graphics processor kernel, built for the way GPUs execute, with no need for tensor cores or expensive preprocessing.

At fifty percent sparsity, MACKO is the first method they know to beat even the dense representation, cutting memory by half again and speeding computation noticeably. Against other sparse libraries the speedups are several-fold. On a pruned Llama2-7B model it delivered the same memory saving with faster inference. Unstructured pruning at moderate sparsity, they claim, is finally worth doing.
arxiv-2511-13361:
Jiyang Zheng and 7 co-authors present MedDCR, a system that learns how to design agent workflows for medical coding. Coding turns clinical notes into standard diagnosis and procedure codes for billing and research. The job needs several steps, from finding concepts to checking codes across documents, and hand-built agent flows miss real variation.

MedDCR runs a closed loop where a Designer proposes a workflow, a Coder runs it, and a Reflector grades results and feeds back advice. A memory archive keeps past designs for reuse and steady improvement. On benchmarks it beat leading baselines and produced clear, adaptable workflows that mirror real coding practice.
arxiv-2511-13761:
Alexander Acker and 5 co-authors test what happens when the compact nanochat training stack meets the DiLoCo distributed training algorithm. DiLoCo lets workers train locally for many steps before syncing, cutting communication by orders of magnitude for sites with weak links. The trade-offs of that shift for final model quality were still unclear.

Wrapped around nanochat's training loop, DiLoCo converged stably with competitive pretraining loss. After later training stages, though, its models scored worse on knowledge, math, and coding benchmarks than the standard parallel baseline. Retraining the later stages in the standard way could not undo the gap, which the authors trace to lasting representation drift from asynchronous updates. Their fork is public as a reference build.
arxiv-2511-13961:
Jiarui Li, Alessandro Zanardi, Federico Pecora, and two co-authors reframe multi-agent path finding, the problem of routing many robots without collisions, as one unified control problem. Most existing work plans routes and executes them as separate stages, with each variant handled ad hoc. Their framework models planning and execution together and allows for uncertainty during motion.

Their algorithm, FICO, uses a factorization method inspired by receding-horizon control to run in a closed loop. It starts execution within milliseconds, scales to thousands of agents, and adapts to delays and new arrivals on the fly. Case studies show computing times up to a hundred times faster than open-loop baselines, with higher throughput.
arxiv-2511-14061:
Hanlin Ren, Yichuan Wang, and Yan Zhong connect three hard problems in complexity theory. Range avoidance asks for a string outside the output range of a stretching circuit. Proof complexity generators are circuits whose out-of-range strings are hard to prove out of range. Demi-bits generators are a cryptographic primitive designed to fool nondeterministic adversaries.

The authors show demi-bits generators imply range avoidance is hard even for nondeterministic algorithms, settling an open question from a 2024 paper. Under extra hardness assumptions the result holds even for constant-degree polynomial instances. They also show the dual weak pigeonhole principle cannot be proved in a weak theory if demi-bits exist, tying cryptography to proof complexity limits.
arxiv-2511-14761:
Keya Hu, Ali Cy, and six co-authors argue that the ARC reasoning benchmark should be treated as a vision task. ARC puzzles ask solvers to find a pattern linking example grids and apply it to a new grid, a core test of abstract thinking. Most attempts hand the grids to language models as text, even though the puzzles are plainly visual.

The team instead paints each puzzle on a canvas and trains a standard vision transformer to map input images to output images. The model learns from scratch on ARC training data alone. Framing the task this way lets ordinary vision tools attack a problem usually reserved for language systems, with results the authors use to press their case.
arxiv-2511-15061:
Haodong Chen, Guido Zuccon, and Teerapong Leelanupab revisit GeneGPT, a system that let users query genomic databases in natural language through a proprietary language model and domain tools. That dependence raised cost, privacy, and scalability concerns, so they first reproduce it with open source models in a single agent design and note its limits.

They then build OpenBioLLM, a multi agent framework with specialists for routing tools, generating queries, and validating responses. It matches or beats the original on most benchmark tasks with smaller open models and no extra fine tuning, while cutting latency by roughly half. Code and resources are shared openly.
arxiv-2511-15661:
Yicheng He, Chengsong Huang, Zongxia Li, Jiaxin Huang, and Yonghui Yang introduce VisPlay, a way for a vision-language model to improve its own reasoning using unlabeled images. Such models answer questions about pictures, but training them with reinforcement learning usually needs human labels or hand-made scoring rules, which are costly to scale. VisPlay instead splits one base model into two roles that train each other.

One role acts as a questioner that invents hard but answerable questions about an image. The other role answers them, producing silver responses used as learning signals, with rewards for diversity and difficulty. Trained on two model families, the system improved visual reasoning, generalization, and reduced made-up answers across eight benchmarks.
arxiv-2511-15961:
Kedar Karhadkar and four co-authors improve how experimentation platforms evaluate variance figures using relative efficiency. Online platforms must prove their confidence intervals can be trusted. Standard A/A tests reduce each experiment to a binary pass or fail, wasting information about effect magnitude. That inefficiency makes false positive rate figures noisy and slow to diagnose problems.

The authors show how to use full experiment results to judge variance estimator quality more efficiently. Better diagnostics catch biased or noisy variance figures earlier. Reliable intervals underpin every product decision platforms support. Customer trust depends on catching interval failures before they mislead experiments. The method extracts more signal from tests firms already run, without new traffic or added experimental cost.
arxiv-2511-16061:
Alex Ning and Vainateya Rangaraju explore pruning neural networks after rotating their representation space. Structured pruning deletes whole neurons or channels, and its success depends on how importance is spread across dimensions. A change of basis can concentrate importance into fewer dimensions, but many standard networks are not invariant to such rotations, so the trick cannot simply be merged into the weights.

They introduce two-subspace radial activations, a family unchanged by rotations applied separately inside two subspaces, making change-of-basis pruning compatible with the network. As a proof of concept, the design costs a modest accuracy drop against a standard control. The authors note open work on activation choices and initialization for this invariant family.
arxiv-2511-16261:
Sarunas Kaubrys studies cohomological Donaldson-Thomas theory for loop stacks of zero-shifted symplectic stacks, a modern algebraic geometry setting for counting objects in moduli problems. The paper compares two views of the same moduli: tangent stacks, treated as additive, and loop stacks, treated as multiplicative.

An exponential map links the two views while preserving the induced shifted symplectic structures. With that bridge, Kaubrys proves a loop dimensional reduction theorem for moduli of objects in certain two-Calabi-Yau categories. A loop version of nonabelian Hodge theory for stacks is also proved in the general linear case. The work extends Donaldson-Thomas machinery to a setting where loop spaces carry the counting information.
arxiv-2511-16761:
L. V. Da Conceição, W. LF. Marcolino, and V. Maria examine how the choice of stellar atmosphere model changes predictions for planetary nebulae lit by Wolf-Rayet-type central stars. These hydrogen-deficient stars drive intense winds, so the blackbody and plane-parallel approximations used for ordinary central stars can badly misstate their ionizing radiation.

Comparing proper expanding-atmosphere models with the two simple approximations, the authors find the extreme ultraviolet spectrum differs strongly below a hundred thousand degrees, where wind opacity cuts the helium-ionizing photon output sharply. For hotter stars the wind matters far less. Feeding each source into the CLOUDY photoionization code, wind models match observed line ratios much better for nebulae with late-type Wolf-Rayet nuclei. The simple approximations, the paper concludes, should be avoided for such stars.
arxiv-2511-17161:
Piotr Pęzik and 52 co-authors describe the instruction dataset behind PLLuM, a family of large language models adapted for the Polish language. Instruction data, examples that teach a base model to follow requests, largely determines how useful the finished model feels. The paper sorts the project's instructions into a functional typology covering organic, converted, and synthetic examples, and explains where each kind came from.

The authors share observations on the trade-offs between human-written instructions and synthetic ones when adapting a model to a new language. They also release PLLuMIC, a first representative subset of the corpus, so other teams can plan similar datasets. For builders of language models in less-resourced languages, the paper is a practical account of what such a corpus takes.
arxiv-2511-17261:
The CMS Electromagnetic Calorimeter Group reports beam tests of upgraded readout electronics for one of the Large Hadron Collider's main detectors. The calorimeter measures electron and photon energies using lead tungstate crystals. Its front-end electronics are being rebuilt for the High-Luminosity phase of the collider, which will flood the detector with far more collisions. Prototypes of the new electronics were fitted to a small matrix of crystals and exposed to electron and pion beams at CERN.

Two test campaigns, in 2018 and 2021, used beam energies from 25 to 250 GeV. The constant term of the energy resolution came out better than six tenths of a percent, and timing resolution for energetic electrons was better than 30 picoseconds. Both figures meet the design requirements, clearing the upgrade for its demanding future environment.
arxiv-2511-17361:
Seamie Hayes and six co-authors present SuperQuadricOcc, a self-supervised system that estimates semantic occupancy around a vehicle, which space is filled and by what kind of object, without manual labels. Self-supervision scales to large driving datasets, but it needs a way to render a three-dimensional scene representation into images for training. The team's representation uses superquadrics, a flexible family of rounded shapes, which earlier lacked a fast renderer.

Their volume renderer indexes superquadrics spatially, so each ray only queries nearby shapes, cutting memory and computing costs sharply. With far fewer primitives than Gaussian-based rivals, the system reached state-of-the-art scores on the standard Occ3D-nuScenes benchmark, ran in real time, and used much less memory. It also beat Gaussian baselines at forecasting occupancy and estimating trajectories, suggesting the shape family is a strong fit for driving scenes.
arxiv-2511-17461:
Jiaxi Liu and seven co-authors redesign how connected vehicles share what they see. Cooperative perception lets cars pool sensor information to see around occlusions. Generic schemes transmit floods of data irrelevant to safety and rely on prearranged partners, both poor fits for dynamic traffic and limited bandwidth. Their framework, SRA-CP, works spontaneously: vehicles continuously broadcast lightweight summaries of their perception coverage, and cooperation starts only when a risk-relevant blind zone appears.

A risk identification module lets each vehicle judge locally whether an occlusion threatens its own driving task. When help is triggered, the vehicle picks peers from their coverage summaries and exchanges only safety-critical content, adapting to the available bandwidth. Against generic cooperative perception, the system lost under one percent of accuracy on safety-critical objects while using a fifth of the bandwidth, and it beat earlier selective methods by a clear margin.
arxiv-2511-17661:
Zhe Li, Haijun Cao, Lijuan Li, Huixia Fu, Mengxue Guan, and Sheng Meng study how flashing light can reshape the quantum states of two atom-thin materials. The base material holds valleys, distinct electron pockets, in a balanced state that supports a quantum spin Hall phase. Its Janus cousin, with unlike faces, already leans toward one valley. Periodic driving by light is used to push each material across phase boundaries.

In the base material a single switch moves both valleys and both spin channels at once into an anomalous Hall phase. The Janus version switches in two stages within one valley, passing through a valley-polarised phase before reaching a stronger final phase. The switches also respond unevenly to the light's direction, a trait that could suit future valley-based devices.
arxiv-2511-17761:
Manuel Kern, Dominik Steffan, Felix Schuster, and five co-authors test intrusion detection systems by staging a capture the flag contest built for stealth. Professional penetration testers attacked a realistic mix of office and industrial systems in stages, and scoring punished teams whose attacks were detected.

Out of many attack techniques tried, several were missed by every detection setup. Open source tools raised many false alarms, while commercial tools raised fewer but missed more attacks.
