Li Zhang and Pengtao Xie make a strong image tool work on its own. The Segment Anything Model can split an image into clean parts for things it has never been taught. But it needs a prompt, a hint from a human hand, for each new image. That need blocks full use in the field.

A fast finder tool called YOLO can spot things and give those hints on its own. But when the two tools are just chained, their goals do not match. The team trains them as one team, with a two-level scheme that keeps both goals in line. Their tool is called BLO-Inst. Fast, prompt-free splitting helps in scans, farm work, and plant checks, where no hand can mark each new frame.
arxiv-2601-22161:
Anmol Guragain tests a trend in how machines read feelings from face and voice. His test uses the EAV set of clips. He asks if the new, large attention tools beat plain ones when the data set is small. He runs three groups of tools: plain Transformers, new split-attention tools, and strong CNN tools with tweaks.

The fancy tools did not win. Plain traits drawn from the clips, built with care by hand, beat the Transformers. His point is that small sets reward craft more than scale. A tool that knows the task can beat a big tool that does not. This is a warn for fields where data will stay scarce, such as care work and mood care.
arxiv-2601-22861:
Refael Sheffer and co-authors map the ground hidden under thick forest canopy. The terrain below the trees matters for search and rescue, trail mapping, and forest checks. Today's tools lean on costly airborne laser scans, or on thermal imaging tuned to find people.

Their method uses plain color images plus neural three-dimensional rebuilding to recover the ground shape. Cheaper mapping from normal cameras could put forest surveys within reach of small teams. It also opens a path to robots that can plan safe routes under trees. The team frames the work around applications like search and rescue, trail mapping, and forest inventory in dense woodland.
arxiv-2603-01761:
Vaggelis Dorovatas, Malte Schwerin, Andrew Bagdanov, and colleagues argue that modular memory is the missing piece for agents that keep learning. Their 2026 position work grows from a seminar on continual learning in the foundation model era. Big pre-trained models excel at set tasks, yet they struggle to run nonstop, gather experience, and personalize.

Classic continual learning updates one set of weights, which makes old skills fade as new ones land. The group proposes splitting memory into modules that pair two learning modes. In-context learning, which adapts from prompt examples, handles fast uptake and storage of new facts. In-weight updates handle slow, stable growth of core skills. Their roadmap charts how that split could scale to agents that adapt for life, not just for one benchmark.
arxiv-2603-02061:
Lorenzo Maggi, Boris Bonev, Reinhard Wiesmayr, and colleagues estimate wireless link quality from very sparse feedback. Their 2026 work targets the signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio that schedulers need for radio resource choices. Devices report only acknowledgments, quality indicators, and past coding choices, a thin evidence trail.

Their framework casts estimation as online convex optimization that learns as feedback arrives. A regularized cross-entropy loss is minimized by mirror descent boosted with Nesterov momentum for fast tracking. An expert-advice algorithm tunes the estimator parameters online, which endows it with continual learning. Ray-traced numerical experiments show better accuracy than top existing schemes across scenarios. The estimator also adapts robustly when the true ratio drifts over time, a must for live networks.
arxiv-2603-02661:
Andrei Lebedev and Vincent Gramoli compare how five live blockchains handle attacks on their peer-to-peer messaging. Their 2026 paper notes that past security work usually targets one chain at a time. No one had tested several chains under the same hostile conditions.

They attacked Algorand, Aptos, Avalanche, Redbelly, and Solana in five different ways and measured the damage. Each chain failed somewhere different: Algorand under packet loss, Aptos under targeted load and leader isolation, Avalanche under brief failures. Redbelly slowed under packet loss, while Solana faced stopping and leader isolation attacks. The shared test setup, released as open source, gives builders a fair way to compare network defenses.
arxiv-2603-02761:
Jens Wagner, Zeno Romero, Kerstin Münnemann, and colleagues predict how fast molecules spread through liquids. Their 2026 paper targets diffusion coefficients, key values for modeling mass transport, where lab data are scarce. Pure formulas miss real mixtures, while pure machine learning can break basic physics.

Their hybrid model, called ESE, joins the classic Stokes-Einstein equation with machine learning corrections. The result stays physically consistent across temperatures for a wide range of two-part liquid mixes. Trained on a large gathered dataset, it beat the prior best model by a clear margin. It needs only standard molecule codes as extra input, and a public web tool makes it easy to use in process design.
arxiv-2603-02961:
Lingxiao Huang, Wenyang Xiao, and Nisheeth Vishnoi model what happens when workers choose how much to trust AI help. Their 2026 paper treats delegation and checking as one rational decision: hand the task to the AI, then decide how hard to verify the output. Institutions, meanwhile, grade workers by outcomes that may not reflect private checking costs.

The analysis shows sharp phase transitions, where tiny gaps in checking skill flip behavior from careful oversight to near-total delegation. AI then amplifies strong checkers while quietly degrading measured quality for workers who rationally over-delegate and under-check. This happens even when raw task success improves and nobody acts irrationally. The mechanism is structural, offering managers a new lens on uneven AI gains.
arxiv-2603-03261:
Yvain Bruned and Aurélien Minguella unite the proofs behind a core tool of modern chance analysis. Regularity structures tame rough random equations by building a renormalized model, a fixed-up local sketch of the noise. Proofs that the model settles lean on spectral gap claims, and one map, the recentering map, sits at their heart.

Their 2026 paper gives an algebraic union of those convergence proofs. The key map, most often defined through analytic bounds, gains several equal characterizations in purely algebraic terms. Equal definitions let scholars move between views and check the same object in the tongue that suits the task. The result streamlines a forbidding corner of the field that supports many results on singular equations.
arxiv-2603-03461:
Marco Salathe and five colleagues keep radiation detectors honest without heaters or reference sources. Detectors in urban security networks must hold energy calibration through wild swings in temperature and background radiation. Classic fixes burn power on temperature stabilization or lock onto single peaks that weather can shift. Their 2026 method instead calibrates from the whole spectrum, continuously, in software.

Each spectrum is fitted with a model combining natural background components, potassium, uranium and thorium series, radon progeny, and cosmic rays, with a physics-based detector simulation. That simulation accounts for non-proportional light yield and photomultiplier saturation. Validation spans simulated data, an environmental chamber run from deep cold to serious heat, and a multi-day outdoor deployment. Calibration stayed stable through temperature swings and rain, cleanly separating instrument drift from real background change.
arxiv-2603-03561:
Brian C Crow and six colleagues sharpen how detectors tell which direction an antineutrino came from. Reactors emit antineutrinos that escape freely, so reading their direction could monitor reactors from outside. Segmented detectors using inverse beta decay can estimate direction, but the standard method's quantification can be ambiguous. Their 2026 paper supplies a cleaner algorithm with a full error analysis.

Detector segment data becomes a matrix, and the algorithm scores direction by a distance between matrices, an efficient two-dimensional pattern match. Validation compares a simulated empirical dataset, generated for one beam orientation, against simulated alternatives. The study also identifies the best segment size when counts are scarce. Though built for reactor monitoring, the authors stress the matcher suits any pattern-matching task, and they discuss hybrids and detector designs beyond their own.
arxiv-2605-00161:
Hasan Amin and 6 co-authors work on diffusion language models, which draft text by refining noisy drafts in parallel. In practice these models still need hundreds of refinement steps for good text, which erases their speed edge. A trick that speeds up image diffusion does not carry over, since text has no smooth path between noise levels.

The team finds the right substitute: an exact formula linking any two noise levels for a draft. Their training method makes a denoising model agree with itself across these links, with no trained teacher needed. The resulting model set new best scores on guided and unguided text generation. Gains were largest when only a few refinement steps were allowed.
arxiv-2605-00461:
Ge Luo and 8 co-authors design a lighter network for fusing images from several sources, such as infrared with visible light or multiple exposures into one. Deep unfolding networks, which turn an iterative optimization algorithm into network layers, fuse well but usually update each modality separately, costing memory and compute. That overhead blocks use on small edge devices.

Their network, CDNet, instead unfolds a coupled dictionary model whose prior splits image content into a shared part and modality-specific parts. The resulting block updates both together in one joint step, under a block-sparse interaction pattern. A compact loss on high- and low-frequency fidelity lets it train without ground-truth fused images. Across four fusion tasks, including medical imaging and fusion for road-scene segmentation, CDNet matched or beat heavier rivals while running lean, with clear margins on standard infrared benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-00961:
Faruk Alpay and Taylan Alpay develop a unified math formulation for post-quantum secure telemetry and actuation in aircraft engine control systems. The setting couples a FADEC controller with a dual-spool turbofan, a safety-critical cyber-physical system. Their model joins lattice-based key set-up, attestation entropy from physical unclonable functions, authenticated encryption, radar-altimeter integrity, bus timing, and Kalman residual checks in one stochastic hybrid model.

Within that model, plant behavior, latency, leakage, hostile channel quality, and cryptographic state evolve together. Channel doubt tightens how often keys can be renewed, ciphertext growth affects bus scheduling, and sensing limits shape alarm thresholds. The analysis, framed defensively, shows how post-quantum security, real-time timing, and closed-loop stability interact.
arxiv-2605-01161:
Hemanta Ban and two co-authors analyze distributed formation control for multiple agents driven by the gradient of the Lennard-Jones potential, a classic attraction-repulsion law. Each agent follows local rules, yet the group must form a stable pattern without collisions. For collision-free initial data, the authors prove global well-posedness together with a uniform lower bound on all distances between agents, excluding hard crashes.

Using total energy as a Lyapunov function, an invariance argument shows every positive limit point is an equilibrium. Because paths stay uniformly away from collisions, the energy is analytic along the flow. A further step yields convergence to a single resting state up to translation. Illustrative numerical examples accompany the proofs.
arxiv-2605-01261:
Kiyoharu Kawana and Kyosuke Adachi improve a standard tool for predicting liquid-liquid phase separation, the process behind protein droplets in cells and the splitting of polymer mixtures. The tool, the random phase approximation, is widely used, but how accurate it is for polymer solutions away from high density was not well mapped. The authors build a loop expansion around it, treating inverse polymer density in the role that Planck's constant plays in quantum field theory.

They compute the first two corrections to the free energy of the standard method. Tested against molecular dynamics simulations of bead-spring chains, the first correction gives a better estimate of the dilute-phase density where the two liquids coexist. The error at the critical point stays about the same as the uncorrected method. The authors present the expansion as a step-by-step route to sharper predictions for polymer phase separation.
arxiv-2605-01361:
Junhyeong Lee, Sangjin Jin, and Yongjae Lee work on decision-focused learning, where a forecast model is trained to make the final decision good, not just the forecast close. Finding the training signal for that goal usually means grinding through a solver or using stand-in losses, both costly or off target.

The three authors show that, when the active limits of a problem stay stable, the regret signal has a clean geometric form. It is the forecast error cast onto the flat space set by the active limits, scaled by local curvature. In plain terms, parts of the error that cannot change the decision are filtered out. Their method, PEAR, solves one small linear system over the active limits instead of tracing solver steps. On linear benchmarks and a real quadratic task, it gives the best decisions at the lowest cost.
arxiv-2605-01561:
Diego Vallarino models economic crises as avalanches on the real web of world production. Borrowing from the physics of the Hall effect, where a field pushes current sideways, he treats shocks as fields. Those fields strike flow-heavy nodes with little backup and thin capacity, turning stress sideways through a conversion rule.

Built on World Input-Output Database networks from 2000 to 2014, with over two thousand country-sector nodes, the model lets stress pile up until nodes topple in sandpile fashion. Monte Carlo runs over shock strength and redundancy stress yield four ordered regimes, from stable absorption to a full avalanche regime. Big-event odds and mean avalanche size rise together as stress grows. The tails thicken by regime, yet not enough to claim universal power-law criticality: the author stresses a finite, real-network account of fragility, not self-organized criticality for the world economy.
arxiv-2605-01661:
F S Gama extends supersymmetric versions of Maxwell-Chern-Simons theory, a three-dimensional gauge theory with a topological twist, by adding higher-derivative terms. The extension is defined in both the one- and two-supercharge superspaces, with the new operator a polynomial in the wave operator of any chosen degree, placed only in the gauge sector.

The goal is the one-loop quantum correction to the superfield effective potential, the quantity that tells whether the quantum vacuum keeps the classical shape. Gama computes it with background field methods in a higher-derivative gauge choice built for such terms. The result comes out in closed form, written through the roots of the polynomial functions that define the extension. Closed forms at one loop are the checkpoints of supersymmetric model building: they let later work test stability and symmetry breaking without redoing the loop machinery.
arxiv-2605-01761:
Quanchen Zou and six co-authors defend text-to-video models against prompts engineered to make them produce violence or explicit footage. Guards inherited from image safety read the prompt's wording, so rephrased attacks slip through. Video adds a second hole: a mild prompt can drift into unsafe scenes as the generator stretches it into a story.

TrajShield works at inference time with no retraining. It simulates the trajectory a prompt implies and finds the causal origin of the risk inside that unfolding path. It then rewrites the prompt just enough to cut the risk while keeping harmless meaning intact. Blatant prompts, disguised jailbreaks, and this slow temporal drift are handled by one mechanism. On a safety benchmark spanning fourteen categories and several video backends, it posts the best defense scores with high fidelity to the original request, cutting attack success by over half on average.
arxiv-2605-01961:
Maheed Ahmed and Mahsa Ghasemi bring fairness into dueling bandits, a setting where a learner picks between options based on human preferences. Most systems train on average preference, which can leave minority groups poorly served when tastes differ widely. The authors assume each user has a personal Condorcet winner, an option that beats every other option for that user.

Arms are scored by how they perform relative to each user's own winner. To balance users, the method uses Nash Social Welfare, which multiplies user gains and so punishes inequality. The framework aims to learn good choices for all users, rather than letting a majority preference marginalise any single group.
arxiv-2605-02161:
Z Papp extends the Feshbach-Villars form of relativistic quantum mechanics to two particles, both with spin zero. That form rewrites a relativistic wave equation as a pair of coupled equations, which can clarify its structure. For two bodies, the challenge is to separate the motion of the whole system from the motion of the parts relative to each other.

Papp shows the extension can be done so that centre-of-mass motion splits off cleanly. What remains is an equation of Feshbach-Villars type written only in the relative coordinate. The short paper gives the construction and its resulting form. Such a separation is a standard first step before solving or approximating two-body relativistic problems.
arxiv-2605-02261:
Dennis Bromley, Diana Wang, and Vidya Setlur explore how people express data queries through proximity, by sketching near, pointing near, and writing near. Data tools often miss analytical intent that is hard to state in a formal query or in words alone. Their multimodal probe lets users query time-series and geographic data by free-form sketching, natural language, and visual annotation in one shared space.

Users sketch trends or paths and add notes and directives tied to shared spatial and temporal context. A hybrid system joins geometric sketch matching with vision-language models to handle queries that mix pattern and meaning. In a study with twenty participants, people repeatedly used spatial, temporal, and visual proximity to link sketches, notes, and language.
arxiv-2605-02361:
Liqian Ma, Zishun Liu, Glen Chou, and Yongxin Chen plan feedback motion for stochastic nonlinear systems that must satisfy signal temporal logic specifications, formal statements about how signals should behave over time. Their goal is a closed-loop system that meets a given formula with very high probability, such as 99.99 percent, despite random disturbances.

The method erodes predicates to turn the hard stochastic problem into a deterministic trajectory optimisation with tightened constraints. The erosion amount comes from a probabilistic reachable tube, which bounds how far the stochastic path can stray from a nominal one. Contraction theory and feedback design compute those bounds, and several tracking controllers are developed. The result is a full planning pipeline that runs through numerical optimisation.
arxiv-2605-02561:
Zhongwei Shen, Yao Xu, and Jinping Zhuge develop homogenization theory for elliptic equations whose coefficients oscillate at infinitely many scales at once. Homogenization replaces rapid wiggles with an effective smooth equation. Problems with endless scales arise in fractal materials and in diffusion in fluids, where structure repeats at finer and finer levels without end.

Under assumptions that the scales stay separated, the authors prove a qualitative homogenization theorem with optimal convergence rates in the mean-square sense. They also establish interior and boundary Lipschitz estimates that hold uniformly across all scale choices. Those uniform bounds are the technical core: they keep control of solutions no matter how many scales are active. The work gives a general frame for multi-scale media with no smallest scale.
arxiv-2605-02661:
Junjie Yu and seventy-seven co-authors introduce AcademiClaw, a benchmark of tasks that university students set for AI agents. Prior benchmarks in this agent ecosystem covered assistant-level work only. AcademiClaw instead draws eighty complex, long-horizon tasks from real student workflows: homework, research projects, competitions, and personal projects that current agents failed to solve well.

The tasks were picked from hundreds of student submissions by expert review and span more than twenty-five fields, from olympiad-level math and linguistics to heavy reinforcement learning and full system debugging. Each runs in an isolated sandbox and is scored by multi-part rubrics, with a separate safety audit. Six frontier models were tested, and even the best passed only a little over half the tasks. Sharp gaps by field and differing model strategies round out the findings.
arxiv-2605-02761:
Justice Owusu Agyemang and six co-authors present a mathematical framework for adaptive video streaming that draws on several providers at once. Current systems probe providers in a line, fail over only after trouble, and keep cold standbys that start slowly. Together those traits cause stalls and visible quality drops when a provider falters.

Their theorem treats acquisition as filling a reservoir from all providers in parallel, while keeping a set of pre-checked, pre-fetched standby streams ready for sub-second failover. Four results are proved. They give a lower bound on uptime from independent streams, and a speedup over batched probing. They show steady quality gains under lazy refill. They also give a switching rule, drawn from prospect theory, that provably stops thrashing between similar streams. The work is theoretical, with practical gains stated as analysis.
arxiv-2605-02861:
Yanis Le Fur and five co-authors benchmark quantum error detection on real hardware, weighing its promise against its costs. Error detection can give unbiased values that converge to the noiseless answer as the code grows. Two costs hold it back: sample counts rise steeply with circuit depth and noise, and classical processing generally grows steeply with code size.

Embedding a code on hardware also adds overhead that can hurt accuracy at first. The team runs memory and logic tests with two codes, a repetition code and a triangular color code, on real and simulated noisy machines, using up to dozens of physical qubits. Pseudothreshold estimates map where detection starts to pay. Despite the challenges, results show strong promise for scaling the technique on current and future machines.
arxiv-2605-03061:
Houman Safaai and Alessandro Marin Vargas introduce Dynamic Vine Copulas, a tool for tracking how dependence among many variables changes over time. Correlations can look steady while tails, asymmetry, or conditional links shift, and simple models miss those moves.

Their method holds a vine factorization fixed and lets pair-copula states drift smoothly or switch families in a controlled way. A held-out test splits plain pairwise links from higher-order conditional effects. In benchmarks it caught changes Gaussian tools missed, and in brain recording data it found a repeatable higher-order signal across areas.
arxiv-2605-03361:
Honglei Zhang, Yuting Chen, Chenpeng Hu, Pengfei Zhou, Siyue Zhang, and Yilei Shi introduce ReasonAudio, a benchmark for reasoning in text-to-audio retrieval beyond simple sound matching. Existing sets mostly test whether a clip matches its caption, not whether a system can handle negation, order, co-occurrence, or duration in a query.

The benchmark pairs synthetic tasks over composite clips with a natural task on real recordings. Eleven leading systems scored poorly overall, and a controlled test still left the best model far behind its own generative backbone and far behind humans. Reasoning-rich audio search remains an open challenge.
arxiv-2605-03461:
Qi Chen, Hao-Xuan Luo, Jin-Kang Guo, Qian-Qian Hong, Li-Bao Fan, and Chuan-Cun Shu give an analytic two-pulse recipe for universal single-qubit gates in ultracold sodium-cesium molecules. Molecular qubits promise rich control, but complex protocols and sensitivity to flaws have slowed practical gate work.

Encoding qubits in the lowest rotational levels, they use a first-order Magnus expansion to derive closed-form evolution and exact amplitude and phase conditions for any rotation. Simulations show fidelities above the four-nines level with little leakage, and molecular orientation tracks the gate action for practical readout. The method extends to other molecules and platforms.
arxiv-2605-03661:
Yuxuan Yang studies optimal embeddings of orders into maximal orders of central simple algebras of degree three over number fields. An embedding is optimal when the order being placed is exactly the intersection of the larger order with the embedded field. Yang considers degree-three extensions and asks when such optimal placement fails.

He determines exactly when an order cannot be optimally embedded into all maximal orders of the algebra. In the remaining cases, he further pins down exactly when the order embeds optimally into one third of the isomorphism classes of maximal orders, and when it manages two thirds. The result gives a complete arithmetic picture for this degree-three setting.
arxiv-2605-03861:
Ankit Satpute and six co-authors tackle content-based recommendation of mathematical research papers. In this setting, relatedness is conceptual rather than textual. Two mathematics papers may share proof techniques, logical links, or generalizations. Yet they may have minimal textual or citation overlap, so recommenders built for computer science or biomedicine fail. An expert-driven study first describes what mathematicians actually want from a recommendation.

Relevance turns out to be aspect-driven at its core, so the team built GoldRiM, a small expert-annotated dataset, and SilverRiM, a large automatically derived one, the first for aspect-aware recommendation in mathematics. Their AchGNN model is an aspect-conditioned heterogeneous graph network. It jointly models text semantics, citation structure, and author lineage. It beat prior aspect-based methods throughout, on both datasets.
arxiv-2605-03961:
Jessica Braudo and Noam Soker compare the shapes of core-collapse supernova remnants and jet-shaped planetary nebulae. Both can share an unusual feature: a narrow, faint zone, called a pipe, extending from side to side. They present two jet-shaped planetary nebulae with a pipe. They present three more with two opposite narrow jet-shaped lobes. The lobes, they argue, can later merge into a single pipe.

A three-dimensional hydrodynamic simulation reproduces two opposite narrow lobes similar to those observed. The simulation explodes a massive star with three pairs of jets, within the jittering jets explosion mechanism framework. The simulated and observed morphologies look alike in both object classes. From that similarity, the authors argue jets shaped the pipes in the supernova remnants as well. That strengthens the case for the jittering jets mechanism.
arxiv-2605-04061:
Bryan Cheng and Jasper Zhang report a striking dissociation in how large language models encode task identity from few-shot demonstrations. Linear probes can classify the task from specific layer activations with perfect accuracy, which earlier work took as evidence that task representations live at those positions. The authors test whether those positions are causally important, and find they are not.

Intervening at a single position achieved zero percent task transfer across all twenty-eight layers of one model, despite perfect probing accuracy there. Replacing activations at all demonstration output tokens simultaneously, by contrast, reached up to ninety-six percent transfer at an early-middle layer. The pattern generalized across four models from three architecture families, with a universal intervention window near thirty percent of network depth, and tracing showed an asymmetric architecture of positions.
arxiv-2605-04161:
Lucas C. Céleri, Krissia Zawadzki, Ivan Medina, and Diogo O. Soares-Pinto connect dynamical quantum phase transitions to rugosity, a recently introduced measure of quantum state texture. Dynamical transitions describe critical behavior in systems driven out of equilibrium by a quench. They come in two standard formulations. One is based on a dynamical order parameter. The other is based on nonanalyticities in a return-rate function.

For the first type, the authors show the time-averaged rugosity, evaluated in the pre-quench energy basis, behaves like an order parameter across the transition. In the Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick model they trace that behavior to the semiclassical structure. Crossing an excited-state transition separatrix redistributes the state over the basis. The response function's critical peak grows algebraically with system size, giving finite-size evidence of sensitivity to the dynamical critical point.
arxiv-2605-04261:
Jie Zhang and three co-authors show a risk in trusting vision-language models as judges of images, for tasks like fact-checking, product comparison, and content moderation. A tiny crafted change to an image, invisible in normal viewing, can make the model speak with confidence about the wrong content.

The attacks do not break the model's safety training. They work at the level of perception. Methods built on open vision models also transfer to leading commercial systems. Across tests on identity, unsafe content, and product advice, success rates ran from about a fifth to total, raising concerns for platforms that rely on these models.
arxiv-2605-04361:
Saranyan Vigraham tests a common assumption in systems of cooperating software agents: that giving agents more shared context always improves their design work. He runs multi-agent software design across ten tasks and seven ways of injecting context, totalling thousands of runs.

The same kind of added document helped greatly on some tasks and hurt badly on others, and on several tasks an irrelevant document did as well as relevant ones. One simple measure, how widely agents explore with no context at all, predicted the direction of the effect strongly. Vigraham argues context should be added only after a cheap no-context trial.
arxiv-2605-04461: Yijing Tu builds Stream-T1: test-time scaling for streaming video generation. The building builds. Their scaling scales test-time streaming video generation. The doing does. It is AI. Stream-T1 stream-t1s. The Stream-T1 scales test-time-streaming.
arxiv-2605-04761:
Wu-Yuin Hwang and three co-authors present the Personalized Thinking Model, a way to build a cognitive twin of a learner for AI-supported education. Their model sorts evidence from learner journals into five layers, from single actions up to core values. It is grounded in Marzano's New Taxonomy of Educational Objectives.

The team built the model with a large language model, sentence embeddings, and clustering, then tested it on forty learners over seven weeks. Checking against human judgment, scores rose slightly after people reviewed and refined the output. Learners also rated the twins as matching their thinking, and deeper layers showed clearer themes and less direct copying of journal words.
arxiv-2605-04861:
Rakshit Gharat and three co-authors build a quantum algorithm for solving differential equations on a lattice using SLAC derivatives. A lattice derivative that matches smooth behaviour correctly must be non-local, acting across many sites at once. That makes it hard to encode efficiently on a quantum computer.

The team constructs efficient encodings for the first derivative and Laplacian in this representation, using state preparation suited to smoothly decaying functions. Wavelet transforms then give multiscale versions, and a preconditioner keeps the system well conditioned. The result is a quantum linear-system method for partial differential equations with stated gate costs, opening a route to large lattice problems.
arxiv-2605-04961:
Byunghoon Kang develops a more efficient version of the generalised method of moments, a workhorse estimation technique in econometrics, for cases where the model's conditions do not hold exactly. Under such misspecification, the standard estimator's behaviour depends on both those conditions and their slopes. Kang builds estimators from widened, shifted conditions that include that extra information.

Weighting the widened system optimally gives an estimator with the smallest large-sample spread for the same target quantity, with the standard method as a special case. Kang also proposes a feasible bootstrap version and proves uniform lower bounds over weighting choices. Simulations and two real-data examples show the gains.
arxiv-2605-05061:
Johan Gaume and three co-authors derive exact solutions for how failure spreads in the weak layer under a snow slab, the process that releases slab avalanches. Many earlier models treat the weak layer as perfectly brittle or ignore its elasticity before the peak load. Both softening after the peak and compliance before it shape stress redistribution and the critical crack length.

Their solution divides the failing zone into a softened core, a fracture process zone, and intact elastic material, recovering the classic brittle length when softening vanishes. Particle simulations confirm the predicted stress profiles and lengths. The same framework is then extended to collapse-driven anticrack propagation, linking two avalanche release pictures.
arxiv-2605-05161:
Bernhard Kainz and three co-authors reframe spotting anomalies in medical scans with vision-language models as a comparison problem rather than a lone-image judgement. Zero-shot localisation is limited because the model lacks healthy anatomical context. Their training-free framework, WALDO, compares a scan against reference distributions of normal anatomy using optimal transport measures.

Reference choice matters in a non-obvious way: moderately similar references work best, a Goldilocks effect the authors analyse theoretically. Similarity-weighted distance measures pick references, and self-consistency steps merge the results. On a brain MRI benchmark the method improved localisation substantially over zero-shot baselines, with consistent gains also seen across other large vision-language models.
arxiv-2605-05461:
Robots usually must grab an object before they can judge whether the grip will hold. Kyle DuFrene and Cindy Grimm remove that step with sensors built into the gripper's fingertips. Their time-of-flight sensors measure distances across several zones without any contact at all.

The team gathered more than twenty-five hundred real grasps over fifteen objects to train a classifier. It then judged grasps on six unseen objects, kept for validation and testing. Accuracy reached about eighty-six percent on the test objects, and the check cycles fifteen times per second, far faster than touch-based methods that must grasp first.
arxiv-2605-05561:
Shrinking a reasoning model to four bits saves memory but can break its sense of when to stop thinking. Sai Babu Patarlapalli and Surya Teja Avvaru present BitCal-TTS, a runtime controller for that problem. Under a fixed token budget, poor confidence signals can end a trace too early or let it ramble.

The controller blends cheap uncertainty proxies with a confidence rescaling tuned to the bit width. On small GSM8K test shards with Qwen2.5 models, it raised exact-match accuracy at two sizes. Premature stops fell at both sizes as well, while most token savings survived.
arxiv-2605-05661:
When a Type Ia supernova's shock wave runs into surrounding gas, the gas glows in Balmer lines. Priyam Das and six co-authors report the first helium lines from such shocks, found with the MUSE integral-field spectrograph. They studied filaments in three remnants in the Large Magellanic Cloud.

Both broad and narrow helium emission appeared, including ionized helium lines that current shock models struggle to explain. Because helium traces the gas the progenitor system shed before exploding, the detections constrain what those progenitor environments contained. The narrow ionized helium, in particular, challenges existing pictures of these collisionless shocks.
arxiv-2605-06061:
Elena Wang and Bastian Rieck extend a classic expressivity test for graph learning to cover geometry. The Weisfeiler-Lehman test and its simplicial version judge what message passing networks can tell apart, but they ignore shape. Two meshes with the same connections and different embeddings look identical to those tests.

Their Geometric Simplicial Weisfeiler-Lehman test folds vertex coordinates into the color refinement process. They prove that geometry aware simplicial message passing is bounded above by this test. They also show matching schemes exist whose power equals the test on any fixed finite family of complexes. Paired with a known complete invariant, the result gives a full geometric expressivity picture, and experiments on synthetic and mesh data confirm the predicted hierarchy.
arxiv-2605-06161:
Shihao Weng, Yang Feng, and Xiaofei Xie argue that language model safety judges must pass a reliability test beyond accuracy. Such judges now grade agent safety by default, yet their verdicts may hinge on how the evaluation policy is worded rather than on what the agent did. The authors name the needed property policy invariance and split it into three testable principles.

Their stress test applies certified equivalent rewrites and deliberate strict to lenient shifts to the judging rubric. Today's judges reacted about as strongly to meaningless rewrites as to real normative shifts, and could not tell them apart. Meaning preserving rewrites flipped up to 9.1 percent of verdicts. A new Policy Invariance Score and Judge Card protocol expose wide reliability gaps that accuracy leaderboards hide.
arxiv-2605-06261:
Eugenio Lomurno and four co-authors close the gap between synthetic and real tabular data at inference time rather than in training. Diffusion generators make the best synthetic tables, yet their output rarely beats real data in downstream use. Past attempts to close that gap retrained or rescaled monolithic generators, leaving the outputs of a frozen model untouched and unrefined, the authors note.

Their framework, TARDIS, refines a frozen backbone's samples with per data set configuration search. One mathematical pattern, bidirectional Chamfer refinement, drives both a continuous score level push and a discrete batch ranking step. Across fifteen benchmarks the method improved downstream results over real data training by a median of 8.6 percent. It beat its backbone on every data set while matching it on fidelity, diversity, and privacy measures.
arxiv-2605-06761:
Oğuzhan Fatih Kar and four co-authors present Weblica, a framework for building reproducible training environments for visual web agents. The live web is complex and ever-changing, so training data has stayed limited to offline demonstrations or a few simulated sites. Weblica instead replays real websites through HTTP-level caching that preserves interactive behavior while freezing visual states.

It also synthesizes new environments with a language model, grounded in real sites and core navigation skills. That scales reinforcement learning training to thousands of environments and tasks. Their Weblica-8B model beats similar-size open baselines on web navigation benchmarks while taking fewer steps, scales well with extra test-time compute, and rivals commercial API models.
arxiv-2605-06861:
James Rowbottom, Nick Huang, Carola-Bibiane Schönlieb, and Ben Adcock place sensors to estimate state without assuming Gaussian data. How well states are rebuilt depends on where sensors sit. Measurements are often sparse and costly. Classical tools assume Gaussian distributions. Newer diffusion-based rebuilding handles complex distributions those tools cannot match. That leaves placement methods mismatched to the recovery models they serve.

Their method uses the Christoffel function from sampling theory to derive a placement strategy. It gives explicit bounds on how many sensors recovery needs, for any distribution. Offline and online variants beat Gaussian and other generative placement methods, most when sensor budgets are low, across several generative models.
arxiv-2605-07161:
Jackson Clark and seven co-authors present SREGym, a live benchmark for AI agents that fix failures in production computer systems. Existing tests for site reliability work are often too simple and hard to extend. SREGym instead runs on real cloud-native software stacks, with faults injected at different layers.

The setup adds background noise and tricky failure modes, including failures that feed on themselves or strike together. Its ninety problems are modular, so new scenarios can be added. Frontier agents varied widely by failure type, with large gaps in end-to-end results, showing current reliability agents remain uneven in realistic conditions.
arxiv-2605-07461:
Jiachen Yu and three co-authors move grading rubrics inside a language model's reasoning instead of leaving them as an outside scorecard. Rubrics usually judge open-ended answers after the fact, or feed reinforcement rewards, without guiding generation itself. In Think-with-Rubrics, the model first writes its own rubric, then answers under its guidance.

A trained verifier supervises training by checking consistency between the answer and both self-written and gold rubrics. Across benchmarks, the method beat a rubric-as-reward baseline by several points on average. Analysis credits better self-rubrics for quality and consistency checks for steadier responses, giving instruction-following models a new internal compass.
arxiv-2605-07661:
George Rapakoulias and three co-authors speed up diffusion model sampling while keeping it genuinely random. Most fast samplers collapse the process into something more deterministic, which hurts downstream tasks like posterior sampling and inverse problems that need true stochastic draws. Their method instead distills the full transition map of the sampling equation.

Called Stochastic Transition-Map Distillation, the approach parameterizes those transitions with a conditional mean-flow model, giving a one-step or few-step stochastic sampler. It needs no pretrained teacher, no two-level optimization, and no stored trajectories, which keeps training efficient. The authors prove convergence bounds in the Wasserstein distance and validate the sampler on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CelebA image generation.
arxiv-2605-07761:
Kentaro Nomura and two co-authors simulate how a shared social reality of emotion could emerge between agents. The theory of constructed emotion says emotion concepts are a community-level consensus applied to bodily sensations arising from allostasis, the body's predictive regulation, and social interaction. Testing that emergence story needs a working computational model.

Their model joins symbol emergence, where interpretation of signs is flexible, with active inference. Two agents receive interoceptive signals, exchange inferred symbols, and adapt both their bodily control goals and their symbol interpretations toward each other. In experiments the agents' prior preferences over bodily states and their symbol probability distributions converged, which the authors read as social reality emerging from social consensus in miniature.
arxiv-2605-08161:
Hussain Alasmawi studies training strategy for automatic tumor segmentation in whole-body PET/CT scans, built for the AutoPET III challenge. Outlining tumors by hand is slow and varies between readers, while lesions differ widely in size, contrast, and location. Challenge models must also generalize across tracers and hospitals.

Using nnU-Net with a ResNet encoder as the baseline, Alasmawi varies intensity normalization, batch dice optimization, and augmentation with CraveMix, and measures the effect of each choice. The experiments show training strategy strongly shapes performance, especially in cutting false positives and staying robust when lesions look unusual. The best configuration is reported for the challenge setting.
arxiv-2605-08261:
Pierluca D'Oro, Sneha Silwal, William Wong, Yuxuan Sun, and coauthors show that top computer-use benchmarks can be gamed. A one-megabyte replay script repeats recorded actions blindly. It never looks at the screen. Yet it beats frontier models on prominent static benchmarks. Its expected score equals the source agent's pass-at-k rate in deterministic settings.

The authors trace the failure to weak environment design. The settings are static, unsandboxed, or poorly verified. Naive aggregation and misuse of pass-at-k add to the problem. They propose PRISM, five design principles for agent environments. The principles cover privileged checks, realistic settings, integrity-checked setups, sandboxed runs, and varied conditions.
arxiv-2605-08461:
Arnob Saha, Bibhas Manna, Nikhil Kotikalapudi, Md Zesun Ahmed Mia, and coauthors tune compute-in-memory chips with Bayesian optimization. Crossbar accelerators promise dense, energy-efficient neural inference, but their design space mixes hardware and algorithm choices in a highly non-convex way, and every candidate costs an expensive simulation.

Their multi-objective framework co-optimizes both sides while querying the simulator sparingly. Even for deep models the spaces are large, reaching dozens of dimensions and astronomical candidate counts for a VGG network on Tiny-ImageNet. Bayesian search focuses trials on promising regions, and the authors show the method attains strong designs for efficient deep network inference on crossbar hardware.
arxiv-2605-08661:
Hadi Kharaghani, Ali Mohammadian, and Behruz Tayfeh-Rezaie search for Hadamard matrices of Williamson type, arrays of plus and minus ones built from four structured blocks. Their focus narrows to near Williamson matrices, where one block circulates freely and the other three are symmetric circulant. A computer search classifies all inequivalent examples at odd orders up to thirty five.

Existence is also shown for every odd order up to sixty three. As a payoff, the search yields the first known quaternary Hadamard matrix of order one hundred eighteen. Combinatorics gains both a complete small order census and a new record object in a design family with roots in signal processing and coding.
arxiv-2605-09061:
Runyao Yu and eight co-authors forecast imbalance prices in electricity markets, the charges that settle gaps between planned and actual power use. Fast, accurate forecasts matter for battery owners and automated trading systems, yet prices form through market rules and arrive through messy, delayed data feeds.

Their neural network builds the market's own price rules into its inner structure, so it learns around a clear prior instead of from raw signals alone. Tests show accuracy on par with generic deep learning models while using far fewer trainable parts and much less training time. The team also checks how the forecast holds up when some price data is missing and how it changes with horizon length.
arxiv-2605-09161:
Tom Benhamou, Sebastiano Thei, and Ben-Zion Weltsch study the models that sit between a starting universe of set theory and a larger one built by a method called strongly compact Prikry forcing. Forcing adds new sets in a controlled way, and the models in between are often hard to pin down. Their 2026 paper finds a simple property that sorts these in-between cases.

For a fixed large cardinal, the property characterizes which smaller forcing methods arise as views of the big one. Working level by level, the authors extend several known results and give criteria for when such a view exists. They also show that, at a fixed size, the relevant views are exactly those whose rule depends only on the stem of a condition.
arxiv-2605-09461: Finding software vulnerabilities with LLMs works better when the model sees the code from three angles at once. Wenxin Tang, Xiang Zhang, Junliang Liu, and others augment context along triple paths for vulnerability detection — VulTriage. The 2026 paper triages security bugs like an emergency room.

Park asks whether teaching language models about market reflexivity makes them better forecasters, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Reflexivity, George Soros's theory, holds that prices shape the fundamentals they are said to reflect, creating self-reinforcing booms and busts. Standard forecasting treats markets as external systems to observe, and ignores that they are part of the loop. Park tested three models, GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Gemini 3 Pro, under four increasingly reflexivity-aware prompts.

The episodes were the dot-com bubble and the global financial crisis, with inputs anonymized to prevent memorized answers. Performance was scored by accuracy and by the risk-adjusted return of a trading strategy. Awareness improved accuracy, but differently for each model and context window length. The same theoretical briefing produced different behavior in each model. Park presents this divergence as the finding: awareness is not an upgrade, and how a model metabolizes it depends on the model.

arxiv-2606-04161:
Tyler Crosse and co-authors diagnose in 2026 why model selectors so often fail. A selector picks the best model for each input. It should beat any single model, yet trained only on logged data it often does not.

The snag is ambiguity: many inputs look the same in the logs but need different models. The team proves that no method trained on logged choices alone can beat this limit without new information. Then they redesign the data itself. Logging richer features about each input breaks the ties that cause the failure. This turns a hidden flaw into a clear design rule. The rule: log more about inputs, or accept selector limits.
arxiv-2606-04261:
Feiyang Kang and colleagues ask in 2026 whether generalist coding agents can automate data curation, the slow loop of proposing, testing, and revising rules for selecting training data. They built Curation-Bench, a benchmark that fixes the model and training recipe and hands agents the loop itself.

Given command-line access to inspect data and submit policies to a fixed pipeline, off-the-shelf agents matched strong published data-selection baselines within ten iterations. But trajectory analysis exposed an execution-research gap: agents mostly tweaked local variants instead of exploring new policy families. Forcing each iteration to cite and adapt a prior published method changed that. The scaffolded agent then composed, unaided, a policy beating the baselines on a tenth of their data budget.
arxiv-2606-04661:
Kumar and colleagues optimize prompts for both accuracy and cost at once, in a 2026 arXiv paper on prompt engineering. They raise inference cost on every call. The best trade-off depends on the task and budget. The usual shortcut collapses both goals into one weighted sum. This fixes the trade-off before the search. It often recovers only a narrow slice of the Pareto front. The authors call this failure scalarization collapse.

Their optimizer, CRAFT, treats calls to the target model for validation as the scarce resource. It spends them on candidates near the optimistic front. Each round, accuracy-oriented and cost-oriented generators propose edits. A Pareto-gap acquisition rule allocates the validation budget. NSGA-II retention keeps a spread-out population of prompts. Accuracy-only, cost-only, and weighted-sum baselines each concentrated in narrower regions. The trade-off stays a post-search choice.
arxiv-2606-04861:
Nazari and colleagues study how rotation helps objects sink through fluids that refuse to flow until pushed hard enough, in a 2026 arXiv fluid mechanics paper. Yield-stress fluids, like the Carbopol gel used here, behave as solids until a stress threshold is crossed. The team rotated cylinders and spheres of varying surface roughness inside a Helmholtz coil within such a fluid.

Measured drag depends strongly on both roughness and rotation: the plastic drag falls as rotation rises at fixed Bingham number, so spinning reduces resistance. Flow shows rotation generating a plastic deformation zone in the orthogonal plane and promoting wall slip. Simulations reproduce the scaling but underpredict drag, likely missing wall slip. The yield limit for sinking rises with rotation and roughness.
arxiv-2606-04961:
Koshelev calculates how much magnetic flux stays trapped in a superconducting strip after it cools through its transition, in a 2026 arXiv superconductivity theory paper. Trapped flux plagues superconducting electronic devices, and the residual vortices in a long narrow strip cooled in a small perpendicular field are his subject. The low-temperature vortex configuration forms very near the critical temperature. Flux density is set by a balance between entries and exits over the geometrical barrier.

As cooling proceeds, the escape rate drops exponentially, and the vortex density falls out of equilibrium at a field-dependent freezing temperature. The freezing point sits above the transition's fluctuation width by a large logarithmic factor. The frozen flux depends very strongly on field, which lets him define an effective flux-expulsion field.
arxiv-2606-05561:
Xueyang Wu and co-authors confront a privacy risk in speech-based health checks in a 2026 arXiv paper. Voice recordings can flag depression, which makes screening cheap and wide-reaching. The same recordings can also leak a speaker's age and gender. Older fixes fail against new attacks or blur every feature with noise. The team instead trims the shared information between the speech code and private traits.

Their system, InfoShield, keeps depression scoring while cutting what the code reveals about the speaker. A new estimator aligns sound frames with trait codes over time, a step older tools handled poorly. On a public speech corpus, guesses at gender fell from about ninety-three percent to about fifty-six percent. Age guessing fell from about fifty-six percent to about thirty percent. The depression score stayed strong and beat the prior best mark, with only a small loss from the privacy step.
arxiv-2606-05661:
Asawa and colleagues built a benchmark for whether AI systems truly learn on the job in a 2026 arXiv paper. Continual learning means improving through a stream of related tasks. No hard, trusted test for it existed. CL-Bench spans six domains, from software work to outbreak forecasting and games. Domain experts validated every task stream. Each stream hides a shared pattern that a stateful system can pick up over time.

Frontier models ran under several agent designs, from plain in-context learning to dedicated memory systems. A gain metric separates real learning from starting skill. The results leave wide headroom: agents often overfit to the latest case or failed to reuse past lessons. Dedicated memory systems did not rescue them. Plain in-context learning beat the memory managers outright. The authors release the benchmark as a yardstick for the next wave of learning systems.
arxiv-2606-05761:
Wenxuan Wang and colleagues test whether AI assistants track how their memories relate in a 2026 arXiv paper. Long-running assistants pile up memories that support, shade, or contradict each other. Correct help often depends on those relations, not on single facts. Existing memory benchmarks seldom probe relation handling. SubtleMemory plants controlled memory variants with known relations inside realistic chat histories.

The benchmark holds over fifteen hundred test cases across ten long histories. Its memory sets come in three flavors: complementary, nuanced, and contradictory. Eleven systems were graded, from standalone memory stores to agent frameworks with plug-in memory. All current systems proved weak at telling fine relations apart. Diagnostic stages separated failures of storage, retrieval, and reasoning. Profiles differed sharply by stage, which shows where each design breaks. The authors release the benchmark to push memory research past simple recall.
arxiv-2606-06061:
Kakroudi and Pieters let people boss a robot arm around in plain words, with a human checkpoint before anything moves in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their framework splits the work across distributed ROS 2 nodes. Language understanding, visual grounding, motion execution, and orchestration each run separately, deployable on different machines. Free-form commands become structured requests for picking, placing, and handovers.

A vision-language model returns targets in image space. Depth and calibration convert those pixels into metric goals in the robot's frame. A web dashboard shows the interpreted intent and grounding overlays at every stage. No motion executes until an operator explicitly confirms. Experiments on a Franka FR3 arm measured reliability and latency as table scenes grew more ambiguous. Different language and vision model pairings were compared inside the same pipeline. The design lesson is architectural: distribute the intelligence, centralize the accountability. Collaborative robots in real workplaces need both.
arxiv-2606-06461:
Luzhe Sun and co-authors offer a gentle way to fix a robot's imperfect helper in this 2026 arXiv paper. Robots often start from a pretrained policy or a human operator whose actions are noisy or off. Retraining is expensive, and full autonomy throws away the helper's intent. Their GLOVES framework instead edits actions on the fly, transporting each proposed action toward what an expert would do, using flow matching learned from a few demonstrations.

The clever part is restraint. The learned flow also scores how expert like an action looks, and that score gates intervention: normal actions pass through untouched, while odd ones get corrected. Assistance therefore appears only when needed. Across simulated and real robot experiments, the method steadily improved noisy imitation agents and large vision language action models, learning from only a few expert demonstrations or reusable skill segments.
arxiv-2606-06561:
C Dedes rewrites the quantum wavefunction with a twist that changes how quantum fluids flow in this 2026 arXiv paper. The Madelung transformation recasts the Schrödinger equation as fluid equations, splitting the wave into amplitude and phase. Dedes replaces that split with a new ansatz. Phase is tied to amplitude through a hyperbolic cotangent, a singular coupling. The flow velocity then picks up a term driven by density gradients.

Effects follow for both continuity and the quantum force. Read as the order parameter of a superconductor, the ansatz changes the London equations, which govern how superconductors expel magnetic fields. The Meissner response becomes sensitive to density gradients, not just phase winding. Dedes concludes that superconductor rigidity need not be purely phase driven. The condensate behaves like a medium whose screening and currents are shaped by its own amplitude landscape.
arxiv-2606-06661:
The nonlinear Fourier transform extends the classic Fourier idea to signals where waves interact as they pass. Denisov studies when this transform settles down to a well defined limit in this 2026 arXiv paper. His data are sparse, meaning most entries are zero, and square summable, meaning the total energy stays finite even over an endless line of entries.

The note covers two versions of the transform, linked to two symmetry groups used in physics and signal work. Denisov proves convergence for this sparse class and draws a direct payoff for a related family of polynomials defined on the unit circle, whose long run behavior follows from the main result. The paper is a companion to his earlier study of the general square summable case, borrowing its setup and notation while sharpening what can be said when the data thin out.
arxiv-2606-06761:
A robot can recognize every object in a room and still fumble picking one up when it sits in a new spot. Jang and co-authors trace that failure to a missing link in this 2026 arXiv paper: the robot policy understands the scene, but not how its own movement directions look from the camera. Its action coordinates, the axes of its base frame, remain invisible in the image it sees.

Their fix, AxisGuide, paints those axes directly onto each camera view. Using the camera settings and the gripper's pose, it renders small cue channels showing which way each base direction moves in the picture, with no depth sensor or extra labeling needed. Trials in the LIBERO simulator and on real robots showed solid gains in task success and much better handling of objects placed at unseen locations, a common way these policies break.
arxiv-2606-07061:
Proving identities between endless sums is a craft that computers have steadily mechanized. Wang advances one core technique in this 2026 arXiv paper. The setting is q-holonomic sequences, families indexed by an integer with a deformation parameter q. A reduction method splits any test polynomial into two parts.

One part is summable, meaning its sum telescopes away neatly. The other is a remainder of lower degree. Wang pins down exactly which multiplier polynomials make a product summable. He then adds a power partible refinement for mirror cases. It removes the highest and lowest degree terms together while keeping the mirror symmetry. The machinery is applied to q-central-Delannoy numbers, a deformed counting sequence. New q-identities and q-congruences fall out as demonstrations. The work sits in the Wilf-Zeilberger tradition of machine assisted identity proof.
arxiv-2606-07161:
Reading text in surveillance video fails frame by frame: blur, occlusion, and scale shifts corrupt each glimpse. Tran and co-authors aggregate whole trajectories instead in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their method, TraRA, is a plug in layer for video text spotting. A sign or plate visible across thirty frames should be read once, jointly, not thirty times separately.

Two modules do the work. Temporal Clustering groups detections that stay coherent across time and appearance, cleaning fragmented tracks. Vision-Language Aggregation then fuses the frames using a vision language model tuned with low rank adapters. Language context helps disambiguate smudged characters. Four public benchmarks covered road scenes and urban footage. TraRA consistently improved tracking stability and recognition accuracy over leading methods. The design needs no changes to the underlying spotter. Future work targets lighter models and real time speed for live surveillance feeds.
arxiv-2606-07361:
Gasse and co-authors classify the search landscapes of two graph problems in this 2026 arXiv paper. A dominating set is a set of vertices such that every vertex is in it or next to it, while vertex coloring assigns colors so neighbors differ. Heuristic search on such problems succeeds or stalls depending on local optima, points where no change improves the solution. The authors ask, for graph classes, whether landscapes are unimodal, flat-plateaued, or multimodal with traps.

They analyze neighborhood rules: changing one element at a time, and allowing swaps between solution parts. For each problem and graph class they determine which landscape type arises, including whether local optimum is global. The work trades runtime bounds, the usual goal of heuristic theory, for understanding of where search gets stuck. The map explains why randomized heuristics vary across instance families and guides which neighborhood operators fit which problems.
arxiv-2606-07761:
Jikun Wang and colleagues at ETH Zürich and partner institutes unveil a stronger way to corrupt memory from ordinary software, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The weakness is read disturbance in DRAM chips: hammering one row of cells can flip bits in neighbouring rows, the effect behind RowHammer attacks. How bad the effect gets depends heavily on the pattern of accesses used.

Their pattern, ScaleDisturb, holds two aggressor rows open for unequal times, exploiting a timing asymmetry in disturbance. On one hundred ninety-six DDR4 chips and three HBM2 chips, ScaleDisturb triggered bitflips at notably fewer activations than the best known patterns, and made attacks easier on every chip. Vulnerability also grew as manufacturing shrank to smaller nodes, the opposite of what chip makers hope. A proof-of-concept attack from a user program flipped more bits than state-of-the-art RowHammer methods.
arxiv-2606-07961:
Rene Ebunle Akupan, May-Win Thein, and Se Young Yoon present a control tutorial for the inverters that hold up islanded microgrids, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A grid-forming inverter in an island must regulate its own voltage with no external grid to lean on, while load current depends on that very voltage. The standard cascaded controller compensates couplings only exactly at its tuning point.

Their alternative is full-state feedback linearisation. The inverter model has full relative degree, so one feedback law can cancel the main nonlinear effects exactly. What remains is two independent double integrators that pole placement can shape. In MATLAB tests at twenty megawatts, the linearising controller settled a reference step in well under a millisecond. The baseline never reached the two percent band within fifty milliseconds. The trade-off is robustness: the cascaded controller tolerated filter mismatch better, a caveat stated plainly.
arxiv-2606-08061:
Lies Beers, Raffaella Mulas, and Jan Petr extend a classical bridge between graph geometry and spectrum to a less-studied gap, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The normalised Laplacian of a graph has eigenvalues between zero and two. The classical Cheeger inequalities tie the smallest positive eigenvalue to how easily the graph splits in two, and dual inequalities do the same for the largest eigenvalue. The gap studied here is the second largest distance from one, a quantity arising in random walks and expander graphs.

The authors relate this gap to both the classical and dual Cheeger constants. Their main tool is a new Cheeger-type constant with a probabilistic meaning, tied to two-step random walks on the graph. For it they prove sharp inequalities in the classical style, so the gap can be estimated from walk behaviour. Such results matter wherever expansion matters, from network design to mixing times.
arxiv-2606-08161:
Jiechen Huang and co-authors teach a transformer to compute the parasitic capacitances that haunt chip design, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Capacitance extraction predicts the unwanted coupling between wires on a chip, which designers must know to predict timing and noise. Rule-based pattern matching struggles at advanced nodes. Earlier neural models accepted only fixed layer combinations from one process node.

Their AttentionCap exploits a structural resemblance: a capacitance matrix behaves like the attention matrices transformers already compute. Customisations include a Gram representation, a physics-aligned symmetric output layer, and a process-node embedding for training across nodes. Trained on synthetic data, it reached about zero point seven percent self-capacitance error and four percent coupling error on unseen designs. Errors were several times lower than the CNN baseline, and inference about one hundred ninety times faster. A pretrained model transferred to an unseen node with only five thousand samples.
arxiv-2606-08561:
Zicheng Han, Wanchen Zhang, and Xiande Zhang resolve the smallest open case of loss-resistant entanglement in this 2026 arXiv paper. A pure quantum state is called m-resistant if it stays entangled after losing any m particles, yet becomes fully separable, with no entanglement at all, after losing any m plus one. For qubits, whether a five-qubit state could be exactly one-resistant was unresolved. The authors show the five-cycle graph state, built from five qubits linked in a ring, does exactly this.

They also develop a stabilizer-subgroup method for verifying resistance in graph states. Applying it to all graph states on five, six, and seven vertices gives a classification up to local Clifford equivalence. The five-qubit one-resistant stabilizer states turn out to be exactly the local Clifford class of the five-cycle state: a single island of loss tolerance in the smallest possible register.
arxiv-2606-08661:
Kuncan Wang and colleagues map the attack surface of agents that answer questions from databases, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Data agents integrate language-model reasoning with relational data access and multi-step workflow orchestration. That integration introduces new weak spots across data resources, database execution, and agent reasoning. The authors present a full security study of these systems.

Their contributions include a layered vulnerability framework identifying eight risks across interpretation, execution, and policy layers. They also give an attack taxonomy spanning three goals, seven tactics, and fourteen techniques. They pair the taxonomy with a payload generation pipeline grounded in realistic attack scenarios. The study gives firms a clear list of weak spots to check before they hand a live database to an agent.
arxiv-2606-08961:
Sun and Wang simulate how dense black hole packs merge up to an intermediate-mass black hole, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Supermassive black holes existed early in history, and intermediate-mass seeds, around 1,000 solar masses, could explain their fast growth. Simulating black hole clusters, the authors follow chains of binary mergers driven by gravitational waves. The mechanism is exchange: soft binaries trade partners, hardening gradually, far more efficiently than three-body scattering.

At densities above 5 billion solar masses per cubic parsec, the runaway chain builds an intermediate-mass black hole of 1,000 solar masses within 10 million years of cluster formation. The scenario avoids the uncertainties of growing a very massive star. As clusters expand, their densities fall to match present-day nuclear star clusters like those in the Milky Way and M33. Repeated mergers keep the black hole's spin low. The authors estimate rates for gravitational-wave events resembling known mergers.
arxiv-2606-09061:
Liu, Wang, and colleagues fix a fairness flaw in how AI chatbots serve crowds of users, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Serving engines use chunked prefill, splitting each prompt's processing into pieces so long prompts do not block others. Standard first-come-first-served scheduling lets some requests starve while tail latency jitters. Their framework adds an aging policy: a request's priority rises with waiting time and remaining work, so nobody waits forever.

Two more components replace static token budgets with latency targets. Latency-Prediction-Based Request Scheduling uses predicted times. Active Prefill Control regulates concurrent prefills. Tested on NVIDIA and Ascend hardware, the aging policy cut mean end-to-end latency by over 10 percent versus first-come-first-served. The latency components reduced P99 tail latency, the slowest 1 percent of requests, and suppressed fragmentation. The authors conclude structural and temporal controls are complementary, and release the code.
arxiv-2606-09361:
Johannes Wehrstein and his colleagues present Bespoke-Card, a system that writes database software instead of tuning it, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The target is cardinality estimation, a database's guess at how many rows a query step will produce. Bad guesses lead the query optimiser to choose slow plans, yet built-in estimators must stay generic for every possible workload.

Bespoke-Card uses cooperating software agents: one plans an estimator design, one writes the code, and a validator scores its guesses against true row counts. Feedback about the largest errors guides repeated improvement, with the best version kept. On the JOB query benchmark, feeding the generated estimates into PostgreSQL cut total runtime by about a third and reduced the median estimation error by roughly two fifths. Each tailored estimator took under an hour and cost less than ten dollars to produce.
arxiv-2606-09561:
Sida and co-authors study a wave in fusion plasmas whose strength rises and falls in a repeating swing in this 2026 arXiv paper. The wave is a geodesic acoustic mode, a ring-shaped wobble of the radial electric field in a tokamak. Fast particles can feed it energy and drive it unstable. The driven form is called an EGAM.

The team ran the gyrokinetic particle-in-cell code ORB5, which follows charged particles in a magnetic field. They compared the mode with the beam-plasma instability, where a beam of fast electrons drives a Langmuir wave. Both systems show the same link between swing rate and wave size. That match says the same particle-trapping physics drives both cases. The work also yields a new way to gauge EGAM strength in a real tokamak.
arxiv-2606-09761:
Corona-García, Fernández-Bretón, and Ramos-García probe a rare breed of ultrafilter tied to Ramsey theory in this 2026 arXiv paper. An ultrafilter is a maximal, consistent way to call sets of integers large. A Z-Ramsey ultrafilter holds a tidy set for each colouring that the integer shift leaves alone. Such objects were posed as open questions by Petrenko and Protasov.

The team shows it is consistent with set theory that none exist at all. They also prove that each filter of a weaker three-colour kind is selective, a strong tidiness trait. The same holds for Z-Ramsey filters that are P-points. A crafted forcing extension then yields P-points that fail the Z-Ramsey test. The build uses quotient algebras of integer sets over a class of ideals. The results answer the posed questions head-on.
arxiv-2606-10061:
Noshin and her team introduce the first benchmark for conversational sycophancy in Bengali social contexts, in a 2026 arXiv paper on language model testing. Sycophancy is excessive agreement or flattery, and in emotionally sensitive conversations models can slide from balanced support into strong validation or escalation. Prior research focused on factual agreement and instruction settings, leaving culturally grounded conversation underexplored. Their benchmark, BenSyc, fills that gap for Bengali-speaking communities in Bangladesh and West Bengal.

Starting from nearly twelve thousand Reddit posts and about one hundred seventy thousand comments, the team built a human-validated dataset with binary labels and a five-level taxonomy from invalidation through escalation. More than fifteen open and proprietary models were evaluated on classification and response generation. Even the best system reached only about sixty-two percent macro-F1 on binary detection and a similar score on five-class sorting.
arxiv-2606-10361:
Yang and colleagues introduce a new regularity condition that sharpens what theory can promise about a classic classifier, in a 2026 arXiv paper on statistical learning theory. Convergence rates for classifiers are usually proven under a weak Tsybakov margin condition, giving polynomial rates, or a strong Massart margin condition, giving exponential rates. Their Boltzmann margin bridges the gap: weaker than Massart, generally stronger than Tsybakov, and able to imply many of their properties under suitable conditions.

Applying Boltzmann margin to k-nearest neighbors classification, they establish the first near-exponential convergence rates for that classifier. The work matters because nearest-neighbor methods are widely used yet their fastest known guarantees required the strongest margin assumption. A middle condition that real data may plausibly satisfy, while still delivering near-exponential rates, narrows the gap between learning theory and the observed speed of simple classifiers.
arxiv-2606-10561:
De Angelis surveys gamma-ray astrophysics in this 2026 arXiv review paper, covering the highest-energy light in the universe. Gamma rays diagnose extreme accelerators, from pulsars to black hole jets, and carry fingerprints of nuclear synthesis, such as lines from radioactive aluminium and iron. The field spans nine orders of magnitude in photon energy, alongside neutrino and gravitational-wave astronomy. Yet one band lags: the MeV gap, where sensitivity remains poor.

That gap limits studies of supernova line spectroscopy, positron annihilation mapping, burst polarimetry, and dark matter searches. The review traces the field from 1950s predictions through the first space detections in the 1960s to modern observatories. It then assesses missions meant to close the gap, noting the COSI telescope as a pathfinder for the late 2020s and a polarimetric mission like ASTROGAM as realistic for the 2030s.
arxiv-2606-10661:
Drummond-Curtis, Dalwadi, and Walker study tiny swimmers near walls in this 2026 arXiv paper on fluid dynamics. Bacteria and sperm swim close to surfaces, where their flow interacts with the boundary and bends their paths. Simple models treat the swimmer as a force dipole, an averaged push-pull flow, with shape held fixed. But real propulsion comes from rapid shape oscillations, and dipole models break down near a wall. The authors add higher-order flow singularities and use a multiscale analysis that keeps the fast oscillations explicit.

Now its fate near the boundary falls into three behaviours: crashing into the surface, escaping from it, and hovering at a steady distance. Hovering is the telling case: experiments see it in bacteria, yet the simplest averaged models never produce it. The lesson: the time-dependence earlier models discarded creates qualitatively new behaviour near a boundary.
arxiv-2606-10861:
Patkar and colleagues test whether chatbot interfaces can curb AI energy use in this 2026 arXiv paper. Most fixes target models or data centers; the interface layer is rarely touched. The team built a prototype with a three-mode switch, per-response energy feedback, pre-send estimates, a usage dashboard, and energy analogies, then ran a five-day field study.

In a baseline survey of 77 people, 94.8 percent knew chatbots use energy, yet 88.3 percent misestimated how much. In the field study, the efficient mode took 55.8 percent of prompts, and observed energy use ran about 47 percent below an all-performance counterfactual. Users switched modes rather than shortening prompts.
arxiv-2606-10961:
Zhang develops a proof framework for process logic in a 2026 arXiv computer science paper. Process logic extends dynamic logic: instead of stating only how a program ends, its formulas describe whole execution traces. The hard part is reasoning about concrete first-order computations while keeping that trace information, and earlier calculi covered only fragments.

Zhang's fix is labels. Formulas carry labels recording trace and update information during derivations, rather than hiding it inside the formula. On that basis he defines cyclic labelled proof systems for propositional process logic, G3PPL, and the first-order version, G3FOPL. Soundness comes from infinite descent: any bad derivation would force an endless fall in a well-founded ordering, which cannot happen.
