bonaventure-itinerarium-mentis-latin-186:
Bonaventure wrote the Itinerarium Mentis in Deum, the Journey of the Mind to God, in 1259. He was on retreat at La Verna, where Francis had borne the stigmata. Karl Joseph von Hefele edited the Latin text in 1861. No English version in the public domain exists, so the Latin stands here as the record of the central Franciscan ascent text.

Six steps, like the six wings of the seraph, lift the soul. They climb through the world, through the senses, and through the mind's powers, to the vision of Being and of the Good. A seventh step is rest, the peace past thought. The little book is dense and burning at once. Generations of mystics climbed by its ladder.
boyle-sceptical-chymist-1661:
Robert Boyle's Sceptical Chymist, published in 1661, is a dialogue that demolishes the old theories of matter. Speaker after speaker defends the four elements or the three principles of the alchemists, and each defense fails. The book is counted the founding text of modern chemistry.

Boyle argues that elements must be found by experiment, not assumed from ancient systems or furnace habits. His careful trials with air, acids, and colors model a new way of asking nature questions. Later chemists looked back to Boyle's dialogue as the moment their science learned to doubt in an orderly way.
brasseur-popol-vuh-1861:
The sacred book of the K'iche' Maya reached Europe in print through Brasseur de Bourbourg in 1861. Popol Vuh: Le livre sacré gives the creation epic in French, its first European edition. Brasseur had found the old manuscript in Guatemala and knew its worth at once.

His French version carried the gods, the making of man, and the Hero Twins to Western readers. The edition tied the Popol Vuh to the wide debate on American antiquity and lost lands. Every later Maya-Atlantis claim leans on the text he brought out. The book is a landmark of American studies in its own right.
camerarius-history-strange-wonders-1561:
Joachim Camerarius was a German scholar of the Reformation age, and his writings on omens circulated widely. This English History of Strange Wonders appeared in 1561. It carried German prodigy lore across the Channel to English readers early in Elizabeth's reign.

Strange births, signs in the sky, and monsters crowd its pages. Each wonder is read as a warning from God about wars, deaths of princes, or sins of the age. Lutheran Germany scanned the book of nature for such omens with great care. The English version shows how fast this habit crossed borders. Fear and faith, more than curiosity, drive the whole collection.
catcott-treatise-on-the-deluge-1761:
Alexander Catcott defended the Deluge as Earth's great agent in his Treatise of 1761. Catcott was a Bristol clergyman of the Hutchinsonian school. That school set Moses's philosophy, drawn from Hebrew scripture, against Newton's system. His treatise reads the Flood as the force that shaped the crust.

Strata, fossils, and mountains all become the Deluge's work in his hands. Remarks on the Bishop of Clogher's account of the same subject join the argument. Catcott writes as a divine who trusts scripture above the new philosophy. His book shows diluvial thought fighting on into the age of geology. It preserves a losing side argued with learning. The controversy itself is the lesson.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-corporation-a: This 1913 reference article on the Corporation Act of 1661 — the Test's forerunner. Bernard Ward unfolds its penal tale. The dissenters were barred from office. The sacramental test excluded the faithful. The law of the Cavalier Parliament. Its repeal came in eighteen twenty-eight.
cia-0000014661: Samuel Novick is the subject of an untitled CIA file dated April 3, 1957. The file draws on an article by Victor Riesel in his newspaper column. Columnists fed the files with names and claims the agency then checked. Novick was a businessman whose left wing ties drew watch in the anti Communist years.
cia-0000014761: Spies in the United States told Russia all is the bold headline of a CIA file dated March 5, 1951. The file describes in detail how agents stole secret data. Headline style files like this summed up the spy scare for busy readers. They also show the alarm that ran through official Washington in the trial spring of 1951.
cia-0000015461: Near Baku, an unconventional flying object was sighted, and a CIA record dated in 1956 lays the report out as a tabulation. A memo came with the table. Baku was a Soviet oil city on the Caspian Sea, deep inside closed land. Turning a strange sighting there into rows and columns was how analysts made distant claims easier to compare and judge.
cia-0000022361: Text on the indictment, noting the Soviet government ordered the U-2 shot down, fills a CIA record dated in 1960. The shoot down order came from the top, by the heading's account. That point mattered, since Moscow wanted the flight framed as a crime met by lawful defense. The legal text and the order together form the Soviet case in brief.
cia-0000037161:
A CIA record dated May 4, 1983 concerns the 1967 crash site of an American Air Force F-4 aircraft. The site lay in My Hao district, in the Haiphong area of North Vietnam. F-4 Phantoms flew many of the bombing missions over the north during the war years. The two-man Phantom was the workhorse of the air war, and many were lost.

The record fixes where one lost aircraft came down, sixteen years after the crash. Crash sites mattered because they often held the answer to a crew's fate. Marking this one kept open the chance that searchers could one day visit the ground and learn what happened to the men aboard.
cia-0000043361:
Cuban government reactions to current crises fill a CIA record dated December 23, 1958. The date is the story: Fulgencio Batista's regime had days left to live. Rebels under Fidel Castro were closing on power across the island.

Inside, Havana's responses to the crises around it are recorded. A government in its final week speaks in a special tone. Orders, denials, and appeals all carry the sound of an ending. Within days, the government issuing them would be gone from the palace. The file preserves that sound from inside the old order, days before Batista fled and the revolution remade Cuba for the rest of the century.
cia-0000046761: Hanoi's running count of claimed American planes downed reached 4,036 in a CIA item dated October 5, 1972. The same dispatch carried word of an F-111 lost, naming its commander. Such tallies were propaganda, but they were filed and studied all the same. Each figure had to be matched against the real losses the air war was costing.
cia-0000049061: Captain Eduardo Avila's travel to El Salvador in 1983 is logged in a CIA item, kept with the Truth Commission records. Avila was named in this series as an alleged conspirator, which made his movements worth filing. The item is a small piece of the paper watch kept on officers tied to the war's crimes.
cia-0000049161: An FMLN representative worked in 1990 to arrange a visit to Costa Rica's president, and a CIA item preserves the effort. Costa Rica, the region's standing mediator, hosted much of the diplomacy that ended Central America's wars. A guerrilla envoy seeking a president's door showed how far the rebels' campaign had moved toward talks.
cia-0000049261: Update number five on the Jesuit killings is preserved in a CIA item from 1990, kept with the Truth Commission records. The numbered series let readers follow the case's slow public life, one bulletin at a time. The fifth adds its week of movement, or of waiting, to the chronicle the series built.
cia-0000049361: Human rights abuses in El Salvador are the subject of declassified CIA document 0000049361, dated February 4, 1983. Carrying a Truth Commission note, the item focuses on abuses rather than on battles or politics. Readers find a brief declassified record whose title states its grim topic directly, kept among the agency's Salvadoran files from the war years.
cia-0000096661: Continued Unrest in Chekiang Province is reported in declassified CIA document 0000096661, dated September 3, 1968. The heading stresses duration, unrest that kept going in one province. The brief file sits one day after the neighboring Wenchou fighting item, and together the two records show the agency returning to Chekiang in consecutive daily filings.
cia-0000102961:
Work Treatment Prophylaxis Camps, Moscow, is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000102961, dated July 1, 1987. The sample covers the years 1977 to 1979 and names five or six such camps near Moscow. Each camp held several thousand people and was run by the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

Entry took a judge's order and a medical exam to show a person could perform hard labor. In practice, treatment for alcohol dependence was almost absent, beyond Antabuse or a few vitamin C tablets. A typical day meant ten hours of construction or heavy labor, plain meals, and political lessons before bed. Guards could be bribed for alcohol, and the camps failed at treating alcoholism.

The contents page names the week's articles, opening with an attempted hijack in London by an unknown gunman. That single named article shows the report's mix: short items on attacks and attempts around the world. The issue is one early installment of the weekly series named in its title.

During that autumn, keeping the sequence current meant keeping pace with a revolution, and the supplement preserves the order of events as the agency assembled it. cia-0000126861: A February 1953 CIA document filed under the name John P. Hayes. The title offers no role, no charge, no context — just the name. Whatever made Hayes interesting to the agency, the answer is inside the file.

cia-0000132661:
The future of the Castro regime is weighed in a CIA paper dated November 4, 1960. The American election was days away, and the new president would inherit the Cuba problem at once. How long Castro could last was the question running through Washington that fall.

The agency's forecasters were split on the answer, and the paper sets out their views. For readers, it preserves a moment of honest doubt before policy hardened. Within five months the invasion at the Bay of Pigs would test every forecast in the file. The paper shows what the experts said before that test came.
cia-0000132761:
Spring tensions run through this CIA briefing on Cuba, dated May 4, 1960. Castro's government was a year old and pressing ahead with its revolution. The United States, still weighing its options, had not yet settled on a course.

May 1960 sits in the hinge of the story: relations were bad and worsening, but the final break was still months away. Briefings from that month record an agency watching land seizures, sharp speeches, and colder diplomacy pile up. The declassified paper preserves the moment before Washington chose confrontation, and it rewards reading beside the harder papers of 1961.

cia-0000136061: From the CIA files comes a cable dated 5 March 1954, long since declassified, on the K Program, a recurring subject in the station files through the spring of 1954. dickens-great-expectations-1861:
Charles Dickens published Great Expectations in 1861, a late novel many call his most perfect. Pip, Miss Havisham, and the convict Magwitch anchor its tight, ironic plot of ambition. Dickens shaped the tale with care and gave it a revised, softer end in print.

Pip, an orphan smith's boy, helps a convict and dreams of a finer life. A secret fortune lets him train as a gentleman in London town and lodgings. He snubs Joe, the kind smith who raised him, and chases cold Estella in vain. The fortune's true source shocks him and teaches him where worth truly lies in men. Few novels trace shame, love, and growth with such clean, hard force.
dircks-perpetuum-mobile-1861:
Henry Dircks, an English engineer, spent years on the hunt for self motive power, and this survey came out in 1861. Men had tried for three hundred years to build a wheel that would turn for ever with no fuel. Dircks set out to list them all.

The book walks through scheme after scheme, with drawings of wheels, weights, and fluids. Dircks shows where each one fails, in plain terms a lay reader can grasp. His survey is still the main guide to the long hunt for a machine that cannot work.
dircks-perpetuum-mobile-first-series-186:
Henry Dircks was an English engineer with a rage for one theme. His Perpetuum Mobile, First Series, came out in 1861. The book lists scheme on scheme for a wheel that runs for all time. Dircks dug through rolls, tracts, and tales of three hundred years.

Wheels with weights, mills with pumps, and craft with magnets all get their due. Most tales end in fraud, flaw, or a hid spring of force. Dircks meant the book as a warn to men who waste life on the dream. The pair of series is the full tale of the vain hunt.
du-chaillu-explorations-equatorial-afric:
Paul Du Chaillu came out of the Gabon forests in 1861 with skins, skulls, and a sensation. Explorations and Adventures in Equatorial Africa made the gorilla a household word in Europe and America. No living gorilla had yet been seen by the crowds who read him.

Du Chaillu tells of hunts, river trips, and tribes of the deep forest, with the great ape as his star. His monster ape, charging and roaring, fixed the gorilla in the public mind for good. Later travelers faulted parts of his tale, but the fame held. The book turned a rumor of the woods into a beast of science.
eisenhower-farewell-1961:
Dwight D. Eisenhower gave his Farewell Address in January 1961. The old general warned against the military-industrial complex by name. No presidential warning since Washington's has been quoted so often.

Eisenhower had led the crusade in Europe and built much of the arms world. Yet he cautions that its vast sway could harm free government itself. He urges balance, thrift, and care for the nation's schools and farms. A soldier's farewell doubles as a prophecy Americans still debate. The speech gains force from the speaker's own unmatched war record in Europe. Only the supreme commander could warn so credibly against arms buildup.
eliot-george-silas-marner-1861:
George Eliot published Silas Marner in 1861, her flawless fable of a betrayed weaver and a foundling child. A betrayed weaver hoards gold until a foundling child redeems him,. Eliot said the tale came to her as a legend meant to show the fruits of a recovered faith.

Silas, falsely cast out by his chapel, lives alone at Raveloe weaving and counting his guineas in isolation. His gold is stolen by Dunstan Cass, and a golden-haired child crawls to his hearth from the snow. Eppie, the child of an opium-dead mother, becomes his treasure and his bridge back to church, neighbors, and human trust in Raveloe. Sixteen years later her choice of the weaver who raised her seals the fable's moral. Its symmetry and warmth make it the Eliot novel most often given to the young.
europmc-pmc10017761:
Zhang and colleagues review engineered exosomes as a tool for targeted cancer treatment in a 2023 paper. Exosomes are tiny parcels that cells release to send signals to other cells. Researchers can load them with drugs and add surface features that steer them toward tumors.

The review covers exosomes from different cell sources and how each source affects their use. It explains how loading and steering are done in the lab. It also weighs safety and the steps left before clinic use. The paper maps a lively field in drug delivery.
europmc-pmc10192861:
Dave, Athaluri, and Singh give an overview of ChatGPT in medicine in a 2023 paper. They cover its applications, advantages, limits, future prospects, and the ethical questions it raises. ChatGPT is a language model trained on vast amounts of text that can hold a fluent conversation on medical topics.

The authors survey uses in study, writing, diagnosis support, and patient communication. They weigh gains in speed against risks such as confident errors and bias. They close with advice on consent, privacy, and oversight. The paper is a balanced early guide to AI in care.
europmc-pmc10495961:
Abril-Pla and a team of co-authors presented PyMC in 2023, a Python library for chance-based models. Such models, called Bayesian, state a guess as a spread of odds, not one fixed number. PyMC lets users write a model in code that reads close to plain math. A math engine then compiles it for fast chips.

The library fits a wide range of models. Abril-Pla lists layered line fits, time series, smooth curve models, and equation-based models. Work can run on plain processors or on graphics and tensor chips. Sample uses walk through common stats tasks step by step. The authors also credit PyMC for growing the open-source scene in this niche.
europmc-pmc10589261:
Hou and co-authors reviewed macrophages in atherosclerosis in 2023, the fatty build-up inside artery walls. Such plaques narrow vessels and can trigger heart attack or stroke. Macrophages sit at the core of each stage, from first growth to rupture and healing. Their states shift with the plaque's local cues.

These cells vary widely and can reshape their fuel use on the fly. Hou shows how low oxygen in a plaque flips a switch, HIF-1alpha, that alters cell acts. Some states stuff the plaque with fat and stir swelling. Others clear dead cells and calm the zone. A ring-shaped sugar, beta-cyclodextrin, helped plaques shrink in past work by aiding fat exit. Drugs that steer these states may yield precise care.
europmc-pmc1088961:
Schug and co-authors hunted for DNA traits that mark genes used in just one tissue in this 2005 paper. Turning a fertilised egg into an adult needs genes switched on at the right place and time. Some genes run in all cells, while others run in one tissue only. The stretch of DNA before a gene, called its promoter, helps set that pattern.

Using human gene activity data from tissue surveys, the team measured how varied each gene's use was. Most genes did vary by tissue in a clear way, they found. They then flagged promoter traits that split tissue-specific genes from those used everywhere. Tissue breadth was scored with Shannon entropy, a maths measure of how spread out a pattern is. Genes used in one tissue scored low on spread, while genes used everywhere scored high.
europmc-pmc11382761:
Su and colleagues review how cells talk to each other and what that means for medicine in this 2024 paper. Multicellular life requires diverse cell types to coordinate their behaviour. Cells communicate by direct contact or at a distance through ligand-receptor pairs, where a signal molecule docks onto a receiver protein. Two processes define the exchange: conduction sends the signal, and transduction lets the receiver process it.

The review first traces the historical milestones of the field. It then details how signal molecules travel and the main pathways they mediate. Diseases caused by faulty communication are surveyed systematically. Clinical applications that target these networks follow. The authors argue that decoding communication networks is critical for grasping cell differentiation, development, and metabolism. They close with the field's open challenges.
europmc-pmc11445061:
Liu, Prentice, and Webber explain how bacterial biofilms resist antimicrobial drugs in this 2024 review. Most bacteria in nature live in aggregated communities called biofilms, glued in a self-made matrix. Cells inside differ deeply from free-floating cells of the same species. Biofilm infections are often chronic and stubbornly hard to treat with antibiotics.

Intrinsic factors drive the tolerance: the matrix barrier, slow growth rates, altered drug targets, and fast swapping of resistance genes. A special cell type, persisters, survives drug exposure by lying dormant. The review describes the biofilm lifecycle and how resistance evolves and spreads within the film. Mixed-species biofilms add cooperation and competition that further shift drug tolerance. The authors argue these features, not single mutations, explain most treatment failures.
europmc-pmc1253661:
Lubin and co-authors tackled detection limits in environmental studies in 2004. Lab tools cannot read values below set limits. Studies often fill gaps with half the limit or random picks. The team tested those habits with simulations.

Half-limit filling biased results unless few values fell below limits. Bias stayed small only when under 5 to 10 percent were censored. Random fill-ins gave unbiased estimates but shaky error ranges. Distortion grew when 30 percent or more were censored. Lubin points to Tobit regression and multiple imputation as sound fixes. Tobit methods fit truncated data of this kind.
europmc-pmc1475661:
Malaria germs must cross the mosquito gut, where most of them die. Dong and co-authors mapped how the mosquito Anopheles gambiae reacts to two malaria species in 2006. One infects humans, the other infects rodents and serves as a lab model. They tracked which mosquito genes switch on during invasion.

The rodent germ stirred a wider change in gene activity. The human germ drew a broader immune reply. Silencing tests on 12 genes found seven that guard against both germs. A few guards were specific to one germ each. Dong shows the mosquito's defense blends shared and tailored weapons.
europmc-pmc1526461:
Proteins that juggle many partners tend to be floppy, not rigid. Haynes and co-authors tested that link in 2006 across four species: worm, yeast, fly, and human. Hub proteins, those with ten or more partners, were compared with proteins holding just one partner.

In all four species, hubs carried more disordered stretches, regions with no fixed shape. Wholly disordered proteins were enriched among hubs, wholly ordered ones scarce. In yeast, hubs tied to regulation and development leaned disordered, while enzyme and transport hubs leaned ordered. Haynes argues disorder gives hubs the flex to bind many unlike partners.
europmc-pmc1550961:
A shared scale for sudden kidney injury needed a real-world test. Hoste and co-authors gave it one in 2006, tracking 5,383 intensive care patients over a year. The RIFLE scale grades injury as risk, injury, or failure, based on kidney function.

Two thirds of patients had some injury. Death rates climbed with grade: 8.8 percent at risk, 11.4 at injury, and 26.3 at failure, against 5.5 with no injury. Over half of those at the risk grade slid to worse grades. Hoste confirms the scale forecasts death and heavy care use, and flags patients likely to worsen.
europmc-pmc161361:
Oxidative stress may start Alzheimer's long before plaques appear. Perry, Cash, and Smith reviewed that case in 2002. Cell changes tied to oxidation, damage by reactive oxygen, precede the disease's hallmark tangles and plaques.

The initial source of the stress stays unclear. Redox-active metals, iron and copper, likely feed the process, since they can spawn damaging oxygen species. Perry argues that pinning down this early chemistry could open new treatments. Most Alzheimer therapies of the time chased late damage; this line points upstream, to the spark itself.  Their focus on metals points to iron and copper handling as a testable lead.
europmc-pmc1764161:
Tiny engineered particles promise much in medicine and industry, but their health effects are largely unknown. Gwinn and Vallyathan reviewed the pros and cons in 2006. Particles under 100 nanometers, billionths of a meter, gain surface traits that plain dust lacks.

Proof from ultrafine particles of human activity suggests harm to heart and lungs. Engineered ones may behave alike, traveling to distant body sites. Beneficial uses, like drug delivery and gene therapy, can themselves cause exposure. Gwinn argues for a precautionary duty: pin down toxic effects now to keep workplace and environmental exposure low.
europmc-pmc1829161:
Bennett and colleagues surveyed people with fibromyalgia online in 2007 to test whether internet surveys can capture this chronic pain condition. The National Fibromyalgia Association built a 121-item questionnaire with expert help and refined it through several rounds of testing. Fibromyalgia causes widespread pain, fatigue, and poor sleep.

A total of 2,569 people completed the survey, and every one of the 50 states sent at least one respondent. Most were middle-aged white women with symptoms for four years or more. The top complaints were morning stiffness, fatigue, unrefreshing sleep, pain, and trouble with focus and memory. Emotional distress, weather changes, insomnia, and hard exertion made things worse. Respondents rated rest, heat, pain medicines, antidepressants, and sleep medicines as the most helpful measures.
europmc-pmc1971061:
Levitt and Peña reviewed anorectal malformations in 2007, birth defects where the anus and rectum form abnormally, often with the urinary and genital tracts involved. They occur in about one in 5,000 live births, in boys and girls alike. Severity spans a wide spectrum.

Minor defects are easily repaired with excellent function, while complex forms are hard to manage, often come with other anomalies, and carry poor functional outlooks. Surgery changed radically in 1980 with the posterior sagittal approach, which let surgeons see the anatomy directly and repair under vision. Better imaging and knowledge of pelvic anatomy at birth further refined early care. The surgeon's core concerns are sexual function, plus control of the bowel and the bladder. With early diagnosis and meticulous repair, patients gain their best chance of good function.
europmc-pmc1994261:
Levine and colleagues used maths and experiments in 2007 to describe how small RNAs control genes in bacteria. These short RNA pieces, called sRNAs, help coordinate stress responses in Escherichia coli. They bind target messages and can block protein making or speed message breakdown. The team studied two distinct classes of bacterial sRNA in detail.

Their results show sRNA control differs from protein-based control in clear ways. It gives a threshold-linear response, where output stays low then rises in a straight line. The threshold can be tuned. The system also resists noise well and allows built-in cross-talk between pathways. These traits may help bacteria coordinate stress relief. They may also guide design of synthetic genetic circuits.
europmc-pmc2117961: A medical paper on the haematozoan infections of birds. The blood parasites of avians. This article preserves that parasitology research. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2124861: A medical paper on effects of mechanical agitation and temperature upon complement. The shaken immunity. This article preserves that immunology. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2125961: A medical paper with cultivation experiments on the globoid bodies of poliomyelitis. The polio bodies, grown. This article preserves that virology. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
europmc-pmc2128361: A medical paper with studies on total bile, effects of operation and exercise. The worked bile. This article preserves that physiology. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
europmc-pmc2128561: A medical paper with studies on the biology of streptococcus, agglutination and absorption. The strep's clumping. This article preserves that bacteriology. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
europmc-pmc2131261: A medical paper on effect of a filterable virus on the growth of a transplantable tumor. The virus-tumor interplay. This article preserves that oncology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2131461: A medical paper on the fundamental properties of the fibroblast and the macrophage, the malignant. The cancer cells. This article preserves that cell biology. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
europmc-pmc2140661: A biology paper with observations on the injurious effects of high temperatures on frog skin. The scorched frog. This article preserves that physiology. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2169261:
Clarke argued in 2007 that clinical trials and systematic reviews need standardised outcomes. Fifteen years earlier, the group that became OMERACT first met to tackle the many outcomes used in rheumatoid arthritis trials. Studies answering the same question often report findings in different ways. That makes evidence hard to combine for healthcare decisions. Even a systematic review can fail when primary studies measure results inconsistently.

Selective reporting makes the problem worse, Clarke warns. Researchers who measure an outcome several ways may publish only the most positive or significant result. Readers then get an overly optimistic estimate of a treatment's effect. That bias can push decisions in the wrong direction. Standard outcome sets, agreed in advance, are offered as the remedy.
europmc-pmc2229861:
Yang and co-workers uncovered new roles in 2007 for the formin protein mDia2 in moving cells. Formins and the Arp2/3 complex build actin filaments, the cell's internal scaffolding, and were thought to split jobs neatly. Arp2/3 was credited with sheet-like lamellipodia, while formins made spiky filopodia. The team depleted mDia2 with interfering RNA and also expressed an always-active version, examining the actin network by light and electron microscopy.

Unexpectedly, depleting mDia2 severely blocked lamellipodia, not just filopodia. The few remaining sheets held abnormally short filaments. Active mDia2 built long filaments, prolonged sheet protrusion, and promoted filopodia. Those spikes formed by lamellipodial filaments gradually converging into bundles. A partner protein, Abi1, targeted mDia2 to the membrane. The authors propose mDia2 creates and protects the long filaments that both structures share.
europmc-pmc2291561:
Zybailov and co-workers catalogued the chloroplast protein set in 2008 for the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana. Chloroplasts power plant growth, yet most of their proteins are made from nuclear genes and imported. The team ran ten independent chloroplast preparations through high-end mass spectrometry, requiring multiple matching peptide pieces for each identification. They also measured protein abundance from spectral counts and examined targeting signals and chemical modifications at protein starts.

They unambiguously identified 1,325 proteins, including new kinases and nucleotide-binding proteins. Nine hundred and sixteen were confidently assigned to the plastid, and 86 percent carried a predicted import signal. Abundances of soluble stromal proteins spanned four orders of magnitude. Forty-eight abundant proteins manage protein upkeep, from proteases to chaperones. A new start-modification motif emerged, and targeting signals differed between Arabidopsis and rice. No evidence supported import through the secretory pathway.
europmc-pmc2292261:
Rodriguez, Ehlenberger, Dickstein, Hof and Wearne built an automated three-dimensional system in 2008 for finding and classifying dendritic spines in microscope images. Spines are tiny protrusions where excitatory synapses form, and their shapes relate to learning, memory and brain disease. Measuring them precisely in 3D was slow and low-throughput. Their software module, part of NeuronStudio, processes laser scanning microscopy volumes automatically, using adaptive thresholding, voxel clustering and a sampling technique to estimate spine diameters.

The system proved more accurate than existing tools and at least ten times faster. Working fully in three dimensions, it resolves spines that two-dimensional tools miss entirely. Diameter profiles classify spines into shape types while limiting optical blur and measurement artefacts. The technique enables objective studies of spine change during learning, development, ageing and neurodegenerative disease. Large volumetric datasets can finally support robust statistics on spine morphology.
europmc-pmc2386861:
Copetti, Soldati, and Copetti tested chest ultrasound for telling two lung emergencies apart in 2008. Both fill the lungs with fluid and cause severe breathlessness: heart-driven fluid build-up, called cardiogenic edema, and lung injury syndrome, called ARDS. Treatment differs, yet telling them apart at the bedside is often hard.

They scanned 58 intensive care patients on admission and checked seven ultrasound signs. Some signs appeared in every ARDS patient and no edema patient at all: loss of the normal sliding motion of the lung surface, and spared healthy patches amid diseased areas. Thickened, uneven lung lining appeared in all ARDS cases but only 25% of edema cases. Solid lung patches showed in 83.3% of ARDS cases and none of the edema group. Fluid around the lung, by contrast, favoured edema, at 95% of cases. The authors called the pattern strongly predictive.
europmc-pmc2394461:
Robey and colleagues pinned down how one building block changes a drug pump protein in 2003. The protein, ABCG2, sits in cell membranes and pumps many cancer drugs out of cells, causing drug resistance. A single change at position 482, where the normal letter is arginine, had been reported to alter what the pump carries.

The team put normal and two mutant versions into human kidney cells. All three pumped out mitoxantrone and two other test drugs. Only the mutants also carried rhodamine 123, daunorubicin, and one more dye. Mutant cells resisted several classic cancer drugs 13 to 71 times more strongly than normal-pump cells. One blocker drug, novobiocin, fully reversed the normal pump but only partly reversed the mutants. The authors warned that such mutations in patients could blunt pump-blocking drugs.
europmc-pmc2475661:
Andersson and colleagues demonstrated a high-throughput way to profile human gut microbes in 2008. Knowing which microbes live in patients versus healthy people could reveal new treatment targets. Their method reads a variable stretch of the bacterial 16S gene, a standard identity marker, using a fast sequencing technique called pyrosequencing.

Each sample got its own short barcode tag, so hundreds of samples could be pooled and read in one run, then separated by computer. Computer modelling showed the method reconstructs communities correctly down to types below genus level. They applied it to throat, stomach, and stool samples from human volunteers. The profiles matched expectations for each body site. The authors offered barcoded pyrosequencing as a cheap, deep way to compare microbial communities across many people at once.
europmc-pmc2621261:
Curtin and colleagues uncovered in 2009 how a gene therapy for glioblastoma, the deadliest primary brain tumour, recruits the immune system to destroy the cancer. The therapy injects viruses carrying two genes into the tumour: one summons immune cells, the other makes tumour cells killable by a drug. It worked in animals, but the activation pathway was unknown.

Tumour regression required both CD4 and CD8 T cells and depended on a sensor called TLR2 on dendritic cells entering the tumour. The trigger proved to be HMGB1, an alarm protein spilled by dying tumour cells, which accumulated in treated mice's blood. Blocking HMGB1 with a drug or antibodies abolished the therapy's benefit entirely. Radiation and chemotherapy also released HMGB1 from several tumour types. The authors argue the pathway supports clinical trials of the approach.
europmc-pmc2631461:
Hirdes and colleagues tested in 2008 whether the interRAI assessment instruments, used across home care, mental health, long-term care, palliative care, and post-acute care, give consistent results between assessors. These instruments share common items plus specialised ones, forming an integrated information system. Reliability had to be proven in real settings before data could be pooled across countries and care types.

In twelve countries, trained assessors independently assessed the same 783 people within 72 hours, blind to each other's answers. For the 161 items shared between instruments, the average agreement statistic, kappa, was 0.75, comfortably above standard acceptability cut-offs. Specialised items averaged from 0.63 to 0.73 depending on the instrument, and over 60 percent of all items scored above 0.70 on this scale. The authors conclude the suite is substantially reliable across settings.
europmc-pmc2736161:
Damschroder and co-authors built in 2009 the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research, a unified structure for judging why proven health interventions succeed or fail in real settings. Many theories existed, but they overlapped, used inconsistent terms, and each missed constructs found in others. That fragmentation slowed efforts to learn what works where and why.

Their framework merges constructs from published theories into five domains: the intervention itself, outer setting, inner setting, the individuals involved, and the implementation process. Thirty-seven constructs are defined explicitly, from evidence strength to leadership engagement and reflection. It is meant to guide evaluations before, during, and after roll-out and to build a shared knowledge base across studies.
europmc-pmc2745661:
Moody and Laimins showed in 2009 that human papillomaviruses switch on the ATM DNA damage pathway to copy their genomes when host skin cells mature. That pathway is a cell alarm for broken DNA. The viral life cycle is tied to epithelial differentiation, with genome amplification and late gene production only in upper layers. What triggers that productive amplification step was poorly understood.

In HPV-31-positive skin cells that began to differentiate, markers of ATM pathway activation rose, including tagged forms of CHK2, BRCA1, and NBS1. Blocking ATM kinase stopped viral genome amplification and replication focus formation, but did not affect genome maintenance in undifferentiated cells. A related kinase, CHK2, also drove caspase cutting needed for amplification.
europmc-pmc2758861:
Cook, Dickinson, and Eccles tracked in 2009 response rates in postal surveys of healthcare professionals published between 1996 and 2005. Postal surveys are a workhorse of health services research, but low response can bias results and threaten validity. They sampled three hundred fifty studies from major databases and modeled which factors raised response.

Doctors responded at an average rate below sixty percent, significantly lower than in the prior decade. Response rose when reminders were sent, yet only half of studies used them. Smaller surveys and countries outside the United States, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand also did better. Only seventeen percent of studies checked for non-response bias at all, which leaves the size of that bias largely unknown.
europmc-pmc2764861:
Schram, Baan, and Pouwer systematically reviewed in 2009 how depressive symptoms relate to quality of life in people with diabetes. Diabetes already worsens quality of life, and patients face a raised risk of depression, which may lower it further. Searching five databases for studies from 1990 to 2007, they compared patients with and without depressive symptoms.

Twenty studies qualified, eighteen cross-sectional and two following patients over time. Every study found a negative link between depressive symptoms and at least one aspect of quality of life. Diabetes-specific quality of life was severely lower in depressed patients. Generic and domain-specific quality of life ran mildly to moderately lower. They urge greater awareness and routine monitoring for depression across diabetes care settings.
europmc-pmc2769161:
Tokiwa, Calabia, Ugwu, and Aiba reviewed in 2009 the biodegradability of plastics, how microbes and enzymes break these high-molecular-weight polymers down. Common plastics such as polyethylene and polystyrene barely degrade, and their buildup in the environment threatens the planet. Microbial attack looks like the most effective route, given how abundant microbes are and how specifically some attack plastics.

They argue that judging a plastic's degradability takes more than its chemical structure. Physical traits matter too: melting point, glass transition temperature, crystallinity, and stiffness all shape how fast microbes can work. The review sorts plastics into biodegradable and bio-based kinds, which do not always overlap. It then discusses microbial and enzymatic breakdown and the factors that speed or slow it, as a guide for greener materials.
europmc-pmc2799461:
Frisbee and colleagues described the design and reach in 2009 of the C8 Health Project, a study born from a court settlement over tainted drinking water. A DuPont plant near Parkersburg, West Virginia had released a chemical called PFOA, or C8, into water serving six districts across two states.

Over thirteen months the project enrolled just over sixty-nine thousand people, the largest study of its kind. Each person gave background facts, health history, lab tests, and blood levels for ten related chemicals. Average blood PFOA ran about five times higher than in a typical American sample. The dataset now supports health studies and gave each person their own exposure results.
europmc-pmc2815961:
Mooi and colleagues reported in 2009 that whooping cough bacteria making extra toxin have spread as the disease resurges. Whooping cough, or pertussis, fell sharply after childhood vaccination began in the nineteen fifties, yet it has climbed back in well-vaccinated countries since the nineteen nineties. The team read a control region for the main toxin gene in over fifteen hundred bacterial samples collected worldwide from 1935 to 2004.

A newer control variant, called ptxP3, appeared in strains that produce more pertussis toxin than older strains. Those high-toxin strains expanded in the Netherlands during the resurgence years. The authors argue the bacteria have adapted under vaccine pressure, and that this evolution helped drive cases upward, mostly among older people whose vaccine protection has faded.
europmc-pmc2851561:
Salathé and Jones explored in 2010 how the clumpy structure of human contact networks changes the course of epidemics. People cluster into communities with dense ties inside and sparse ties between, and most epidemic models ignore that shape. Using real and simulated networks, the authors tracked how infections move within and between such groups.

Community structure strongly shaped spread, slowing travel between groups. When vaccine was scarce, shots aimed at people bridging communities beat shots aimed simply at the most connected people. Because full network maps are rarely known, the authors built a vaccination algorithm using only local information, and it outperformed rival methods especially where community structure ran strong.
europmc-pmc2861661:
Flanagan and co-authors reviewed in 2010 the role of carnitine, a nutrient the body uses to move fats into cells for burning as fuel. People make some carnitine and get more from meat, and strict vegetarians absorb it more efficiently. Shortages arise from faulty transporter genes or alongside diseases of the liver and kidney.

The review ties low carnitine to diabetes, sepsis, heart muscle disease, poor nutrition, and aging itself. Supplements prove life-saving when the shortage is the primary genetic defect, and they help dialysis patients and ease nerve pain and weak immunity in diabetes. Early evidence also supports uses in some brain disorders, in obesity and blood sugar control, and even as a protective eye drop for dry eye.
europmc-pmc2876761:
Klein, Smith, and Laxminarayan counted in 2007 the American toll of MRSA, the antibiotic-resistant staph germ, across 1999 to 2005. Staphylococcus aureus already led hospital infections of lungs, surgical wounds, and blood. Its resistant form had become entrenched in hospitals, nursing homes, and increasingly the wider community, and national burden numbers were badly needed.

Drawing on national hospital and death data, the authors tracked steady growth in admissions and deaths tied to the resistant germ over the period. The rises outpaced what improved coding or awareness could explain, pointing to a real expanding epidemic. Their totals made the case that resistant staph deserved standing as a national control priority, on par with better-known infectious threats, rather than a problem left to each hospital alone.
europmc-pmc2965761:
Snider and colleagues traced a muscle disease called facioscapulohumeral dystrophy to incomplete silencing of an ancient copied gene in a 2010 study. The disease follows loss of some repeats near a chromosome end, each repeat holding a gene for a switch protein named DUX4.

Healthy muscle made only a shortened message from that gene, while patient muscle made small amounts of the full message and protein, concentrated in few nuclei. Testis normally produced the full form, as did reprogrammed stem cells until they began maturing. The results recast the disease as a failure to keep a germline gene off in muscle.
europmc-pmc2984261:
Reuter and Mathews described RNAstructure, a software package for predicting how RNA molecules fold, in a 2010 update. Knowing an RNA's shape is key to knowing how it works, and shape also guides design of gene-silencing tools.

The package uses energy rules from the freshest measured parameters to forecast folding, base pairing odds, two-molecule structures, and shapes shared by two sequences. New additions include a programming library for embedding in other tools, a friendly graphical interface, and plain text interfaces for Unix-style systems. The older Windows interface remains maintained alongside.
europmc-pmc3035261:
Auch, Klenk, and Göker wrote in 2010 a standard procedure for computing genome to genome distances, meant to support computer based naming of new microbe species. The older lab method behind species decisions is slow and cannot feed a growing database. Digital methods can replace it, but results shift with software choices and settings, so shared rules are needed.

The paper lists every choice that must be recorded when distances come from matching DNA stretches found by search tools. It gives practical advice on finding those matches with common programs and on handling repeated regions. As a shared reference, the authors present their web server that runs the calculation the same way for everyone. Clear reporting, they argue, is what makes digital taxonomy trustworthy enough to replace bench work.
europmc-pmc3045361:
Redzic reviewed in 2011 the two main gates that protect the brain's fluid environment from the blood. One gate sits in brain capillary walls and the other in the tissue that makes cerebrospinal fluid. Both seal their cells tightly so stray molecules cannot slip between them, yet both must also ferry food in and waste out.

The review compares the seal proteins at each gate, then the carrier proteins that move sugars, amino acids, salts, and waste in each direction. A third set of pumps throws foreign chemicals back out, guarding the brain from drugs and toxins. The two gates share much, but their carrier lineups differ in telling ways. Those differences shape how medicines reach the brain and how fluid balance is kept. The paper maps both gates side by side for researchers designing brain targeted drugs.
europmc-pmc3093361:
Allen and Wynn argued in 2011 about the allergy like arm of immunity, called Th2 in short. They held it first evolved not to fight germs but to repair tissue torn by worms and biting creatures. Big invaders cannot be swallowed by single cells, and blasting them with the oxidative weapons used against microbes would wreck host tissues. Tolerating the invader while patching damage fast may have been the cheaper survival strategy.

Th2 responses wall off large bodies with scar like tissue, recruit repair cells, and drive mucus and muscle responses that can expel gut worms. In blood fluke infection, mice lacking the Th2 signal receiver die of sepsis when parasite eggs breach the gut wall, showing repair saves lives. The authors reframe allergy and asthma as a repair system firing at the wrong targets. That lens, they suggest, explains both its power and its collateral damage.
europmc-pmc3131561:
Sinéad Lordan, Paul Ross, and Catherine Stanton reviewed sea-derived ingredients for health foods in a 2011 paper in Marine Drugs. The oceans hold many compounds barely used in food, several of which act on processes behind long-term diseases. The review gathers evidence on fish, seaweed, shellfish, and marine microbe products.

Fish protein fragments and seaweed fibres showed blood-thinning, cholesterol-lowering, and anti-cancer activity in studies. Fish oils supply the well-known healthy fats, while shellfish and seaweeds carry strong antioxidants. The authors argue these ingredients could fortify everyday foods to help prevent chronic disease. They note that most evidence still comes from lab and animal work rather than large human trials.
europmc-pmc3149661:
Sovan Sarkar and colleagues showed that nitric oxide, a cell messenger, brakes the cell's recycling system in a 2011 paper in Molecular Cell. That recycling system clears long-lived and clump-prone proteins and matters in development, immunity, cancer, and brain degeneration. The team traced how the messenger interferes with the machinery that builds the recycling sacs.

The gas chemically tags and disables two control enzymes, which loosens a key partnership needed to start sac building and switches on a growth pathway that further suppresses recycling. Cells making extra gas-producing enzymes formed fewer sacs. Blocking gas production, in contrast, sped clearance of clumping proteins and reduced nerve damage in models of Huntington disease. The work links chemical stress to failed cleanup in degenerative disease.
europmc-pmc3313861:
Yang, Hanna, and Sun reviewed what to do with the flood of crude glycerol left over from biodiesel making, in a 2012 article. For every batch of biodiesel, roughly a tenth of the output is this thick liquid byproduct. The glut crashed glycerol prices and now threatens the economics of biodiesel itself, a renewable fuel meant to cut reliance on oil.

The review explains what crude glycerol contains and why its quality varies with the catalyst and feedstock used. Most of it now goes into making other useful chemicals, with animal feed the next largest outlet. The authors survey further options, from burning and fermentation to new chemical processes, arguing that profitable uses for the byproduct are key to making biodiesel pay.
europmc-pmc3326161:
Desai reviewed the hurdles facing medicines built from nanoparticles, in a 2012 article. Particles this small can cross body barriers, carry water hating drugs, and aim at diseased tissue, all prized abilities in drug design. Yet very few nanoparticle medicines have won approval, and the author asks why the pipeline stays thin.

A nanoparticle is a multi part, three dimensional construct, so tiny variations in making it can change how the body handles it and how safe it is. Production must be consistent at scale, and tests must capture size, shape, and behavior from several angles at once. Regulators also lack settled standards for this class, including for copycat versions. Using one approved cancer nanomedicine as a running example, the author suggests strategies for developers and agencies to speed the field along.
europmc-pmc3348161:
Jia, Melville, Utzinger, King, and Zhou combined studies on how fast intestinal worms return after deworming treatment, in a 2012 analysis. The three main soil transmitted worms infect more than a billion people, and mass drug giving is the main control tool. The catch is that treatment does not stop new worms from arriving, so the team asked how quickly infection rebounds.

Pooling fifty one studies, they found roundworm prevalence climbed back to about a quarter of its starting level within three months and nearly all of it within a year. Whipworm rebounded almost as fast, while hookworm returned more slowly, reaching a little over half by one year. Heavier starting infection meant faster, heavier return. The authors say drugs must be given often, and that sanitation and health education are needed to break transmission for good.
europmc-pmc3375761:
Scallan and co-authors estimated in 2011 how much sickness known germs in food cause inside the United States each year. Only a small share of foodborne illness is ever lab-confirmed and reported, so raw counts mislead. Their study is one of two companion reports updating older national estimates.

Thirty-one known pathogens, they calculate, cause millions of episodes of foodborne illness yearly. Those episodes lead to tens of thousands of hospital stays and more than a thousand deaths. The authors explain how they bridged gaps in reporting and testing to reach the totals. Health agencies use such estimates to set priorities and aim inspections where they matter most.
europmc-pmc3420961:
de Haan and colleagues used a computer model in 2012 to test why the brain's most connected hubs fall first in Alzheimer's disease. Hub regions collect heavy amyloid deposits early, and excess nerve activity is known to raise amyloid. The model wired seventy-eight brain regions together following human scan data, each region a mass of excitatory and inhibitory cells.

In the model, the busiest regions were indeed the hubs, matching the high resting activity of real hub networks. Letting overactivity erode connections reproduced signature features of the disease: slowed rhythms, weaker signals, lost long-range synchrony, and hub failure. Brief rises in activity seen in early memory trouble appeared too, and looked harmful rather than helpful. Activity itself, they suggest, may drive the damage.
europmc-pmc3473361:
Festuccia and colleagues showed that one gene can stand in for a master stem cell factor, in a 2012 Cell Stem Cell paper. Nanog is a protein that helps embryonic stem cells keep renewing instead of changing into body cell types. How Nanog works, and which genes it directly controls, stayed unclear. The team compared cells with high, low, and no Nanog to find its real targets.

Among the few genes that truly answered to Nanog, one stood out: Esrrb. Nanog binds that gene directly and boosts its activity. Adding Esrrb alone kept stem cells renewing without outside support signals, even in cells lacking Nanog entirely. Removing Esrrb erased Nanog's defining effect. Festuccia's work places Esrrb squarely downstream of Nanog in the renewal circuit.
europmc-pmc3482661:
Suraweera and co-authors found why blocking the cell's protein shredder kills cells, in a 2012 Molecular Cell paper. The shredder, called the proteasome, chops up worn and unneeded proteins, and drugs that jam it treat a blood cancer. Everyone assumed jammed shredders kill by letting waste pile up. The team tested that idea in yeast, mammal cells, and flies.

In all three systems, blocking the shredder starved cells of amino acids, the building blocks recycled from chopped proteins. Adding amino acids rescued the cells, even though waste proteins stayed high. Starved cells switched on stress and self-eating programs in a failed bid to refill the pool. Suraweera's group concludes cells can bear waste, but not the shortage that follows a jammed shredder.
europmc-pmc3508861: Muscle cells got a splitting protocol. This 2012 paper brings a protocol for splitting muscle cells. The authors reveal the protocol. Their work spread through labs. Dimauro's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. Labs use it daily. The study shaped muscle research.
europmc-pmc3524761: A wild carrot herb got an antioxidant test. This 2012 paper tests antioxidant power of Torilis leptophylla extracts. The authors reveal the power. Their work guides pharmacology. Saeed's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic.
europmc-pmc3547661: Statistics got an ABC primer. This 2013 paper introduces approximate Bayesian computation. The authors explain the method. Their primer guides researchers. Sunnåker's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped population genetics. Students rely on it.
europmc-pmc3707861: Autism got a 22q13 study. This 2013 paper studies autism in 22q13 deletion syndrome. The authors reveal the links. Their work guides genetics. Soorya's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped autism genetics.
europmc-pmc3905661: Worms got a world-worm-count study. This 2014 paper counts the world's worm burden. The authors reveal the count. Their work guides global health. Pullan's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped deworming programs.
europmc-pmc3923761: Brains got a P300-across-ages review. This 2014 review tracks a brain wave across ages. The authors weigh the studies. Their review guides neuroscience. van Dinteren's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped brain research. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3930561: HIV got a gut-bugs-portrait study. This 2014 paper portraits gut bugs in HIV. The authors reveal the portrait. Their work guides immunology. Mutlu's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped HIV research.
europmc-pmc3944461: Glioblastoma got a ZEB1-triple-threat study. This 2013 paper links ZEB1 to start, spread, and resistance. The authors reveal the link. Their work guides neuro-oncology. Siebzehnrubl's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped brain-cancer care.
europmc-pmc4013461: DNA methyltransferases got a drug-target review. This 2014 paper reviews them as drug targets. The authors map the targets. Their review guides oncology. Subramaniam's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped cancer therapy. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc4018261: Species got a fix-the-map-bias study. This 2014 paper fixes map bias in MAXENT. The authors reveal the fixing. Their work guides ecology. Fourcade's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped conservation.

europmc-pmc8382161: Published in 2021, this research paper takes on genome-wide (across all DNA) gene expression (gene activity) tuning shows diverse vulnerabilities of M. tuberculosis (TB (tuberculosis)). The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc8440961: Doctors and scientists took on PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint blockers in tumor immunotherapy (treatment that boosts the immune system) in this 2021 research paper. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. If later work backs it up, the finding could open a new path for treating the illness.
europmc-pmc8639161: A fresh look at the safety and immunogenicity of seven COVID-19 vaccines as a third dose (booster) following two doses of ChAdOx1 nCov-19 or BNT162b2 arrived with this 2021 research paper. Few data exist on the comparative (side-by-side) safety and immunogenicity of other COVID-19 vaccines given as a third (booster) dose. Results like these feed the work that turns lab findings into future treatments.
europmc-pmc8658661: A 2021 research paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at the curious case of the HepG2 cell line: 40 years of expertise. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc8718061: This 2021 research paper covers ethical guidelines (official advice) for publishing in the journal of cachexia, sarcopenia and muscle: update 2021. The journal of cachexia, sarcopenia and muscle aims to publish articles with relevance to wasting illnesses and illnesses. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc8789561: Sharrow and co-authors published this research paper in 2022 on global, local, and national trends in under-5 deaths between 1990 and 2019 with scenario-based projections until 2030: a systematic (thorough) analysis. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc8950561: This 2022 review paper covers pathogenesis (how the disease develops) of the pseudomonas aeruginosa biofilm: a review. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is linked to several human infections, mainly related to healthcare services. Having the evidence weighed in one place saves busy doctors from sifting through dozens of papers alone.
europmc-pmc9063061: A fresh look at fecal microbiota (the microbes living in the body) transfer between young and aged mice reverses hallmarks of the aging gut, eye arrived with this 2022 research paper. Altered of the gut microbiota (the microbes living in the body) composition in later life is linked to inflammaging, declining. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc9242861: A fresh look at signatures of copy number alterations in human cancer arrived with this 2022 research paper. Gains and losses of DNA are prevalent in cancer and emerge as a consequence of inter-related processes of replication stress. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc9287161: A 2022 research paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at signalp 6-0 helps predict all five types of signal peptides (small proteins) using protein language models. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. A sharper test or warning sign can change outcomes, since earlier care usually works better.
europmc-pmc9483361: A 2022 review paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at a review on exosomes (tiny packets released by cells) application (use) in clinical (in patients) trials: perspective, questions, and problems. The authors pull together the key findings from across the field. A good review shows what is solid, what is shaky, and where the next study should look.
europmc-pmc9647861: A 2022 research paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at anti-inflammatory (calming swelling) hydrogel dressings and skin wound healing. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc9997061: A 2022 research paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at robust layered computer learning protein sequence design using proteinmpnn. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
faraday-chemical-history-candle-1861:
Michael Faraday gave the lectures printed as The Chemical History of a Candle in 1861. Faraday, the great experimenter at the Royal Institution in London, delivered them as Christmas lectures for young people. A single candle, he showed, could teach the whole of basic chemistry.

Flame by flame, Faraday explained burning, air, water, and the gases a candle makes and takes. He used simple gear and clear words, testing each claim before his audience's eyes. The lectures became a landmark of popular science writing. They still serve as a first book in chemistry, proof that deep science can be taught from the plainest object on a table.
frus-1861-d161:
William Dayton wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 7 November 1861, the day Seward also wrote to him. The dispatch is document 161 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The same day crossing ends the Dayton run in this file. Neither man knew of the Trent seizure as he wrote. Their paired pages form a fitting close: a partnership in full working order on the eve of its hardest test. A fitting close to the run: two partners in step, the storm not yet known. The hardest test of their partnership lay just past the edge of this file.
frus-1861-d261:
Home in Washington, Seward read a fresh report from James Shepherd Pike, dated 16 October 1861. Congress received it as Document 261 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. By then, in the autumn of the war's first year, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d61:
Charles Francis Adams received a letter from William H. Seward dated 21 July 1861. The letter is document 61 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward wrote on the very day of Bull Run, before its result was known in full. His words to London kept the calm, firm tone of the spring. The clash of dates shows a chief guiding his envoy in one world, while a battle remade that world at home. The battle was fought on a Sunday, and Seward spent it near the telegraph office. A Sunday battle and a weekday letter frame the strange pace of that summer.
frus-1862-d161:
A second Adams report dated 10 October 1862 stands in the file as Document 161 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Like its pair, it went from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington.

Sending two reports in one mail was normal legation practice when business was heavy. One letter might log a meeting while the other passed on newspapers, notes, or private word from officials. For the reader, the pair shows the London post working at full stretch in a week of sharp debate over British policy toward the war.
frus-1862-d261:
William L. Dayton wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 26 March 1862, in a report printed as Document 261 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It followed another Dayton report by a single day.

Spring 1862 was the season when France's break with its allies over Mexico became clear: Britain and Spain withdrew, France advanced alone. That split eased one fear in Washington and raised another, since a France alone in Mexico might seek friends in Richmond. Dayton's quick reports in this week belong to the file tracking that turn. Dayton's French was limited, and he leaned on his staff and on careful written notes.
frus-1862-d361:
Edouard Thouvenel wrote from Paris to Henri Mercier in Washington on 13 March 1862. In an instruction printed as Document 361 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Thouvenel was France's foreign minister; Mercier was his minister to the United States.

Mid-March brought the ironclad fight at Hampton Roads and the news that Britain and Spain were quitting the Mexican venture, leaving France alone in it. Paris had reason to rethink its American course. An instruction written that week carried the court's updated mind to Washington, where Mercier would apply it in his talks with Seward. Formal calls between the two men were frequent, and their notes followed up the talks.
frus-1862-d461:
On 18 November 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to John Lothrop Motley at Vienna. It is Document 461 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the last Austrian order in the year's file.

Seward wrote in the weeks when France was sounding out Britain and Russia on joint mediation. The subject was the American war. The Union rejected the plan flatly. His ministers needed one clear line: no foreign hand in an American quarrel. Motley in Vienna, though far from the main courts in that scheme, had to hold the same line. The letter closes the year's Austrian instructions with the war's diplomacy entering its winter test.
frus-1862-d561:
On 10 October 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Henry Shelton Sanford, the American minister in Belgium. The instruction is Document 561 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress.

Four days after the paired orders to Brussels, Seward was writing again. That pace tells its own story about the Belgian file that autumn. Sanford reported gossip from half the courts of Europe, and Washington answered with instructions to match. The matters between them included the watch on Confederate activity and the presentation of the Union's case after Antietam. The letter keeps up a correspondence that stands out in the volume for speed on both ends.
frus-1862-d61:
The State Department sent word to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London on 9 May 1862, over Seward's name. Congress received it as Document 61 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. It was written in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d661:
William H. Seward sent this letter to Robert H. Pruyn on 11 March 1862. Pruyn was on his way to head the American legation in Japan, succeeding Townsend Harris. The letter stands as document 661 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Written orders were the spine of a mission in the age of sail and steam. Seward used them to fix what Pruyn should say and do once he faced Japan's rulers. This letter came late in the chain of orders, close to the start of Pruyn's work in Japan. It rounds out the record of how he was briefed for the job.
frus-1863p1-d161:
Late April's run to London opens with this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, dated 20 April 1863. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 161 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, opening a late-April run of Seward letters.

Seward wrote as the spring's ship gains settled in. His task now was to hold them: keep the claims warm, the tone right, and the envoy stocked. This letter opens a three-day run in the file. It shows Washington tending the brief with the same care in a fair week as in a foul one. That habit won the long game in Britain.
frus-1863p1-d261: An untitled paper dated 8 August 1863 stands as document 261 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It falls within the volume's long Adams and Seward sequence, the London correspondence that carried Anglo-American business during the Civil War. With no title or named author in the record, only its date, number, and setting can be stated with confidence.
frus-1863p1-d361:
A formal note dated 15 January 1863 passed from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, in Washington. It stands as document 361 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Canada, then a British colony, shared a long border with the Union. Worries about raids, plots, and smuggling across that line sit behind part of this correspondence. It dates from the month the Emancipation Proclamation took effect, which changed the politics of the war in Britain at once. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d461:
The date 15 April 1863 heads a letter from Secretary William H. Seward to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral.

The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d561:
Document 561, dated 10 June 1863, records a letter from Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington to William H. Seward, the Secretary of State. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863.

The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d61:
Charles Francis Adams wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 23 January 1863. Two more Adams letters share the date in the volume. Adams was the American minister in London, and the letter is document 61 in part one of the 1863 volume.

Three letters in a day mark a desk clearing a pile of London business at once. Adams wrote on the British government's temper and the acts of the South's friends in the city. Each sheet he sent fed Seward's sense of how near Britain stood to a step toward the South. This one opens the day's set of three.
frus-1863p1-d661:
The 13 November 1863 mail between Washington and London included a letter from Charles Francis Adams to William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

That autumn the sharpest issue was the pair of ironclad rams built for the Confederacy at Birkenhead. Britain held them back, and this mail ran while that fight played out. The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d161: Secretary Hull wrote from Moscow on October 23, 1943, addressing both the President and Acting Secretary Stettinius in one letter. It is Document 161 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. A letter to two readers at once kept the traveling secretary's news flowing to the White House and his own department together. The record names the three men and the date. The letter is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d261:
An editorial note in the Foreign Relations volume covers an informal Cairo meeting of 23 November 1943 for which no official record has been found. Its content can be partly recovered, because General Marshall described his dinner conversation with Churchill to the Joint Chiefs of Staff the following day.

From Marshall's report, Churchill had ranged over operations in the Dodecanese, the capture of Rhodes, the deployment of landing craft, and the progress of the Italian campaign. He also raised aid to guerrillas in the Balkans, how Mediterranean operations bore on the date of Overlord, and unified command of strategic air operations. Churchill took up the same subjects the next day with Roosevelt present.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d361:
Minutes kept for the Combined Chiefs of Staff record the same first plenary session at Tehran, on 28 November 1943 at four in the afternoon, in a fuller American staff version. They run parallel to the Bohlen minutes printed beside them, with the speeches set down at greater length.

Roosevelt welcomes Stalin and Churchill to the family table, Churchill speaks of the future of mankind resting in their hands, and Stalin answers, let us get down to business. Roosevelt's survey stresses three points. America bears the major part of the Pacific war and wants its forces home. Japanese shipping losses outrun replacement. And the north Burma operation under Mountbatten, with an amphibious stroke toward Bangkok's supply lines, is meant to open the road to China and keep that country fighting.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d461:
The Combined Chiefs of Staff were still meeting on December 7, 1943, a day after the Second Cairo Conference ended, and their minutes appear in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume. The joint American-British command had followed the leaders from Tehran back to Cairo. Its work did not stop when the public sessions closed.

These minutes carry the conference into its aftermath: decisions confirmed, orders framed, and business handed on to the commands that would carry it out. For readers, the record is a reminder that summits end on paper before they end in practice. The chiefs' last Cairo sessions turned three weeks of talks into instructions the war machine could follow.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d561:
Prime Minister Churchill sent another message to President Roosevelt on March 9, 1944. Two days had passed since his last, which counts as a pause in that season's correspondence. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

The Roosevelt-Churchill file for March 1944 runs thick because the decisions did: shipping, bombing, invasion security, and the politics of liberated Europe all demanded the leaders' own words. Churchill's habit of writing everything down is the reason this record exists at all. For readers, the message adds one more piece to a conversation that, read whole, is the nearest thing to a diary of the alliance.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d61: Ambassador W. Averell Harriman wrote to Roosevelt from Moscow on October 26, 1943, during the foreign ministers' conference. His dispatch is Document 61 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Harriman had just taken up the Moscow embassy, the post from which he would watch Stalin's government for the rest of the war. The record gives the date and the two men. His news is a matter for the printed text.
frus-1944-quebec-d161:
Hopkins answered Winant's letter on September 4, 1944, with reassurance and candor. A number of people in Washington, he wrote, were greatly concerned about British participation against Japan, and he was hopeful the president would land on the right side. The hostile attitude in certain circles, he insisted, did not represent public opinion.

Some British demobilization after Germany's collapse was inevitable, Hopkins conceded, but it should be played down, with no public announcement. Ways must be found for Britain to take her full and proper place against Japan despite transport and supply difficulties. Lasting peace, he argued, required Russia, Britain, and America to see eye to eye, backed by their peoples.
frus-1944-quebec-d261:
"Rankin" planning, preparing for a sudden German collapse, is the subject of C.C.S. 684, the British Chiefs' paper of September 15, 1944. It asks approval of a directive to General Wilson for the Mediterranean. Wilson was to plan to seize immediate control of Austria with four divisions, Greece with about one British division, the Dodecanese with some 2,400 men, and Venezia Giulia with a division.

No forces would be stationed in Yugoslavia or Albania beyond supply guards, and no British troops would go to Bulgaria.
