British naval help on the Danube, including mine clearance, required prior agreement with the Russians. The force calculations exclude American troops, who would withdraw, and the four Indian divisions, who would not be used for Rankin duties.
frus-1944-quebec-d61:
H. H. Kung, China's minister of finance, addressed this letter to President Roosevelt on September 8, 1944. Kung was China's chief financial official and a brother-in-law of Chiang Kai-shek. The letter appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

China's finances were collapsing under inflation that autumn, and Kung's appeals to Washington sought the aid that might hold his government together. A finance minister writing directly to the President shows the depth of China's need and the personal nature of wartime aid. For readers, the letter brings the fourth ally's distress into a volume dominated by the two Western leaders.
frus-1945-50-intel-d161:
The title "Central Intelligence Group Directive No. 14" heads a text dated 19 July 1946. It survives in print as document 161 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. The first peace-time setup paired the National Intelligence Authority at the top with the Central Intelligence Group below it.

Orders of this kind turned broad policy into daily rules. They name the office in charge and the work to be done. The shelf of such orders, read in order, is the true org chart of the system as it grew. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d261:
A memorandum dated 11 March 1948 links two senior offices. The sender was the Chief of the Special Procedures Group(Cassady). The reader was the Deputy Chief of the Special Procedures Group (Dulin). It is document 261 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. Across Washington, the new security bodies were moving from setup work to the real business of the Cold War.

A short memo could set a meeting, kill a plan, or start one. This one played its part in that daily traffic. That plainness lets a reader see how an issue moved from a working office up to the men who decided it. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d361:
A letter from Robert Blum of the Office of the Secretary of Defense reached Allen W. Dulles on 7 February 1949. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 361 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. The Council had sent in an outside team to grade the CIA, and the whole town knew a blunt report was coming.

Writers chose a letter when they wanted a stance to count. The text gives the sender's side in full. Many of the big fights of these years can be followed letter by letter. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d61:
Minutes dated 26 December 1945 record a meeting held in the quiet week between Christmas and the new year. The intelligence question did not rest for the holiday. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Late December meetings in Washington are usually small and pointed: the men who attend are the ones who must finish the work. These minutes belong to the final clearing of ground before the January directive. Readers can use them to date the moment when argument gave way to drafting. The volume's long autumn of rival plans ends in this season. The papers of the new year open with a president's signature instead of another committee's view.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d161:
Roosevelt passed Stalin's New Year answer on Poland to Churchill on 4 January 1945. His telegram quotes the Soviet reply in full for the prime minister's information. The exchange is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations.

Stalin writes that he is extremely sorry he failed to convince the President of the Soviet position's correctness. Events, he hopes, will prove that the Polish National Committee has given the allies real help against Hitler's Germany. The London émigré government, by contrast, spreads disorganization and so aids the Germans. As for delay, Stalin pleads one hard fact. On 27 December the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet already told the Poles it intends to recognize their provisional government.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d261:
The Kurile Islands get a full territorial study in this paper of 28 December 1944. Written by the Division of Territorial Studies, it is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Its problem is stated in one line: the future disposition of the Kurile Islands.

The chain runs some 690 miles from Hokkaido to Kamchatka: forty-seven volcanic islands, thinly peopled. About 17,550 permanent residents, all Japanese, swell by tens of thousands of seasonal fishing hands in summer. Fish give the islands nearly all their economic worth. Their history is a see-saw: Russia yielded the whole chain to Japan in 1875, in exchange for Japan's withdrawal from southern Sakhalin. The paper weighs the islands' strategic value to Japan, Russia, and the United States alike.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d361:
Ships for freed Russians are the subject of a memorandum from Admiral Emory Land, the War Shipping Administrator, to Secretary Stettinius on February 5, 1945. Land reported that the American chiefs had agreed to use troopships for repatriation. The lift would match British help: 10,000 men a month across the Atlantic.

The deal held only while overland routes stayed closed. Once Germany fell, redeployment would need every troopship. Land added that Eisenhower had asked for two large troopships to move Russians gathered at Marseille. The memo turns Eden's prisoner diplomacy into tonnage, ports, and sailing dates.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d461:
Churchill edited like a proofreader, and this list of his changes to the draft communiqué, dated February 11, 1945, preserves his pencil at work. In the part on Germany's defeat, one word should become another throughout. Coordination should read as concert, launched should gain the word continuously after it, and joint should give way to combined.

On occupation and control of Germany, jointly becomes together, and coordinated becomes united. The last change is substance, not style. France, the new sentence should say, would be invited by the three powers to take a fourth zone. She would also sit as a fourth member of the Control Commission. The list shows the communiqué's final polish.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d61:
Keeping the Yalta trip secret is the subject of a 20 January 1945 note from Charles Bohlen to Under Secretary of State Joseph Grew. Bohlen, an assistant to the Secretary of State, reports a White House decision on press censorship. The note is printed in the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences.

Two days earlier, Hopkins, Admiral Wilson Brown, and Stephen Early had agreed to invoke the censorship code from 19 January. It barred any speculation about the time, place, or general area of the coming meeting. Staff were also told how to answer questions about absent officials. The only allowed reply was, “He is out of town.”
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d161:
President Truman answered Stalin on recognizing the ex-enemy states in a message sent through Harriman on June 18, 1945. The telegram carrying his words is document 161 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Stalin had proposed restoring diplomatic relations with Romania, Bulgaria, Hungary, and Finland.

Truman fully agrees that recognition would be a constructive step, the message says. But the two governments stand differently toward each state: nothing blocks instant American ties with Finland, while the internal situation in Romania, Hungary, and Bulgaria differs country by country. He is studying the matter further. The practical course, he proposes, is to discuss it at their coming meeting and reach a uniform agreement there. The draft was written in the State Department and approved by the President.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d261:
Naval aide George Elsey filed a one-sentence research note on the great rivers, submitted July 1, 1945. The note is document 261 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Elsey had combed the Map Room files to see what the two presidents' papers held on questions that might arise at Berlin.

His whole finding is negative. There has been no reference to the free use of the Rhine and Danube rivers in Roosevelt's and Truman's messages and papers in the Map Room. The tiny memo still earned its place. Free navigation of the Danube in particular was a live question at Potsdam, pressed by Eisenhower among others. And the President's staff needed to know one thing. No past presidential word committed the United States either way.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d361:
What to do with captured German war material is the problem in a Combined Chiefs of Staff report dated June 28, 1945. The Combined Administrative Committee drafted a reply to a request from the supreme commander in Europe. He had asked authority on two points: filling London Munitions Assignment Board needs from stocks in Germany and Austria, and scrapping surplus enemy gear.

The report notes informal talks at government level. Some nations, it says, wanted enemy war material shared out among the United Nations. Those nations opposed the wide destruction of German equipment. The paper shows that even captured guns became a diplomatic question in the summer of 1945.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d461:
Tito's charges against Greece are answered in MacVeagh's cable from Athens of July 10, 1945. Tito had broadcast on July 8 that Greeks were firing across the border to provoke the Yugoslavs. He claimed thousands of Macedonians and Greeks were being fed in Yugoslavia after escaping terror by Greek reactionaries. Premier Voulgaris called on MacVeagh in alarm.

The Premier planned to fly to Salonika the next day, quietly, to learn the facts himself, then make a temperate factual broadcast on his return. American observers in northern Greece, MacVeagh reports, fail to confirm Tito's statements. Conditions on both sides of the border were disturbed, but the refugee figures struck him as unquestionably fantastic.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d561:
Marshal Tito and Field Marshal Alexander signed an agreed note at Duino on June 20, 1945. It is document 561 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The note covers civil rule in the part of Venezia Giulia placed under Allied military government.

The Yugoslav side would not accept the Allied plan for running the zone. It reserved the right to raise the matter through normal state channels. A Yugoslav note attached argues that the old Italian system should not come back. The zone's own wartime organs should be kept if they work well. It also states that Slovene and Italian tongues are equal, and that Rome's government should have no say in the zone.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d61:
President Truman replied to Ambassador Harriman on June 14 or 15, 1945, with early word on his party for the Berlin conference. The telegram is document 61 in the Foreign Relations volume on Potsdam, answering Harriman's question about what to tell the Russians. It gives a first picture of the American group being put together.

Eisenhower, Truman says, has orders to arrange rooms and meeting space, but has not yet been told who is coming. The President plans to bring his Chiefs of Staff, the Secretary of State with his aides, two or three other high officials, plus servants and Secret Service men. Names and numbers will follow once they are fixed. The message shows the trip still taking shape a month before departure.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d661:
A Soviet demand on Tangier reached Washington on July 2, 1945, and is recorded in document 661 here. The Secretary ad interim, Grew, relayed it to Ambassador Winant in London. Moscow had just learned of the three-power expert talks set for Paris on July 3.

The Soviet ambassador told Grew his government was interested in Tangier. It was surprised its opinion had not been asked and no Soviet expert invited. It asked that the experts' meeting be postponed until a Soviet expert could attend. Grew records the answer he gave in reply. The United States, he pointed out, never signed the 1923 statute and never joined Tangier's administration. Its presence rested on the interest shown by keeping a diplomatic agent there.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1061:
Secretary of State James Byrnes wrote this letter to Molotov at Potsdam on July 19, 1945. It proposes joint Allied supervision of the approaching Greek national elections. Allied duties to Greece, and the pledges made at Yalta, are given as the grounds. Responsibility to the Greek people, Byrnes argues, makes shared supervision wise.

Four governments would share the task: Britain, the Soviet Union, France, and the United States. Greece's own government has agreed to elections under their watch. That consent rests on Article 9 of the Varkiza Agreement, which provides for Allied supervision. Byrnes closes with earnest hope that the Soviet government will agree to join.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1161:
Washington tabled this proposal on 22 July 1945, late in Potsdam's first week. American papers at this stage laid out what the United States wanted from the postwar order. Each one gave the British and Soviet teams a clear stand to answer.

A proposal fixed words that others had to accept, amend, or refuse. That made the drafting itself a form of power. This paper is part of the American opening hand, played once the first speeches were done. Kept word for word in the record, it lets readers judge what Washington sought before the trades began.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1261:
A second Sato cable to Togo bears the date 30 July 1945. The Moscow embassy sent its last July reports in pairs as the crisis thickened. Each tested the Soviet mood one more time and found it unchanged.

By then the pattern was fixed. Moscow gained by waiting, and Tokyo's need grew by the day. Sato's twin reports of 30 July hold that pattern at its end. Within a week the atomic bomb and Soviet entry would end the waiting by force. This cable is part of the record of the days just before, when paper was still Japan's only weapon.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1361:
Henry Villard, chief of the Division of African Affairs, wrote to the acting secretary of state on 27 July 1945. Villard's division handled American ties with Africa inside the State Department. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

Africa rarely tops the Potsdam story, yet the department kept a full division on it, and its chief could write straight to the acting secretary. Questions of colonies, bases, and trade crossed Villard's desk in 1945 as empires began to loosen. This paper brings that corner of the department into the record. It reminds readers that the postwar world was being argued over on every continent, not Europe alone.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-161:
Thompson's minutes close his conference run with a session of August 1, 1945. He had recorded Potsdam meetings since the first week. His sets, printed in the second Potsdam volume, form one of its most complete spines. This last set covers the closing day, when the final protocol was adopted.

Readers who followed Thompson across July meet a familiar, steady hand. The style stays plain to the end. That steadiness is the value: one observer's record, kept the same way throughout. The minutes let the conference be rebuilt day by day. They end where the work ended, with the deal in hand.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-61:
George Allen memoranda'd a foreign ministers' exchange on the Italian colonies, written up on July 24, 1945. It is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. The discussion itself took place at the ministers' meeting of July 22.

Molotov recalled that Moscow had declared at San Francisco its intent to apply as a trustee power. He then turned on a Commons statement by Eden that Italy had lost its colonies in Africa and the Mediterranean. By what right, Molotov asked, had Great Britain decided this question? Who, he demanded, had found the colonies? Eden answered in kind, in a few words. Italy had lost her colonies to the British Army, he said. They sat under British military occupation pending their final disposal in the peace treaty with Italy. Molotov said his delegation had presented a paper on the subject for the next meeting.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d761:
Grew wrote to Byrnes on July 17, 1945, the opening day of the Potsdam Conference. Document 761 is an early letter in the Acting Secretary's channel to the field. Grew held Washington while the leaders met in Germany. His letter joined the second Potsdam volume of the official record.

An opening-day letter sets the home office's tone. Grew could pass first news and steady the travelers' rear. Readers see the partnership between the two men at its start. The document pairs with Byrnes's reply of the same week. Together they frame the link that let the summit function at a distance from its own capital.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d861:
Document 861 is a working paper of the United States delegation dated July 20, 1945. It closes this run of the volume's papers. Staff drafted it at the end of the conference's first week. The paper stayed in the delegation files and was printed in the second Potsdam volume.

A week's-end working paper shows positions after first contact. The drafters had heard the other sides and written again. Readers can use it as a hinge in the run: behind it, preparation; ahead, the hard second week. The document ends this set where the conference itself paused to breathe, with the largest questions still open and the paper still flowing.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d961:
Secretary Byrnes handed this American proposal on German reparations to Molotov on July 30, 1945. He gave it just before the foreign ministers met that day. Russian and Polish claims would be met from the Russian zone. Two additions would come from the Ruhr, in the British zone.

The first addition is a quarter of the surplus factory equipment there. It would be traded for equal value in food, coal, potash, zinc, timber, clay goods, and oil goods from the Soviets. The second addition is a further 15 percent of such equipment. That share would pass to the Soviet government free, with no payment or exchange in return.
frus-1950v07-d161: A 1950 FRUS telegram from the Joint Chiefs to the Korea commander. The Korean War's early months demanded decisions. This document preserves that cable. Tomorrow's readers will find it. It retains its place in time. The archive guards it with care.
frus-1969-76v21-d361: Minutes of a meeting on Chile from the 1969-1976 FRUS volume. The coup's shadow. This entry preserves those minutes. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
galileo-discourse-floating-bodies-salusb:
Galileo Galilei's Discourse on floating bodies, written in 1612, appears here in Thomas Salusbury's 1661 English translation, A Discourse Concerning Bodies in Water. Galileo wrote the work in a dispute at the Medici court over why ice floats. His opponents held Aristotelian views on shape and density.

Galileo argued that floating rests on the weight of the body compared with the water it pushes aside, not on flat shape. Experiments with wax and water backed his account of hydrostatics. Salusbury's translation, printed in London, first brought Galileo's physics to English readers in their own tongue. The short work shows Galileo's style: court debate turned into careful test and proof.
galileo-mathematical-collections-salusbu:
Thomas Salusbury published Mathematical Collections and Translations in 1661 in London, a landmark set of Italian science in English. Salusbury chose and Englished works that English readers could not otherwise reach. Galileo stands at the center of the volume.

The set gives the first English forms of Galileo's Mechanics and his early work On Motion, called De Motu. Works by Castelli and Torricelli, Galileo's heirs in the study of water and motion, stand beside them. Salusbury meant to import a whole school of science at once. It shaped how English thinkers, in Newton's age, first met the Italian founders of modern study of motion.
gao-gaoreports-b-296861: EDO Corporation took its September 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Defense firms get the same full hearing as all.
gao-gaoreports-b-296961: Fort Mojave/Hummel took its October 2005 contract fight to GAO as a joint venture, and this ruling is the verdict. The venture said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Joint ventures get the same full hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-297061: ADC took its October 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing. The process stays the same for all.
gao-gaoreports-b-298761: BST Systems doubled its December 2006 protest — two case numbers, one tech fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-310261: This 2007 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Command Management Services, Inc. Losing bidders can ask GAO to review whether an agency ran the competition fairly. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts.
gao-gaoreports-b-310661: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Karrar Systems Corporation. The January 3, 2008 ruling examines how the agency evaluated the bids. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts. The library keeps it as part of the public record.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-261: The post office's mail plant shuffle lacked clarity in 2005, and GAO's report says the realignment strategy needed clearer criteria. The review asks for the map. The sorting centers deserved the honest plan. The clarity had to come. The sorting centers deserved the honest plan.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-461: Climate change funding reports needed clarity in 2005, and GAO's report says federal reports should be clearer and more complete. The findings demand the transparency. The report warns that the warming planet deserved honest books. The reports had to be clearer.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-661: Census Bureau IT management was progressing in 2005, and GAO's report says many key practices were implemented, though more actions were needed. The findings balance credit and need. The report warns that the headcount's tech deserved finishing. The actions had to be taken.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-961: Independent and special counsel spending got a GAO audit in 2005, and the report examines expenditures for the six months ended March 2005. The findings grade the accounting. The report shows the prosecutors' tabs were checked. The spending had to be sound.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-161: Counting the counterterrorism dollars needed work in 2006, and GAO's report examines determining and reporting federal funding data. The findings target the fog. The report warns that the terror-fighting money deserved honest counting. The data had to be determined. The terror-fighting money deserved honest counting.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-261: The nuclear weapons certification approach needed refining in 2006, and GAO's report says the NNSA had to better manage its new assessment method. The findings demand the rigor. The report warns that the atomic arsenal's health checks needed care. The approach had to be refined.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-361: Sarbanes-Oxley needed tailoring for small companies in 2006, and GAO's report says key principles should guide implementation for smaller firms. The findings prescribe the approach. The report warns that the corporate reform should not crush the little guys. The principles had to guide.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-661: Measuring student growth stumped the states in 2006, and GAO's report says states faced challenges that federal initiatives might help address. The findings detail the struggles. The report warns that the testing regime needed workable measures. The growth had to be measured.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-161: Reading First was working, mostly, in 2007, and GAO's report says states saw better reading instruction, though clearer federal procedures were needed. The findings balance credit and critique. The report asks whether the littlest readers were really winning. The youngest readers were counting on it.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-361: Hiring an army of census takers needed a plan in 2007 — GAO's report says the bureau should sharpen recruiting and train its temp field force better. The findings target the people pipeline. The report's warning: the count is only as good as the counters.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-461: The Pentagon's must-protect list needed prioritizing in 2007 — GAO's report says the effort to name and rank critical sites wanted real guidance. The findings demand a method for the madness. The report's logic is plain: you cannot guard everything, so guard smart.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-561: Cargo in transit was slipping past the watchers in 2007 — GAO's report says weak spots in the in-bond system hampered border enforcement. The findings target the tracking gaps. The report warns that the shipment nobody watches is the shipment that matters.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-761: Buried bomb waste had no final plan in 2007 — GAO's report says the schemes for the most dangerous buried transuranic junk were unfinished, with cost guesses still soft. The findings describe the nation's hottest garbage in limbo. The report demands a real plan before the bill comes due.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-361: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at homeland Security: Strategic Solution for US-VISIT Program Needs to Be Better Defined, Justified, and Coordinated. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-561: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at veterans' Benefits: Increased Focus on Evaluation and Accountability Would Enhance Training and Performance Management for Claims Processors. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-661: The Government Accountability Office dug into afghanistan Security: Further Congressional Action May Be Needed to Ensure Completion of a Detailed Plan to Develop and Sustain Capable Afghan National Security in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
heine-poems-bowring-1861:
Edgar Alfred Bowring translated the complete poems of Heinrich Heine into English in 1861. The volume holds the Book of Songs, the young Heine's lyrics of love and loss, and the later cycles that darkened his tone. Schubert and Schumann set many of these lyrics to music that still fills concert halls.

Heine's short poems turn on a dime from tender to ironic. A love song can end with a shrug that undoes its own sweetness. Bowring kept the meters close to the German so English readers could sing along in spirit. German schoolchildren have learned these poems for generations. Bowring's volume long gave English readers their fullest Heine in verse.
herzen-my-past-thoughts-1861: Herzen's My Past and Thoughts (1861) memoirs span Russia's revolutionary ferment. Exile sharpened his pen. The Tower library holds the full text. It remembered struggle. Czars ruled. Exiles wrote. Hope burned. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
holmes-elsie-venner-1861:
Oliver Wendell Holmes published Elsie Venner in 1861, calling it a romance of destiny. Holmes, a professor of anatomy, wanted to test a medical idea in fiction: how far is a person responsible for traits fixed before birth? The novel is the first American work of biological determinism.

Elsie Venner's mother was bitten by a rattlesnake shortly before her birth, and Elsie grows up beautiful, strange, and half serpentine in temper. Her schoolmaster falls in love with her while a doctor watches the case like an experiment. Holmes weaves New England village life around the central question of inherited sin and free will. The idea came from his medical lectures, and readers argued about Elsie for decades.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lowy-albert-101:
Albert Löwy (born 1816) was an English rabbi and communal worker born at Aussee in Moravia, and a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind gives his career. He studied Hebrew and Arabic at Vienna, then became a minister of the Reform Synagogue in London. He served there for fifty years, retiring in 1892.

Working with Professor Marks, Löwy helped compile the congregation’s prayer book, and he helped found the Anglo-Jewish Association, serving as its secretary from 1871 to 1889. The article stresses his scholarship: he catalogued Samaritan manuscripts, printed the first specimen of an Aramaic dialect spoken by Jews of Urmia, and catalogued the City of London’s Hebrew books. St. Andrews gave him an honorary doctorate in 1893. The entry shows a minister whose learning served both his synagogue and wider Jewish scholarship.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-manetho-greek-m:
Manetho, the Greco-Egyptian priest who wrote Egypt's history, is treated in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. He was high priest of Sebennytus in the Delta and lived under the first two Ptolemies. His history was written after 271 before the common era. Its value rests on his direct use of hieroglyphic sources.

The article explains how his work reaches us. Josephus is the only writer who gives connected extracts from it. Later chronologers copied out his tables of dynasties and kings. The writers warn that Josephus's extracts are full of confusion, above all on the Exodus. Some errors are Josephus's own. The Hyksos material holds real information, but tying those kings to Israel fails. Once blunders are corrected, the Exodus tale seems built from the Bible plus Egyptian folk stories. The entry teaches readers to use a priceless source with open eyes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-maskil-plural-m:
“Maskil” is a Hebrew word with two very different lives. Joseph Jacobs, Peter Wiernik, and Gotthard Deutsch explain it in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. In its older use the word was a title of honor. It meant a scholar or enlightened man. In parts of Italy it belonged to rabbinical students, while in the East it could name the overseers of the poor.

The second half of the article follows the word eastward: among the Jews of the Slavonic lands, a maskil was a self-taught Hebrew scholar. He was drawn to the Haskalah, the Jewish enlightenment that spread from the circle of Mendelssohn. Such men worked mostly as teachers and writers. They taught a generation of Russian Jews to read Hebrew and built the new Hebrew literature. Yet each generation of them had to be recruited fresh from Orthodox ranks.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meinek-moses-sa:
Moses Säkel Meinek was a German scholar, editor, and probably printer at Offenbach in the early eighteenth century. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn give him a brief entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Almost everything known of him is three dated imprints: in 1715 he published, under his own name, “Teutsche Apothek” by Naphtali Pappenheim. In 1717 he issued a riddle in Judaeo-German verse by an anonymous author. Schudt reprinted it with a German transcription in his “Jüdische Merckwürdigkeiten,” calling Meinek a printer.

In 1722 he edited an anonymous guide for the reader of the Law. It is the “Siyyumah ha-Parashiyyot meha-Torah,” which the entry judges he probably wrote himself. That is the whole record. The editors assemble it from the bibliographies of Steinschneider and Wolf. Small as it is, the notice preserves a figure of the German-Jewish book trade, whose men rarely left any trace.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mendelsohn-mart:
Martin Mendelsohn was a Berlin physician. He belonged to the generation that made nursing a science. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman profile him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Posen in 1860. He took his medical degree at Berlin in 1885. He spent a postgraduate year in Paris. He rose through the first medical clinic and the Charité. He reached a privat-docentship in 1895. He reached the title of professor in 1899.

His cause was the care of the sick as a discipline in itself. From 1894 he edited the "Zeitschrift für Krankenpflege," the journal of nursing. His books circle the bedside. They treat opium and the comfort of the patient. They treat medical art versus medical science. One, in 1896, treats the influence of cycling on the human organism. About a hundred journal essays complete the count. They mark a busy clinical career.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meyer-rachel-10:
Rachel Meyer, a German novelist born in Danzig on March 11, 1806, is remembered in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry by Isidore Singer and S. J. Levinson, published in 1906. She married her late sister Frederika's husband and, while raising and teaching children and giving to charity, kept up her own self-education. Noted men were guests in her home.

Her first book, Zwei Schwestern, appeared at Berlin in 1853 and praised love's triumph over self within marriage. In Vienna she wrote a sketch of city life and a novel about the great actress Rachel, published in 1859. Her last novel, In Banden Frei of 1869, studied her friend Lina Davidson. Practical under her idealism, she even sketched the inventor Stephenson to stir a nephew's practical spirit.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-montelimar-hebr:
Montélimar, capital of the Drôme in France, held a large and comparatively prosperous Jewish community from the early fourteenth century, as Richard Gottheil and S. Kahn write in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Jews had a synagogue on the Rue de la Juiverie, a school by the Porte Saint-Martin, a cemetery, and a slaughter-house whose privilege the Dauphin Louis confirmed in 1455.

Scholarship passed through: in 1339 Samuel ben Judah of Marseilles revised there his Hebrew version of Alexander Aphrodisius on the soul. The turn came in 1439, when the lords imposed the Jewish badge the town's consuls had long spared them; in 1453 the Jews were ordered to attend Christian preaching. The entry names the community's leading men across two centuries.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-musa-of-tiflis-:
Musa of Tiflis, a native of Za'faran in Persia, was a Karaite who founded a sect of his own in the early ninth century. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. His followers were called Abu Imranites, Meshwites, or Tiflisites. The Karaites themselves counted him an apostate.

Musa kept several Karaite rules, such as counting the fifty days from a Sunday. But his chief teachings broke away: he held that God, after creating the world, left it to run itself. He also denied the resurrection of the dead. His month began when the old moon vanished, not when the new one showed. The entry also weighs whether he is the Moses ben Amram quoted by Ibn Ezra.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nabon-or-navon-:
Nabon, or Navon, is the name of a Turkish family that produced rabbinical writers from the seventeenth century on. Gotthard Deutsch and M. Franco wrote the Jewish Encyclopedia article on it. One branch sat at Jerusalem and another at Constantinople. The earliest known member is Hanun Nabon, whose sermons the bibliographer Azulai saw in manuscript.

The article gives short lives of eight Nabons. Jonah Nabon of Jerusalem taught the great Azulai and left responsa and a work on divorce. Judah Nabon wrote notes on Maimonides' code, and Ephraim Nabon gathered responsa at Constantinople. Two later Nabons became chief rabbis of Jerusalem. Jonah Moses, in 1836, was the first to bear the title Rishon le-Ziyyon.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nathan-ben-jose:
Nathan ben Joseph Official was a French rabbi famed for debate. Isidore Singer and S. Kahn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived at Sens in the later thirteenth century. His son called him the prince of polemists. Nathan argued in public with church leaders and baptized Jews.

He debated bishops from many French towns, one by one. He also faced the king's confessor and Paris bishop Guillaume d'Auvergne. In 1273 he debated Pope Gregory X on a Bible verse. Nathan spoke with striking freedom in these contests. No book of his survives today. His notes on Bible verses are quoted in later works.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nissim-ben-mose:
Nissim ben Moses of Marseilles was a French philosopher. Joseph Jacobs and Isaac Broydé wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. About 1306 he wrote on the Pentateuch. His age was split by a war over philosophy.

Orthodox Jews and philosophy's friends fought hard then. Nissim still gave reasoned readings of the miracles. Sodom's fall, he said, was a volcanic eruption. He pointed to Ischia's eruption of 1302 as its like. His commentary survives in several manuscript copies. It goes under three titles in those copies. They are Ma'aseh Nissim, Sefer ha-Nissim, and 'Ikre ha-Dat. Schorr also credits him with a homily on Ruth.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oedenburg-sopro:
Oedenburg, also called Sopron, is a city in Hungary. Gotthard Deutsch and Miksa Pollak wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its Jewish group counts among the oldest in Hungary. A text of 1526 traces it to the tenth century. Fire gutted the town in the year 1317.

King Charles Robert asked Jews to settle there in 1324. They lived in peace for thirty years of that age. Then Louis the Great cast them out in 1354. Most went to Wiener-Neustadt, in Austria. A few years on, they were let back in. By 1379 the group numbered eighty souls in all. By the close of the next age it reached 400. Kings at times shielded them from town attacks.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-organ-11761:
The organ is a wind instrument with pipes and keys. Cyrus Adler and Judah David Eisenstein wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jewish sages say it was one of the Temple's tools of music. The link rests on a verse in Psalm 150. That verse names stringed tools and organs in English.

Scholars think those two terms may be swapped in place. The true word for organ may be the first, not the last. In new Hebrew, one word serves for organ and piano. The Temple tool was the magrefa, by Talmud accounts. It had ten pipes, each pipe with ten holes. So one hundred notes could be got from it in all. An older tale gives it a square ell of size. It gives it pipes for a full one thousand tones.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-palagyi-melchio:
Melchior Palágyi was a Hungarian writer born at Paks. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born there on December 26, 1859. His first name at birth was Silberstein, as was his brother's. His father gave him his first school lessons at home.

Melchior then went to high schools at Temesvar and Kassa. In 1877 he went to the trade school at Budapest. In 1881 he passed his tests as a school teacher. His fields were the science of sums and of nature. Five years on, he was a professor at a trade school. As a pupil he wrote a treatise on sums in 1880. The Academy of Sciences put that work out in print. He then turned to deep thought as his main field.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-paz-duarte-de-1:
Duarte de Paz was a Portuguese Marrano who lobbied at Rome. He acted as agent for Portugal's New Christians, the forced converts. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He died about 1541, after years of double dealing.

Duarte had won King John the Third's trust in war. He lost an eye fighting in the African war. Sent on a mission, he went to Rome instead. There his gifts and speeches swayed the cardinals. In 1532 the pope voided the bull that set up the Inquisition. Masked men later stabbed Duarte, but hidden armor saved him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-peshitta-or-pes:
The Peshitta is the oldest Syriac version of the Bible. Emil G. Hirsch and M. Seligsohn wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its name means the simple one. It covers both the Old Testament and the New. Syriac Christians still use it as their Bible.

No single translator made the whole version. The work grew over several centuries of labor. Tradition ties its start to King Izates of Adiabene. The Pentateuch may date to the first century. By the fourth century the full Bible stood in Syriac. Church fathers quoted it widely by then.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pine-pnie-samso:
Samson Pine was a German Jewish translator of the 1300s. Gotthard Deutsch and A. M. Friedenberg wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was likely born at Peine, in Hanover. He later lived and worked at Strasburg. Such teamwork across faiths was rare in that age.

Two Christian poets preserve his name for us. In 1336 they continued Wolfram's great poem Parzival. Pine rendered the French text into German for them. He also invented rhymes for their verses. Their manuscript thanks him twice in ten lines. Both times it names him plainly as a Jew.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-primo-samuel-12:
Samuel Primo was a follower of the false messiah Shabbethai Zebi. Gotthard Deutsch and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Jerusalem in the seventeenth century. He died, in all likelihood, at Constantinople. He was one of the first men to join Zebi's cause.

Primo served Zebi as his private secretary. He did so on the trip from Jerusalem to Smyrna in 1665. He lent the false messiah an air of state and honor. From Smyrna he spread the news through foreign lands. The messiah had come at last, he told the Jews. With a few close friends he planned a bold step. They would do away with rabbinic Judaism itself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-quetsch-solomon:
Solomon Quetsch was an Austrian rabbi and Talmud scholar of Nikolsburg. Isidore Singer and Gotthard Deutsch wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born there in 1798. He died there in 1856. He learned at the yeshivah of his home town. His teacher was Mordecai Benet, whose dearest pupil he was.

Quetsch served as rabbi at Piesling and then at Leipnik. Last he served at Nikolsburg, his own home town. There he came after Samson Raphael Hirsch in the post. He held it for a few months only at the end. He was a rabbi of the old school in all things. Yet he stood out from that school in clear ways.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-randar-or-arend:
A randar was a tenant who leased farms, mills, or taverns. Isidore Singer and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The word was used in Poland, Lithuania, and nearby lands. Whole villages could be held under such a lease.

The article notes that Jews leased most of these taverns. The Jewish tavern keeper became a stock figure in Polish writing. In Pan Tadeusz he appears as Jankiel, a loyal helper. He gives advice and even plays the cymbals well. The entry also notes many Russian rules on Jewish taverns. It shows how one job shaped both daily life and literature.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reif-abraham-12:
Abraham Reif was a Galician poet born at Mosciska in 1802. Isidore Singer and M. Margel wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He died in 1859. Early on he followed the Me'assefim school of Hebrew writing.

The article says he later broke away from that movement. Tobias Feder's sharp satire deeply shaped his work. Alexander Langbank introduced him to secular sciences. Reif's ready wit made traditionalists fear him, they say. He opened a school for Bible and Hebrew in his town. That school produced leading Hebraists. His dramas picture Galician Jewish life in vivid scenes. Too poor to print them, he gave copies to pupils. His language stayed pure Biblical Hebrew throughout.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rime-12761:
Rime is the matching of sounds at the ends of words. Crawford Howell Toy and I. M. Casanowicz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Some writers credited the early Hebrews with knowing rime. Judah Provencal even called Hebrew poetry mother of all poetries.

The article says Samuel Archevolti found rime in the Bible. He thought it existed but was not fully developed. Moses ibn Habib claimed it for other early Hebrew verse. Modern writers like Reuss gave rime a large role too. Yet most agree rime was no formal rule in the Old Testament. Matching line ends arise from grammar, they argue. Such echoes are not an organic part of composition. The entry separates chance sound likeness from true poetic form.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenthal-david:
David Rosenthal was a Polish physician born at Tarnogrod, in the Lublin region, in 1808. Herman Rosenthal and Max Rosenthal wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. His father was a district physician on the Polish army staff.

Rosenthal studied at Vienna and was sent to fight cholera in 1831. He served Warsaw's Jewish hospital for decades, as chief physician from 1844 to 1879. He also taught hygiene at the Marymont institute near Warsaw. His account of an 1847 typhus outbreak described what was later called recurrent fever. He wrote as well on glanders in human beings.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sambari-cattawi:
Joseph ben Isaac Sambari was an Egyptian chronicler of the seventeenth century. Joseph Jacobs and M. Franco wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Of lowly origin, he worked for a rabbi at Alexandria in Egypt.

Sambari spent his leisure on history, using a famous rabbi's great library. He knew Arabic, Hebrew, and Spanish, though his Hebrew is faulty. His first chronicle, a general history from Abraham onward, is lost. The second, Dibre Yosef, survives in two copies, at Oxford and Paris. It covers Egypt's Fatimite califs, Spain's Abbassids, and the Ottoman Turks.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-san-francisco-1:
Cyrus Adler and Jacob Voorsanger wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on San Francisco. The city was California's chief port and trade center on the Pacific coast. The village of Yerba Buena took the name San Francisco in 1847. Jews likely lived there early, though records are thin. The gold rush of 1849 changed everything.

That year large numbers of Jews reached the city. Some came on the first Pacific mail steamer in February. Others crossed overland or sailed from Europe and Australia. In autumn 1849 over one hundred Jews were in town. About fifty gathered for the Day of Atonement in a room above a store. In the summer of 1850 the two main congregations formed. One drew German and American Jews. The other drew Polish and English Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-scheuer-jacob-m:
A. Peiginsky wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, issued with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board in 1906. It profiles Jacob Moses David Scheuer, called Tebele. He was a German Talmudist. Scheuer was born at Frankfort-on-the-Main early in the eighteenth century. He died at Mayence in 1782. He ranked among the foremost pupils of Jacob Cohen, Frankfort's rabbi.

Scheuer served as a judge at Frankfort under the author of Pene Yehoshua'. In 1759, at an advanced age, he became rabbi of Bamberg. There he mediated a long dispute between Jews and gentry. His work produced the ceremonial agreement of 1760. A baptized Jew then slandered him to the prince-bishop. Bamberg became impossible for him. In 1767 he accepted the district rabbinate of Mayence. He stayed there until his death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sfej-abraham-13:
Abraham Sfej was a rabbinic author born at Tunis early in the eighteenth century. Gotthard Deutsch and M. Franco wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He left Tunis and settled in Jerusalem, pausing at Constantinople on the way. He died at Amsterdam in 1784.

Sfej died while raising funds for the Jerusalem community. His book Ene Abraham comments on Maimonides' great code, the Yad ha-Hazakah. It was printed at Amsterdam in the year of his death. The entry is brief, but it keeps the name of a North African scholar who crossed the Jewish world for learning and duty.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shemoneh-esreh-:
Shemoneh Esreh is the set of blessings at the heart of daily Jewish prayer. Cyrus Adler and Emil G. Hirsch wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. Its name literally means eighteen, for its blessing count. Jews say it morning, afternoon, and evening each day.

An extra service on Sabbaths and holy days includes it too. As the prayer itself, it is called the Tefillah. Sephardic Jews call it the Amidah, the standing prayer. Worshipers must recite it while standing on their feet. In fixed form the blessings actually number nineteen. They group into praise, petitions, and closing thanks. The entry maps the prayer that structures Jewish worship every single day.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-henry-n:
Henry Naphtali Solomon was an English Hebraist and educationist born in 1796. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born in London and schooled by his father. His father kept a school at Brixton in London. Henry became head master of the Jews' Free School in 1817.

In 1822 he opened his own school in Queen's square. It later moved to Hammersmith and then to Edmonton. He taught at Edmonton for more than forty years. He helped found a Jewish literary and scientific institution. He also preached for years in the St Albans Synagogue. He translated the Jewish prayer-book and wrote very widely.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-spingarn-joel-e:
Joel Elias Spingarn was an American educator born in New York in 1875. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born in New York city on May 17. He graduated from Columbia University in 1895 with honors. He took postgraduate courses at Harvard and Columbia as well.

He earned his doctor's degree in 1899 at Columbia. That year he became a tutor at his alma mater. In 1900 he rose to adjunct professor of comparative literature. His chief book traced literary criticism in the Renaissance. It appeared in 1899 and was translated into Italian. He also wrote The New Hesperides and American Scholarship, both in 1901.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-synagogue-archi:
Synagogue architecture covers how Jews have housed worship through the ages. Joseph Jacobs and A. W. Brunner wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Ancient Jewish art survives mainly in the Temple's remains. Judea's place and history discouraged a lasting art tradition. Old synagogue ruins give builders only meager guidance today.

The Kafr Bir'im synagogue is the best preserved ancient example. Its front held three doorways with carved frames. The central door bore a rounded, enriched arch. Inside, the plan ran rectangular with a columned portico. The door faced west and the Ark stood east. The reading platform sat near the center. Men filled the side spaces while women used a gallery. The entry weighs what ruins can teach modern builders.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tashlik-14261:
Tashlik is a rite of casting sins away at New Year. Isidore Singer and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Its name comes from a passage in Micah. Micah says God will cast sins into the sea's depths. Jews gather by running water to act that verse out.

On the afternoon of New-Year's Day the congregation assembles. They recite Micah's closing verses beside the stream. Penitential prayers and hymns follow the reading. When and where the custom began is uncertain. One view links it to a decree in Josephus. That decree let Jews pray by the sea at Halicarnassus. The Zohar hints that what falls into the deep is lost. Talmud and early codes never mention the custom, though. The entry weighs hints against a long silence.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-theodotion-1436:
Theodotion, a Greek translator of the Old Testament, is treated through his Daniel. Crawford Howell Toy and Emil G. Hirsch wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. His version of Daniel replaced the Septuagint in church use. Only one Greek manuscript kept the older Daniel text.

Origen placed the Septuagint in his Hexapla but quoted Theodotion instead. Jerome blamed the Septuagint's faults for its rejection. Earlier fathers had already favored Theodotion's wording. Yet he did not translate straight from the Hebrew-Aramaic text. The additions to Daniel were Greek in origin, scholars argue. An Aramaic version of them adapts the Greek, not the reverse. The article untangles a tricky textual puzzle.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-toul-hebr-or-za:
Toul, a French town in Meurthe-et-Moselle, had Jews from the thirteenth century. Isidore Singer and S. Kahn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. R. Eliezer of Toul, a tosafot author, once lived there. His brother Abraham studied under Isaac the Elder of Dampierre. Meir Abulafia addressed learned letters to Abraham's circle.

In 1708 the Bishop of Toul sought to expel Jewish bankers. His petition against the Levy family failed. Duke Leopold let 180 Jewish families stay in 1721. They could worship and trade without molestation. Leon Cohen represented Toul at Napoleon's Paris assembly in 1806. The Nancy consistory governed the small community. By 1905 it held forty or fifty families.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ugolino-blaisio:
Blaisio Ugolino was an Italian scholar who gathered a vast treasury of Jewish antiquities. Crawford Howell Toy and Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Born at Venice around 1700, he knew Talmudic literature deeply. He was said to be a Jewish convert. His Thesaurus ran to thirty-four Latin volumes.

The set appeared at Venice between 1744 and 1769. It reprinted most seventeenth-century treatises on Jewish antiquities. Bochart, Buxtorf, Selden, and Reland all stand inside it. Topics run from festivals to burial customs. Priests, Temple, Talmud, and law each fill several volumes. Ugolino translated many tractates himself from Hebrew. Menahot and Zebahim were his own renderings. Full indexes close the thirty-fourth volume.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-veit-philipp-14:
Philipp Veit was a German painter of portraits and religious scenes. He was born in Berlin on February 13, 1793. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. His mother was a daughter of Moses Mendelssohn. His stepfather, Friedrich von Schlegel, had him baptized as a boy.

Veit studied art at Dresden and Vienna. In 1813 he joined the army and fought Napoleon. He won the Iron Cross for bravery. From 1815 he worked in Rome with the neo German school. He painted frescoes there with Cornelius and Overbeck. Later he directed the Staedel Institute at Frankfort. His large canvas Germania became his best known work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wallich-11161:
Wallich was a German family rich in doctors. Joseph Jacobs, Gotthard Deutsch, and M. Seligsohn wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The name may come from the Hebrew form of Falk. Its earliest known members lived at Worms. Joseph ben Meir and Moses Joshua Wallich practiced there in the fifteen hundreds.

A 1615 document lists many family physicians at once. Fathers and sons signed it together as doctors. In the seventeen hundreds, Wallich doctors practiced across Germany. Abraham ben Isaac studied medicine at Padua. He settled at Frankfort in 1657. His Hebrew medical book argued that body and soul ail alike. The entry traces the family's long medical line.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weltsch-samuel-:
Samuel Weltsch was an Austrian cantor. He was born at Prague on September 12, 1835. Isidore Singer and Alois Kaiser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He died at Prague on August 5, 1901. Cantors filled his family line. He sang at Prague's Meisel synagogue while still young. Prague's conservatory gave him his music training.

In 1865 Weltsch took a post in New York. He served Ahawath Chesed congregation until 1880. He worked to improve American synagogue music. He helped compile the first volumes of Zimrat Yah. That song collection serves all seasons of the year. It is still widely used today. He also led charities and schools in Prague.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yannai-ben-ishm:
Yannai ben Ishmael was a scholar of Palestine in the third century. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived at the same time as Zeera and Abba bar Kahana. A few of his rules of law live on in his name.

One rule treats a line of the set prayer of each day. A query on that same prayer came to him from Zeera. A rule on the cutting rite for slaves is told in his name. His tales have lived on as well as his rules. One tale treats the meet of Adam with the angels. One is a parting speech built on a verse in Judges. In a sick spell Zeera and Abba came to his bed side. There they fell to a debate on the groves of Solomon.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zamzam-15161:
Zamzam is a holy well in the mosque at Mecca in Arabia. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Muslim lore ties it to the spring of Hagar and Ishmael. That spring is named in the Book of Genesis as well.

Some Arab minds read the name as fill, fill in tongue. Hagar bid her son fill the jar at that spring. One mind read it as stay, stay in the Egyptian tongue. Hagar bid her son cease his road at that well. The spring is held to be a work of pure grace. Its water is prized for drink and for wash rites. Men ship it to far lands for the sick and the devout. The fast of the holy month is oft broken with it. Men wet their eyes with it to make sight more keen.
kardec-le-livre-des-mediums-1861:
Allan Kardec trains the seer in Le Livre des mediums, his French guide of 1861. The name means the book on mediums. Kardec had set out his faith's creed in his prior book. Here he turns to craft: how sittings should run, what kinds of seers there are, what frauds and risks to watch, and how to weigh words from the dead.

Rules, types, and warns fill the guide in calm prose. His faith took it as its chief hand book at once. In French, it is the school text of a world faith. Its order is its strength.
kennedy-inaugural-1961:
John F. Kennedy delivered his Inaugural Address in the snow in 1961. A new generation takes power in his crisp, ringing phrases. Ask not what your country can do for you, he tells Americans.

Ask what you can do for your country, the famous line concludes. Kennedy pledges strength for liberty's defense anywhere on the globe. He calls foes to talks and friends to shared, bold ventures. Grace, vigor, and high purpose mark the speech from its first words. The address defined the New Frontier and an era's bright, brief hopes. Its balanced sentences are still quoted at graduations across the land.
la-fontaine-des-amoureux-de-science-comp: Achille Genty edited this 1861 French edition of an old poem on the fountain of the lovers of science. Its author is named as Jehan de La Fontaine, a writer of an earlier age. The hosted sample shows only scanner notes. The title and editor still ground the book's identity. It is a short old French poem tied to the lore of science and alchemy. Genty's edition brought that rare text back before nineteenth-century readers.
la-fontaine-des-amovrevx-de-science-comp: This 1861 edition presents the same old French poem on the fountain of the lovers of science. Jehan de La Fontaine is named as its composer. Achille Genty served as editor. The hosted sample shows only scanner notes. Readers get a second copy of a rare alchemical poem. Its archaic spelling, with amovrevx for amoureux, marks its age. Such poems hid lessons about the philosophers' stone inside love imagery and verse.
leila-or-the-siege-of-granada-complete-p:
This complete edition of Lytton's Leila opens in summer 1491. Ferdinand and Isabel's armies invest Granada, Spain's last Moorish city. Moonlight touches the Sierra Nevada above the Spanish camp.

Leila, a Jewish maiden, loves across the lines of war. Her father's plans and her own heart conflict sharply. Kings, friars, and soldiers all shape her fate. The romance moves through ambush, trial, and siege to battle. Readers get Lytton's full tale in one undivided text here. David Widger produced this complete Gutenberg text. Five books in one file suit readers who dislike split volumes.
levi-clef-des-grands-mysteres-1861:
Eliphas Levi drew his whole creed into one book in La Clef des grands mysteres, out in 1861. The title means the key to the great riddles. He links the lore of the Jews, the cards of the tarot, and a bright force he calls the Astral Light.

Levi claims one key can unlock faith, lore, and rite at once. The book is dense, bold, and meant for keen minds. French occult groups took it as core creed. It is the ripe fruit of his thought, in his own tongue. Ranks of signs and keys crowd the last parts of the book. Keen fans used them as a map for their own rites and drills.
lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-literat:
Lippincott's March 1875 number opens with an escape from Siberia. Australian scenes and adventures begin alongside it. Charlotte F. Bates offers a poem called Forecast. Ita Aniol Prokop's Matchless One concludes its tale of American society.

William Black's Three Feathers reaches a farewell in chapter twenty-eight. Emma Lazarus retells a tradition, La Madonna della Sedia. Harriet Prescott Spofford contributes Playing with Fire. Trollope recalls the Tuscan court under Grand Duke Leopold. Munich as a pest-city and Mitchell's scientific life add nonfiction. Recollections of the Tuscan court continue across this number too.
macaulay-history-england-vol-5-1861:
Volume 5 of Macaulay's History of England from the Accession of James II appeared in 1861, after Thomas Babington Macaulay's death. Friends prepared the unfinished volume from his papers. It carries his story of William III's reign toward the end of the seventeenth century.

War with France, plots against the king, and fights over taxes and trade fill the chapters. Macaulay kept his vivid style, painting scenes and judging men with confidence. The volume stops short of the full span he had planned. Even unfinished, it closed the most popular English history of its age, a work that taught generations how to picture the Glorious Revolution and its gains.
maine-ancient-law-1861:
Sir Henry Sumner Maine published Ancient Law in 1861. Maine, a law professor who later served in India, compared the oldest legal records of Rome, India, and other lands. He asked how law itself began and how it changed as societies grew.

Maine's famous summary runs from status to contract: early law fixes each person's place by birth, while modern law lets persons make their own bargains. He traced property, wills, and crime from family rule toward individual right. The phrase and the book founded comparative legal history and the sociology of law. Later research corrected many details, but Maine's questions still organize the study of early law.
memoirs-of-louis-xiv-and-his-court-and-o:
Volume two of Saint-Simon's memoirs opens at chapter nine, in 1695. Harlay, Archbishop of Paris, died of epilepsy at Conflans that August. He had lost favor with the King and Madame de Maintenon.

He had stood against the word of her marriage to the King. Envious clergy took joy in his fall from high place. Gardeners raked out his footprints as he walked with the Duchesse de Lesdiguieres. On the 8th, the King gave his cardinal's nomination to the Bishop of Orleans. The Bishop knelt and held the King's knees at the news. Grace and piety marked him, and he gave most wealth away.
military-reminiscences-of-the-civil-war-:
Jacob Dolson Cox, formerly a major-general commanding the Twenty-Third Army Corps, wrote this memoir of the Civil War. Volume One covers April 1861 through November 1863. In his preface Cox says he aims to reproduce his own experience. He wants readers to see how the war's duties appeared to one active participant.

Cox tested his memory against the government's Official Records of both armies. He knew many prominent officers and civilians intimately, and shares what he learned of them. Some chapters first appeared in Battles and Leaders of the Civil War. The volume offers a personal narrative meant to supplement formal campaign histories.
mill-representative-government-1861:
John Stuart Mill published his book on elected rule in 1861, a classic theory of how free peoples should govern. Mill argues this form is best for nations that have grown mature. It trains men and women by giving them a share in rule. He backs a wide vote, with tests he thought kept it sound.

Mill gives the first strong case for fair shares of seats by votes cast. He calls this plan a great step forward. He also weighs town rule, unions of states, and rule over subject lands. On that last point, later readers fault him. Students still read the book beside On Liberty.
mill-utilitarianism-1861:
John Stuart Mill published Utilitarianism in 1861, first as magazine essays and then as a short book. Mill defended the moral theory he had learned from Jeremy Bentham and his own father. Its rule is simple to state: the right act is the one that brings the greatest happiness overall.

Mill answered the charge that the theory is a pig philosophy by ranking pleasures of mind above those of body. He argued for liberty, justice, and rules that protect the weak as parts of happiness itself. The essay is short, clear, and argued with care against named critics. It remains the canonical statement of utilitarian ethics, the first text most students read on the subject.
morin-astrologia-gallica-1661:
Jean-Baptiste Morin was a French royal astrologer and professor whose Astrologia Gallica appeared in 1661, after his death. The work runs to twenty-six books in Latin, the fruit of a lifetime at the art. It is the last great Latin system of judicial astrology.

Morin rebuilds the judgment of nativities on strict rules for a planet's state, place, and aspects within the whole chart. He scorns cookbook reading and demands that each chart be weighed as one living configuration. Modern traditional astrologers still study Morin in translation as the master who gave their art its firmest method.
narratives-of-new-netherland-1609-1664-p:
J. Franklin Jameson edits this set of Dutch narratives of New Netherland. The years run from 1609 to 1664, the colony's full span. Writers include Hudson's men, De Rasieres, and Father Jogues. Their letters and journals tell the founding of New York firsthand.

This Gutenberg file is an early edition of the same collection. V1 calls the tales invaluable, vivid, and direct. Mohawk life, trade, missions, and war fill the pages. The Dutch speak in their own voices, plain and close to events. For colonial history the set is raw material of the best kind, later used in school and college alike.
njals-saga-dasent-1861:
George Webbe Dasent published The Story of Burnt Njal in 1861, his translation of Njal's Saga. The Icelandic saga, written in the 1200s, is often called the greatest of its kind. Dasent, a scholar of Norse tales, gave it its first English form.

Njal, a wise and peaceful farmer, tries to hold back the feuds that grip his kin and neighbors. His friend Gunnar's pride and others' envy light a chain of killings that law cannot stop. The feud ends in the burning of Njal's house, with him inside. The saga blends law, fate, and stark dialogue. Dasent's version remains a landmark English dress for a masterpiece.
oe-epistola-alexandri-cockayne-1861:
The Old English Letter of Alexander to Aristotle survives in a single famous manuscript, Cotton Vitellius A.xv. That same book holds Beowulf. Thomas Cockayne edited the letter in 1861, printing the Old English text for students of England's earliest literature.

Alexander reports the wonders of India to his old teacher. Monster races, giant beasts, and deadly lands fill the letter, now told in the tongue of the Anglo-Saxons. English monks translated the marvels because wonder itself seemed worth saving. Cockayne's edition pairs the text with learned notes. It is England's earliest monster lore, written in the language of its first poets.
openalex-w1589514561:
Paloma de Sales and four co-authors wrote this review. It appeared in a Canadian pharmacy journal in 2012. All five authors worked at the University of Brasília. Alpha-amylase is an enzyme that helps digest starch. Blocking it may help treat diabetes and obesity, they note.

Plants offer many compounds that can block this enzyme. The review gathers crude extracts and pure compounds tested. Many extracts showed clear blocking action in the studies. Flavonoids showed the strongest action among plant compounds. Their strength rose with more hydroxyl groups, the authors report. The review maps plant sources for future drug work.
openalex-w2039755861:
Marcelo Aizen, Carolina Morales and Juan Morales studied how alien species change pollination networks. Their paper appeared in PLoS Biology in 2008. Plants and pollinators depend on each other unevenly. That uneven pattern may keep networks stable. Alien species can join these webs. Their effect on web structure was little explored.

The team compared ten plant-pollinator webs. Most webs came from southern Andes forests. Two came from oceanic islands. Heavily invaded webs showed weaker mutual dependence. Alien species took over key links from native generalists. Links among native species fell in invaded webs. Overall web connectivity did not change much. The authors warn that invasion quietly erodes native pollination ties.
openalex-w2090738461:
Tomoo Sawabe, Yoshitoshi Ogura, Yuta Matsumura and colleagues updated the family tree of Vibrio bacteria. Their paper appeared in Frontiers in Microbiology in 2013. Vibrios live widely in marine waters. The family holds well over a hundred named species. Gene-based grouping needed revision as data grew.

The team used multi-gene family trees for the update. They proposed eight new clades in the family. A clade groups species by shared ancestry. They also described one new species formally. It was named Vibrio tritonius. Clearer grouping helps labs identify samples correctly. It also aids studies of disease-causing vibrios. The paper sets a reference framework for the family.
openalex-w2143196261:
A. Roderick Escombe, Clarissa Oeser, Robert Gilman, and colleagues published this study in PLoS Medicine in 2007. They asked whether natural ventilation can protect against airborne infections like tuberculosis in hospitals. Sealed isolation rooms with machines are costly, so poorer settings need a low-cost option that truly works.

The team studied seventy naturally ventilated rooms in eight hospitals in Lima, Peru. They compared them with twelve modern negative-pressure rooms. Hundreds of tracer gas tests measured how fast air changed in each room. Opening windows and doors gave a median of twenty-eight air changes per hour. That was more than double the rate of the machine rooms, at a fraction of the cost.
openalex-w2171184561:
Raymond Lee, Bosu Seo, Steve Hladkyj, and colleagues published this meta-analysis in Human Resources for Health in 2013. They gathered what predicts physician burnout, a problem tied to care quality and to doctors quitting or moving away. Their focus was emotional exhaustion and depersonalization, the two classic faces of burnout.

Sixty-five physician samples from many regions and specialties were pooled. Exhaustion rose with workload, rigid structures, workplace conflict, and work-life strain. It fell with autonomy, positive work attitudes, and a strong safety culture. Depersonalization followed the same pattern more weakly. Some links flipped by region or specialty: strong safety culture protected doctors in the Americas most, while positive attitudes mattered more in Europe.
openalex-w2189732261:
B. Abelev and colleagues in the ALICE Collaboration published this measurement in the Journal of High Energy Physics in 2015. They measured elliptic flow, the oval spray pattern of particles, for identified particle types in lead-lead collisions. Sorting the flow by particle identity tests how the hot, dense collision matter expands as one shared fluid.

ALICE data covered pions, kaons, protons, and several heavier short-lived particles across collision classes. At low momentum, heavier particles flowed less, exactly as a common expanding velocity field predicts. Fluid calculations matched the light particles well for head-on collisions but missed the heavier ones. At higher momentum, particles grouped by type, mesons apart from baryons, with modest deviations from quark-counting rules.
openalex-w2262245161:
Mauro Fisberg, Irina Kovalskys, Georgina Gómez, and colleagues published this protocol in BMC Public Health in 2015. They present ELANS, the Latin American Study of Nutrition and Health. Obesity is climbing fast across the region, yet no representative multi-country study had combined diet and activity measurement in one design.

The survey spans eight countries, from Argentina to Venezuela, with nine thousand urban participants aged fifteen to sixty-five. Sampling was layered by sex, age, and social level to mirror each nation. Teams measured food intake, activity, and body size under one shared protocol, with pilot runs first. The dataset enables cross-country comparison of eating patterns and energy use.
openalex-w2280838961:
Betty Abelev and colleagues in the ALICE Collaboration published this measurement in the European Physical Journal C in 2015. They measured two short-lived strange baryons in proton-proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. These particles carry strange quarks created fresh in the collision, so their yields test models of how hadrons form.

ALICE recorded the particles' momentum spectra near the collision midline. Popular quantum chromodynamics-inspired models generally predicted fewer of them than the data showed. The team also searched for a claimed five-quark particle, a pentaquark, in one decay channel. No sign of it appeared. The measurements now serve as the proton baseline for judging stranger behavior in heavy-ion collisions.
openalex-w2295283661:
Robin Chazdon, Pedro Brancalion, Lars Laestadius, and colleagues published this perspective in AMBIO in 2016. They ask when a forest counts as a forest, in an era betting heavily on restoration. Official definitions were built to count forest stocks, and they blur natural woods with plantations, hiding how regrowth is really going.

The authors trace how forest concepts changed alongside management aims through history. They argue restoration needs definitions that reveal a patch's quality and direction within a shifting landscape. New sensing tools and community-based assessment can make such definitions practical. Their framework shows how each management objective should weight forest state, change, and surroundings differently, guiding policies that protect and regrow forests.
openalex-w2517886161:
Erik E. Cordes, Daniel O. B. Jones, and Thomas Alfred Schlacher led a large team behind this 2016 review in Frontiers in Environmental Science. It surveys the environmental impacts of the deep-water oil and gas industry. Deep-sea habitats hold many rare species living at low numbers. Most recover very slowly after disturbance, which makes them sensitive to human activity.

The authors gather what is known about typical harms from offshore drilling and production. They then review the rules and management strategies used in different places. Options include closing some areas, restricting methods, and limiting work to certain seasons. Success rates have varied widely between jurisdictions. From this record they build recommendations for a general strategy to limit damage. The goal is management grounded in how fragile deep-sea life really is.
openalex-w2971222961:
Deepanway Ghosal, Navonil Majumder, Soujanya Poria, and colleagues published this paper in 2019. It presents DialogueGCN, a computer model that recognizes emotions in conversation. Knowing the emotion behind each line of dialogue has uses in health care, education, and human resources.

The model treats a conversation as a graph, linking each utterance to its speaker and neighbors. It uses both a speaker's own past lines and the influence of other speakers to judge emotion. This design fixes a weakness of older sequence models, which let context fade over long exchanges. The authors report that DialogueGCN beat the best prior methods on several standard test sets for emotion classification.
openalex-w3033069661:
Tijl Verhoelst, Steven Compernolle, Gaïa Pinardi, and colleagues published this validation study in Atmospheric Measurement Techniques in 2021. It checks the nitrogen dioxide data from TROPOMI, an instrument on the Copernicus Sentinel-5 Precursor satellite. Nitrogen dioxide is an air pollutant tied to traffic and industry.

TROPOMI has produced readings in daily operation since April 2018, but satellite data need ground truth. The team compared its measures of the gas in lower, upper, and whole air columns against three ground networks. Those networks use light-absorption instruments at sites around the world. Matching the two views shows where the satellite product can be trusted for air quality and climate work, and where it still drifts.
openalex-w3036296561:
Hans ter Steege, Paulo Prado, Renato de Lima, and colleagues published this study in Scientific Reports in 2020. It produces bias-corrected estimates of tree species richness for the Amazon rainforest. The Amazon holds a huge share of the world's tree species, but raw counts from field plots can mislead.

Plots cluster in accessible places, while vast areas stay unsampled, so plain tallies skew the picture of the whole basin. The authors correct for those biases to estimate how many tree species the Amazonian flora truly holds. A sound total matters for conservation planning and for judging what deforestation puts at risk. The paper's long author list reflects the many plot teams whose field data feed the estimate.
openalex-w3045864561:
Stephen Rogerson, James Beeson, Moses Laman, and colleagues wrote this opinion piece in BMC Medicine in 2020. It warns that COVID-19 harms malaria control, a side effect drawing little attention. Malaria remains a major killer, above all in places with the fewest resources.

Recent gains against malaria are fragile, and progress had already stalled for five years. Pulling back proven measures invites rapid resurgence, threatening young children and pregnant women most.
