Within days she developed diarrhea, vomiting, and falling blood pressure, along with a widespread rash, eye inflammation, and a bright red, bumpy strawberry tongue.

The picture pointed to streptococcal toxic shock syndrome, a dangerous toxin-driven reaction, and she was moved to intensive care on several antibiotics. The authors note that strawberry tongue is a recognized clue to this syndrome, and they report, for the first time, the tongue's surface peeling as she recovered. They urge clinicians to weigh the diagnosis in shocked patients showing the sign.
pmc-13247061:
Ghallab, Shaheen, and Elkorany compared error-correcting radio schemes for smart power grids in this 2026 Scientific Reports paper. Smart grids must move monitoring and control data reliably over noisy, bandwidth-limited links spread across wide areas. The authors set out the mathematics of trellis coded modulation, which merges coding with multi-level signaling to gain reliability without extra bandwidth, and of its turbo extension, which adds iterative decoding.

Simulations under plain noise and fading channels tested both against uncoded transmission. The simpler trellis scheme delivered the highest data rates in several settings, including multi-antenna channels, while the turbo variant emphasized robustness. The authors discuss adding artificial intelligence driven adaptive coding and fifth-generation grid networks, arguing dependable communication underpins the modern energy system.
pmc-13248961:
Li, Huang, and Li examined transfusion crises in pregnant patients with thalassemia, in a 2026 article. People with this inherited blood disorder need regular transfusions, and pregnancy raises the demand. Repeated transfusions can train the immune system to attack donor blood, or even the patient's own blood, and such reactions are easily mistaken for ordinary pregnancy changes.

The authors analyze three cases where transfusions stopped working as expected. From those cases and current guidelines they build a step-by-step pathway. At the first sign of trouble, teams should screen for antibodies and run a direct antiglobulin test. That separates immune causes early, so treatment can target the right one, protecting both mother and fetus.
pmc-13249061:
Armstrong and colleagues lay out a trial protocol for virtual reality pain relief in children, published in 2026. Laser treatments help many skin conditions but hurt, and eye protection limits ordinary distraction tricks. The planned crossover trial enrolls forty young patients who need at least two outpatient laser sessions at a Midwestern children's hospital.

Each child will play an immersive game during one session and wear a darkened headset during the other, with the order assigned randomly. Pain, anxiety, and medicine use will be compared between the two visits, alongside sickness symptoms from the headset. Enrollment finished with forty children completing both visits, and results are expected in mid 2026.
pmc-13249761:
Marseglia and colleagues update the practical handling of severe allergy attacks in children, in a 2026 European Journal of Pediatrics review. Searching guidelines and studies from 2020 onward, the authors cover anaphylaxis, the fast, whole-body reaction that can kill. Food remains the top trigger in childhood, with drugs, bee stings, and exercise-related cofactors gaining weight as children age.

Adrenaline injected into muscle stays the only life-saving first step, yet it is still given too late outside hospitals. A needle-free nasal spray version is coming, easing needle fear, though pediatric evidence is still thin. Newer long-term options, an antibody drug and gradual food exposure therapy, lower everyday risk without replacing emergency readiness. Discharge planning and family training close the authors' checklist.
pmc-13250861:
Zeng and colleagues track mouth bacteria inside jaw cysts to predict how well bone will regrow after treatment. Their 2026 Journal of Oral Microbiology study follows patients treated by marsupialization, where a tooth-related jaw lesion is opened and left to shrink slowly. Bone regrowth after this gentle surgery is slow and hard to predict.

Samples from saliva, tissue, fluid, and swabs across treatment showed that the closed lesions held a distinct bacterial community rich in Fusobacterium and Clostridia. Opening the lesion let ordinary saliva bacteria take over, and later a different community settled in. A swab signature at three months predicted twelve-month bone regrowth with high accuracy. Lingering early bacteria meant poorer healing, giving doctors a possible early warning tool.
pmc-13251761:
Durbhakula and colleagues ask why some knee replacement patients hurt long after surgery while others recover cleanly. Their 2026 Journal of Pain Research analysis covers fifty-eight adults having a first total knee replacement. Blood inflammation markers were drawn before surgery, and oxidative stress was measured during the operation itself.

Patients starting with higher inflammatory cytokines showed a tighter link between surgical oxidative stress and pain six months later. At low cytokine levels, oxidative stress showed no relationship with later pain at all. The authors call the pairing a biological double hit that primes lasting pain after surgery. Because the analysis was exploratory and small, they stress the findings are hypotheses for larger cohorts to test.
pmc-13251861:
Byunggul Lim and co-authors watch hunger and blood sugar in daily life in this 2026 study. Adults with overweight or obesity, even without diabetes, can show unstable sugar control, and real-time hunger might foreshadow the swings.

Eighty-four adults wore continuous sugar monitors for 14 days and answered phone prompts about hunger six times a day. Hunger reports came with lower sugar at that moment and half an hour later. Over the next three hours, though, sugar climbed, and the odds of a sharp post-food spike rose by about a quarter in the first hour after hunger. The authors suggest hunger alerts could time just-in-time support.
pmc-13253661:
Geoffrey Kaye and co-authors report a 2026 study of smooth pursuit, the eye movement that tracks a moving target. People tracked a target while doing mental math on digit streams they saw, heard, or both. The team also checked whether working memory, the mind's short-term store, changed the results.

Tracking stayed steady when focus went to visual input but grew shaky when focus went to sound. When heard digits clashed with seen digits, math errors rose while eye tracking did not worsen. People with stronger working memory tracked a bit more steadily under hard sound tasks, which the authors link to shared brain circuits.
pmc-13253761:
Fauve van Veen and colleagues explore family choices in a 2026 interview study on genodermatoses, inherited skin diseases. They spoke with 30 people aged 16 and older who had such a disease and wanted children now or later. The talks covered how the disease shaped that wish, what options they knew, and what advice they got.

Most wanted to avoid passing the disease to a child, a wish shaped by fear from their own hard years. Two main themes and nine subthemes came out of the talks. Many said doctors did not offer counsel on reproductive options as routine care, which the authors urge clinics to fix.
pmc-13257961:
Koji Mizukoshi and colleagues present a 2026 study asking whether sharper face images change how attractive a face looks. High-resolution photos of 180 Japanese female models were taken with an 8K camera system. Blurred low-resolution versions were made from the same photos by pixelation, meaning breaking the image into coarse blocks. Both versions were shown on an 8K display, and each viewer rated every face on a six-point scale.

Faces in high resolution got slightly higher attractiveness ratings than the same faces in low resolution. The boost was strongest for faces already rated as more attractive at the start. Ratings fell with the model's age in both versions. The authors suggest extra visual detail can strengthen the cues people use when judging attractiveness, even if the effect is small.
pmc-13258061:
Charles E Hoogland leads a 2026 secondary analysis comparing in-person and online recruitment to a smoking cessation trial for adults facing food insecurity. Food insecurity means lacking steady access to enough food. Eligible adults had used food aid in the past thirty days, smoked at least five cigarettes a day, and were willing to try quitting within seven days. Baseline surveys were done on tablets in person or on personal devices after online adverts.

Online recruits reported deeper food insecurity, more schooling, and higher income, but lower motivation and confidence to quit, plus more loneliness and depressive symptoms. Online enrollment ran much faster, at 64.8 people per month against 7.7 in person, with 324 online enrollees against 178 in person. Eligible online recruits were also more likely to enroll, at seventy-one percent against forty-nine percent.
pmc-13259361:
Deniz Dudukcu and co-authors survey what happens when blockchains guard software-defined networks. Software-defined networking centralizes control, which is handy but paints a target on the controller. Their 2026 unified survey organizes a scattered literature on blockchain-backed defenses.

Six territories structure the tour: industry uses, security mechanisms, defense plans, attack-specific shields, artificial intelligence, and performance. Prototypes blunted denial-of-service floods, man-in-the-middle tricks, and spoofing across internet-of-things, vehicle, and smart-grid settings. Consensus delays and scaling limits still bite hard in big deployments. The authors close on missing standards that keep these designs out of production.
pmc-13259961:
Marina Mello Villalba and colleagues wrote a 2026 controlled intervention study of co-contraction training in older adults. In co-contraction training, opposing muscles are tightened against each other at the same time, so no weights or machines are needed. Thirty-four physically active adults aged sixty to eighty-five were assigned by chance to co-contraction training, traditional machine training, or a control group. Both training programs ran twice a week for eight weeks.

Muscle size grew in both training groups, by up to ten percent with co-contraction and fifteen percent with machines. Strength, however, improved only in the traditional group, while the co-contraction group showed a small reduction in one strength measure. All groups improved on functional capacity tests like sit-to-stand and walking, with no differences between groups. The authors call co-contraction a workable low-cost option where machines are unavailable.
pmc-13260161:
Shoichiro Amari, Masato Eto, and Hiroshi Oyama present a 2026 feasibility study of a standalone virtual reality system for neonatal resuscitation training. Neonatal resuscitation is the emergency care that helps newborn babies breathe. Repeated practice is needed, but mannequin training is limited by cost, space, and instructor time. Thirty-two already-certified perinatal professionals, including eleven physicians, fourteen nurses, and seven midwives, tried an app focused on positive-pressure ventilation.

All thirty-two finished the session, a completion rate of one hundred percent, with no one stopping over side effects. Median usefulness and willingness to recommend both scored five out of five. A standard usability score came to 65.0, which the authors call moderate. Simulator sickness was low, and three people reported mild symptoms that cleared within ten minutes. Realism and involvement ratings need improvement, the authors say.
pmc-13260461:
Domenico Del Turco leads a 2026 mouse study of a protein called synaptopodin in brain cells involved in learning. Synaptopodin sits inside dendritic spines, the tiny receiving knobs on nerve cells, and is required to build the spine apparatus, a small calcium store inside the spine. The team engineered mice whose dentate granule cells made about three times the normal amount of the protein, then examined spine structure and electrical activity.

In the engineered mice, the protein appeared in twice as many spines as normal. The number of spine apparatuses rose about threefold, while spine density and head size did not change significantly. Electrical recordings showed about a 3.5-fold increase in the frequency of small excitatory currents, indicating more active synapses. The authors suggest extra synaptopodin enlarges the pool of synapses available for strengthening during learning.
pmc-13262861:
Nigus Telele and colleagues compare two self-sampling methods for human papillomavirus testing in a 2026 journal article. The virus can cause cervical cancer, and self-sampling could widen screening where clinics are scarce. Girls and women aged 15 to 25 in Bangladesh, Nepal, and Pakistan provided both a self-collected vaginal swab and a first-void urine sample.

Paired samples from 753 people were tested the same way for high-risk virus types. Rates for 14 high-risk types were 8.6 percent by swab and 7.2 percent by urine, and rates for vaccine-covered types were close. Each method caught some types the other missed, and samples with less virus were more likely to disagree. Overall agreement stayed high, supporting either method for large surveys.
pmc-13263761:
Louise Heyzer and colleagues ask which kinds of frailty make walking while thinking so costly for older adults. Dual-task cost, the slowdown when mind and legs work together, signals vulnerability. Their 2026 Singapore study examines two hundred eighty-one community dwellers across physical, social, and oral frailty.

Participants walked while counting backward or naming animals, taxing two mental systems. Frontal executive function, measured by a bedside battery, predicted cost in both tasks most strongly. Social and oral frailty seemed relevant to the arithmetic task until cognition entered the model, where their effects faded. Sharpening executive function, they propose, is the promising intervention target.
pmc-13267561:
Yangpeng Li and colleagues wrote a 2026 review of optical mapping, a method for filming the heart's electrical waves. Special dyes make heart tissue glow as signals pass, giving films with fine detail in space and time. The review covers how the method is used to judge drugs meant to fix irregular heartbeats.

Optical mapping can track many electrical measures at once and can be paired with other methods. The authors list drugs already tested this way and show how the films reveal how rhythm problems start. They also note limits, including the gap between lab hearts and patients. The review aims to give a full framework for using the method in drug work and to guide its move toward clinical use.
pmc-13268161:
Yi-De Tai and colleagues present a 2026 study of wireless power for brain interfaces placed inside blood vessels. Such devices record or stimulate the brain without open surgery, but current versions trail long wires through vessels to the chest. Wires raise infection and clot risks. Removing them means beaming power through skull and tissue within safety limits.

The team designed coil pairs shaped for vessel use and tested them in computer models, on the bench, in sheep tissue, and in living sheep. Power crossed at useful depths: peak transfer reached about 11 percent at shallow depth and about 2 percent at double that depth, still delivering meaningful power under safety limits. One coil pair won at short range; a ferrite-core design won farther out and forgave misalignment better. The authors call wireless powering of these implants feasible.
pmc-13268261:
Brian E Bunnell and colleagues report a 2026 feasibility trial of virtual reality therapy for specific phobias. Exposure therapy works, and VR can stage feared situations at home, but therapist and client had never been shown sharing one remote VR session. Adults afraid of dogs, snakes, or spiders were randomized to twelve weekly sessions by standard video care or by a multiuser VR platform.

The trial enrolled 54 people, well above its target of 30. Follow-up data collection beat every benchmark, and rated treatment fidelity reached 90 percent. Fear outcomes did not differ between groups in this small sample. Client satisfaction, though, improved significantly more with VR. The authors calculate a full trial needs about 160 participants and say the approach is ready for that test.
pmc-13268361:
Ramazan Kerim Yılmaz and colleagues present a 2026 image-based case report on emphysematous pyelonephritis, a dangerous kidney infection. Gas-forming bacteria destroy kidney tissue, and diabetes is the main risk factor. Their patient had diabetes and high blood pressure and arrived with flank pain and fever. CT scans showed a swollen left kidney with pockets of gas in its lower part.

Blood cultures grew a drug-resistant strain of E. coli. Strong intravenous antibiotics were given, and after two weeks the patient improved enough to go home, keeping the kidney. The report contrasts older aggressive surgery with today's more conservative drainage-plus-drugs approach. Its images show the trapped gas that marks this emergency, where quick recognition and antibiotics can prevent kidney loss or death.
pmc-13269561:
Willinton Hernan Pinchao Pinchao and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on zinc oxide nanoparticles given to Santa Inês ewes around lambing. Tiny zinc particles may be absorbed better than standard zinc. Thirty-three ewes received no supplement, nano zinc, or standard zinc particles, at 300 milligrams a day from late pregnancy to weaning.

Body weight, parasite egg counts, and most blood and immune measures did not differ between groups. The nano group showed higher counts of one white cell type and higher albumin than the standard particle group. Several protective antioxidant enzymes, which guard cells against damage, also responded clearly in the nano group. The authors conclude that nano zinc improved antioxidant response with no signs of poisoning at that dose.
pmc-13269961:
Linfa Chen and co-authors published a case report in 2026 about a woman in her late 50s who arrived with sudden speech trouble. Brain scans showed many calcium deposits inside the skull plus a fresh stroke in the left front of the brain. Gene sequencing found a new frameshift variant, a spelling shift that truncates the protein, in a gene called SLC20A2.

The same variant appeared in her son and eldest daughter, who both showed brain calcification on scans. Her second daughter lacked the variant and had clean scans. The variant was classed as likely disease-causing under standard guidelines. The authors say the case widens the known range of faults behind primary brain calcification and supports genetic testing and counseling.
pmc-13270661:
Christian Kempny is lead author of a 2026 scoping review, a broad survey of a new field, on how large language models are used in qualitative research. Qualitative research works with words, interviews, and themes, and its reporting guides say little about documenting model use.

Searching five databases for studies from January 2020 to May 2025, the team screened thousands of records and kept 75 studies. OpenAI GPT models appeared in 93 percent of them. Help with coding data and finding themes were the most common uses. Reporting of basic technical settings was patchy: only 13 studies gave temperature settings, and only four gave another key setting, top_p.
pmc-13272261:
Carolyn Ten Holter and Mira Wolf-Bauwens wrote a 2026 journal article on dual-use quantum technologies in defence, technologies that can serve civilian and military ends at once. New technologies never develop in a moral or political vacuum, they argue, so funding, use cases, and context shape how quantum tools should be judged.

The authors argue the label dual-use is inadequate for moral judgement because it mixes a plain description with an ethical verdict and misses context and process. They propose building Responsible Innovation frameworks into quantum development, enabling case-sensitive ethical assessment and practical guidance. Their way forward engages critics of military quantum uses while respecting current geopolitical realities.
pmc-13273161:
Katarzyna Czarzasta leads a 2026 study in rats of how offspring recover from maternal depression around birth, focusing on brain chemicals by sex. Maternal stress during pregnancy and nursing had earlier caused depression-like and anxious behavior in young offspring, more in females, but not in adults. The team measured signal chemicals in three brain regions of adult offspring.

Female offspring of stressed mothers showed the biggest changes, with lower levels of a dopamine breakdown product and of protective amino acids in the hippocampus and frontal cortex. Male offspring showed only lower serine in the frontal cortex. The authors suggest these sex-dependent changes may underlie recovery in adult offspring.
pmc-13274161:
Mengmeng Jie, Qiushi Liao, and Cheng Liu wrote a 2026 review article on circular RNAs in inflammatory bowel disease. This long-term gut inflammation covers Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, and present drugs help only partly. Circular RNAs are ring-shaped genetic messages that fine-tune cell behavior and show altered patterns in patients.

The review maps how these rings interact with classic signaling routes inside gut cells, including the JAK-STAT and NF-kappa-B pathways that drive inflammation. Several rings already look promising as blood or tissue markers for spotting and staging the disease. Others might become drug targets. The authors note the field is young, with clinical use still to be proven.
pmc-13274761:
Yu-Ting Wei and colleagues report a 2026 journal article testing whether acupuncture changes how brain signals flow in Alzheimer's disease. Sixty patients were randomly assigned to the standard drug donepezil alone, or donepezil plus acupuncture, for six weeks. Resting brain scans were analyzed for the frontoparietal network, a system for attention and control, before and after treatment.

Both groups improved on a standard thinking test, with larger gains in the acupuncture group. Patients' frontoparietal wiring looked scrambled yet partly rebuilt compared with seven healthy adults. After treatment, the acupuncture group showed its own pattern of changed connections, including paths from the right insula and the precuneus into a left temporal region. The drug-only group's changes followed a different route.
pmc-13275061: Dongyue Jiao and co-authors issued a 2026 correction notice for their 2024 eLife article on a signaling pathway that sustains protein production in cancer cells. During a self-review, the authors found that representative microscope panels in Figure 4F, showing cell invasion and migration assays, had been inadvertently duplicated. Similar-looking raw images were mixed up during figure assembly. The notice stresses the error touches only those specific images, not the captions, the measured data, or the paper's conclusions. A corrected figure is supplied, and the authors apologize for the oversight.
pmc-13275561:
Cristina Bridi and a large team present a 2026 journal article testing the weedkiller 2,4-D on the earliest life stages of a South American frog, Physalaemus gracilis. The chemical is widespread in surface waters, and this frog is known to be sensitive. They compared the pure active ingredient with two shop-bought formulations at five low doses matching Brazilian freshwater limits.

The pure ingredient raised a cell-damage marker at low doses and weakened an antioxidant enzyme at high doses. The two products diverged on heart rate, one slowing it at higher doses, the other speeding it at every dose. Effects differed in size and direction by compound, complicating simple safety claims.
pmc-13275961:
Marios Platon Dimopoulos and co-authors report a 2026 case series on a rare, severe narrowing of the aorta, the body's main artery. Nicknamed coral reef aorta, the condition fills the vessel with hard, jagged calcium. Open surgery is the standard fix but is risky for frail patients.

The team treated three patients with intravascular lithotripsy, a method that sends soft sound pulses through the vessel to crack the calcium. A pressure-based measure, called FFR, tracked blood flow before and after. All three procedures worked, and flow improved clearly in each case. One patient developed a tear in the vessel wall, fixed with a stent. The others needed no stent. At checks up to a year later, all three still felt better with open vessels.
pmc-13277761:
Aleksandra Janiszewska leads a 2026 study of louse flies, blood-feeding parasites of birds, across migrating species in Central Europe. The team screened more than 100,000 birds from 157 species caught during autumn migration. They then used family-tree-aware models to ask which host traits track with parasite rates.

Seven louse fly species turned up, with two dominating the sample. Most host species carried the parasites, but only about two in a hundred individual birds were infected at the median. Body size, rainfall in the breeding range, habitat, diet niche, and migration distance all shaped rates. The two common fly species responded to host traits in opposite ways, warning against one-size predictions as climate shifts migration.
pmc-13278061:
Debra R Milamed and John Hedley-Whyte wrote a 2026 biographical reflection on Sir Benjamin William Rycroft, an ophthalmologist who shaped Hedley-Whyte's early education. Rycroft led eye care at a military hospital at Musgrave Park outside Belfast in 1940 to 1942, where he also taught the young Hedley-Whyte and became godfather to his brother.

Born in Yorkshire in 1902, Rycroft trained in medicine, moved into eye surgery, and served with distinction in the Mediterranean during the war. Afterward he advanced burn reconstruction, corneal grafting, and tissue banking in Britain. The piece also recalls his organ playing, gardening, and royal connections, and his 1964 memorial lecture in Belfast on plastic surgery and ophthalmology.
pmc-13279561:
Zia Ullah and colleagues report a 2026 case of brucellosis that inflamed both sacroiliac joints. Brucellosis is a germ illness caught from farm animals or raw milk. It often hits one sacroiliac joint, the joint that joins spine to pelvis. Two sided joint harm is less typical and can mimic tuberculosis or joint swelling diseases. Blood tests showed high swelling marks, and a standard test found Brucella antibodies, germ fighter proteins. MRI scans proved two sided joint swelling with bone wear and fluid in the bone. Care began with two antibiotics, doxycycline and co-trimoxazole. Two sided pain with fever in raw milk users should prompt this test.
pmc-13280461:
Yuntao Hao and team report a 2026 gene study of familial ovarian immature teratoma, a rare ovary germ cell tumour. Past work by the team found a germline fault in BMP15 as a risk factor in one family. Yet not all female carriers in that family had the tumour. The team ask if a second gene acts with BMP15 to cause disease. Subjects came from two three generation families.

Unlike the two unaffected sisters, both affected second generation members held a germline fault in CDHR2 as well. It was a truncating fault, which cuts the protein short. Harm was predicted by standard gene tools and graded by gene guidelines. Lab tests of CDHR2 levels used PCR, protein blots and fluorescence microscopy. Two hits may explain why just some carriers fall ill.
pmc-13280661:
Yuh-Shan Ho and colleagues mapped thirty years of research on false teeth and mouth repair in a 2026 study. They counted and sorted papers from 1991 to 2024 in a large science database. More than thirty-eight thousand papers fit their search. They grouped the work by words in titles, short summaries, and keywords.

Implants, tooth materials, and digital tools led the field across all three decades. The team found four broad themes, from implant-based repair to function-focused care. Three newer themes grew fast in the last period. They were three-dimensional printing, checks on digital accuracy, and the use of smart software. The map shows a field moving from hand craft toward digital work.
pmc-13281561:
Ahmed Adly and colleagues tested how tooth caps are made in a 2026 lab study. Partial caps cover part of a tooth rather than the whole crown. A cap must fit tight at its edge, or decay can creep in. The team used forty-eight sound human upper premolars. Teeth were shaped in two designs, a thin classic cut and a wide cut that spans all faces. Each design was copied three ways: a putty mold, and two mouth scanners.

All caps were glued in and cycled through hot and cold baths to mimic the mouth. Fine microscopes then measured the edge gap of each cap. One scanner gave the tightest fit in both designs. Its wide-design caps beat the putty mold by a clear mark. Most clear wins in the study traced to that scanner. The authors say scanner choice shapes fit as much as tooth design.
pmc-13281861:
Khalid Abdukadir Osman and colleagues set size norms for testicles in Somali men in a 2026 study. Testicle size is a basic sign of male hormone and fertility health. Norms differ by population, yet Somalia had no sound-scan norms of its own. Doctors there leaned on foreign charts that can mislabel healthy men. The team read scans of two hundred twelve men with normal findings in Mogadishu. The men, aged eighteen to eighty-four, were scanned from 2022 to 2025.

Size averaged about ten milliliters on the right and a shade less on the left. The healthy range ran from roughly five to eighteen milliliters. The right side was reliably the larger one. Size did not track with age. Somali values differed clearly from European, West African, and Asian charts. The authors give a cutoff for when a side gap counts as real. They urge local use of these first Somali norms.
pmc-13282161:
Yan-li Chen and Jin-hua Wang present a 2026 case report built around working backwards from an ultrasound clue to a hidden narrowing of the aorta. The aorta is the body's main artery. A birth narrowing, called coarctation, can drive high blood pressure and stroke yet stay missed in adults. Their patient was a thirty-two-year-old man admitted with sudden right-side weakness and slurred speech, after ten years of uncontrolled high blood pressure.

Ultrasound of his kidney arteries showed a slow, delayed waveform pattern on both sides, known as parvus et tardus. That downstream clue prompted scans upstream, which found a severe narrowing at the start of the descending aorta. Blood pressure in his arms was far higher than in his legs. Later dye scans confirmed the tight segment. The authors argue this cheap clue can trigger early screening in young patients.
pmc-13282861:
Sugar handling in the fungus Nakaseomyces glabratus is the subject of a 2026 laboratory study led by Jolien Vreys. The fungus lives in host sites where sugar levels rise and fall. The team asked how its sugar kinases, the enzymes that first process sugars, control entry into energy pathways.

Laboratory tests covered five predicted kinases. Only three processed glucose, fructose, or mannose, and each had a distinct role. One kinase worked best when sugar was scarce, while others handled larger amounts. A compound tied to trehalose storage blocked two kinases and slowed sugar uptake. The results show layered control that helps the fungus grow when food is limited.
pmc-13282961:
What does a rare muscle disease cost American health plans each year? Amanda A Hill and associates answer with 2026 claims work. The disease weakens face, shoulder, and arm muscles over time. Its cost to health plans had not been measured before in this country.

Claims from 2018 to 2021 covered 383 patients and 1,915 matched controls. Yearly medical costs per patient were far higher for patients than controls in both plan types. Drug claim costs were also higher, even for patients without other conditions. Stroke-related disease and ear problems were more common in patients. The authors call the totals a cautious first estimate of direct medical cost.
pmc-13283161:
Airway cells washed from ventilated COVID-19 patients sort into sparse and dense profiles in Franklin Pereira Araujo's 2026 analysis. The virus can drive intense lung inflammation and cell change. The team studied cells drawn from the windpipe of patients on breathing machines.

Samples came from 48 draws in 28 patients with severe disease. Cell counts split samples into sparse and dense profiles for comparison. Dense samples showed more basal cells, young cells, and lung lining cells with odd shapes. They also held more active immune cells and more virus spike signal. Dense profiles arose more often in patients who died. A surface marker called EpCAM rose on lining cells in dense samples.
pmc-13284461:
Elizabeth Anne Breen writes a 2026 commentary on RNA treatments for Alzheimer disease and related tau disorders. A recent review by Rajbanshi and colleagues surveyed new RNA tools, hurdles in translation, and trials now under way. Breen notes strong skill at hitting molecular targets, yet patient benefit has stayed hard to prove.

The commentary argues that target contact alone will not be enough. Immune dysfunction in the brain, wide differences between patients, and disease stage all shape whether a drug can help. Future success, Breen suggests, will need precise tau control plus proof of lasting gains in thinking and daily function, with trial designs that match patient biology and timing.
pmc-13285361:
Live X-ray guidance during front-approach hip replacement ties to a slightly lower early redo rate in Dutch registry data analyzed by Marije C. Vink and co-authors in 2026. Guidance may help place parts well, but proof of better results was thin. The study covered 49,878 first hip replacements done from 2022 to 2024.

Raw redo rates at two and a half years sat close in both groups, near two percent in the figures reported here. After adjustment for body size, past surgery, and fixation, the guided group showed a lower redo risk. No clear gaps appeared for redo due to bad alignment or breaks near the implant. The authors note gains are small.
pmc-13286361:
Anna Mertens and colleagues map the grip system that moves a cell convoy in living zebrafish in a 2026 developmental study. A cell cluster called the lateral line primordium crawls along the embryo's flank, and its grip on the sheet beneath mixes several related anchor proteins. Knocking out anchors singly and in stacks let the team see which ones truly share the work.

Two anchor types sat in overlapping zones of the cluster and covered for each other. Only stacked losses broke the shared anchor hub, sped up stray protrusions, and slowed the march. A sheet protein, laminin alpha5, guarded the floor's soundness but not motion by itself. Pairing its loss with one anchor loss stalled migration outright and sprouted invasion-like fingers, proof the convoy runs on backup grips.
pmc-13288161:
Touqeer Rehman and co-authors report in 2026 a baby aged four months. The baby arrived with seizures, a rash around body openings, and hair loss. Dangerous blood acidity first looked like blood infection. Urine chemistry showed a pattern pointing to a rare, treatable fault in how the body uses the vitamin biotin.

Firm proof tests were not available at their centre, so the diagnosis stayed unconfirmed. Even so, starting biotin at ten milligrams a day brought fast clinical and chemical recovery. Combined with a review of earlier cases, the report urges doctors to weigh this vitamin fault in infants with the same trio of signs.
pmc-13288361:
Zahid Ahmad Paul and co-authors profiled yarrow plants gathered in Kashmir in 2026, testing alcohol extracts and two separated fractions for antioxidant and germ-fighting strength. The herb has a long folk history for wounds, fever, and pain, and the team used chemical fingerprinting to name its active parts.

The ethyl acetate fraction fought oxidation most strongly and also hit a bacterium and a fungus hardest in dish tests. Fingerprinting named diosmin, pelargonin, and epicatechin as key compounds. Computer docking showed diosmin gripping a bacterial growth protein most tightly. The authors propose guided separation of the active parts as leads against drug-resistant germs.
pmc-13288861:
Dennis A Eichenauer leads a large expert panel writing 2026 European Hematology Association guidelines for Hodgkin lymphoma, a B-cell cancer that often strikes young adults. Staging rests on PET and CT scans plus risk factors, and the document walks through diagnosis, treatment by stage and age, salvage care, and follow-up.

Early favorable disease usually gets two cycles of ABVD chemotherapy followed by low-dose targeted radiotherapy, with stronger or gentler variants for unfavorable early disease depending on scan response and age. Advanced disease options include the BrECADD combination or nivolumab with AVD, again adjusted by interim scans. Relapsed patients are steered toward checkpoint inhibitor salvage, high-dose chemotherapy, and stem cell transplant when eligible.
pmc-13289661:
Luis Felipe Ensina and colleagues review a 2026 set of options for chronic spontaneous urticaria that resists omalizumab. Omalizumab helps many who fail high-dose antihistamines, yet some respond partly or not at all, and sorting true resistance from missed diagnosis matters first.

Validated scores over seven days and control tests should judge response, the authors advise. pmc-13289761: Editors and the publisher of OncoTargets and Therapy issued a 2026 retraction notice for a 2019 article on Atractylodes polysaccharides and colorectal cancer by Feng and coauthors. A third party raised integrity concerns in 2025 about Figure 3, and the authors themselves asked for retraction in March 2026. Checks found Western blot overlaps with papers from related and unrelated groups representing different samples. The notice lists the suspect figures but presents no replacement science, so its content stays narrow.
pmc-13290461:
Robotic surgery for gallbladder cancer matches open surgery on cancer outcomes and beats it on several recovery measures, a 2026 meta-analysis by Piyun Zhang and colleagues concludes. Robotic removal has spread in recent years, but doubts about safety and cancer control have lingered.

Searching five databases, the authors found five propensity-matched studies covering 629 patients, 202 robotic and 427 open. The robotic group had fewer major complications, less blood loss, lower pain scores, and a shorter hospital stay. Mortality, overall complications, operating time, lymph node counts, clear-margin rates, and three- and five-year survival all came out statistically alike. Zhang and colleagues call robotic surgery a safe option while asking for randomized trials to confirm the recovery edge.
pmc-13290561:
Patience, treated as a resource teams can hold, gets a measuring stick in a 2026 study by Risheng Qiao and colleagues. Their subject is patient capital, a concept usually tracked with money metrics, here rebuilt from interviews and surveys in organizational settings.

Starting with grounded-theory coding, the team distilled five dimensions: self-control and patience, steady persistence, long-term goal drive, emotional and social skill, and adaptability. pmc-13290661:
Semen quality in Emirati men wobbled over a decade while sperm movement slid steadily, Temidayo Omolaoye and colleagues report in a retrospective study from 2026 from a UAE fertility center. Middle Eastern data are scarce in the global debate over falling sperm counts.

pmc-13290861:
Small tested nudges lifted survey recruitment among Muslim immigrants in Indianapolis, Olanrewaju Onigbogi and colleagues report in a quality improvement study from 2026. Weekly completions rose from a mean of 20.9 to 30.0 during the nudge phase, then settled at 25.9, still above baseline, with 709 surveys completed overall. pmc-13290961:
Akiyuki Okamoto and co-authors present a 2026 case report on early rehabilitation started inside an intensive care unit during a myasthenic crisis. Their patient was a 67-year-old woman newly diagnosed with myasthenia gravis who developed breathing failure and needed a ventilator.

Exercise began on hospital day 3, with the team watching vital signs and muscle tiredness as the load rose step by step. Standing practice started on day 12, and walking practice followed on day 17 while ventilation continued, with no adverse events reported. She left the ventilator on day 24, walked on her own with a cane by day 64, and went home on day 78.
pmc-13291061:
Swallowing trouble after head and neck cancer treatment may be getting missed in routine follow-up, argue Sinead Rothrie, Grainne Brady, and Justin Roe in a 2026 service evaluation. A separate group of 74 patients screened with a concerns inventory found that most reported at least one unmet quality-of-life need. The authors press clinics to ask about swallowing and wider concerns directly, rather than waiting for patients to raise them.
pmc-13291161:
Telling schizophrenia from bipolar disorder is hard, and Zefeng Wang leads a 2026 study using brain scans to help. The two illnesses share many symptoms. Mistakes in diagnosis are common. A light-based brain scan during a word task may offer a fairer test.

The team built a learning model called TimeMIL for these time-based scans. It took data from 52 healthy people, 50 with schizophrenia, and 67 with bipolar disorder. The model finds key time segments on its own. It sorts the three groups with high accuracy in tests. Added tools show which brain areas drive each call. That openness may help doctors trust the output.
pmc-13291361:

pmc-13291661:
Ocean eddies feed tiny plants in barren subtropical seas. Alexandra E. Jones-Kellett leads a 2026 study of these swirling refuges. Gyre waters hold few nutrients on average. Yet many plant plankton types coexist there.

Freshly mixed waters hold eddy-like plankton counts. Horizontal mixing thus spreads the eddy benefit wide. Diversity rests on motion, not calm. The carbon food web gains from that churn.
pmc-13292061:

pmc-13292261:

pmc-13293061:

Treated loads also fell faster over time. Load testing may help target care.
pmc-13293561:

The authors warn of workflow friction and alert fatigue, and call for ongoing tuning so safeguards help rather than hinder care.
pmc-13293661:

pmc-13293761:

Clustered cells sprouted and migrated together better than loose cells, with higher vessel and matrix gene activity. pmc-13294261:
Yating Jin and colleagues test whether brain stimulation over visual or parietal areas changes perceptual learning in a 2026 experiment. pmc-13294361:
Samah A M Abou-alfitooh and coauthors test new green-made flooding chemicals for squeezing more oil from mature reservoirs in a 2026 study. pmc-13294461:

Speaking valves and caps were tolerated at once by most, suction needs dropped, and secretions thinned.
pmc-13294561:
Koji Hasegawa and coauthors appraise a failed heart drug trial in a 2026 viewpoint on non-obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Better patient picking, endpoints, and dosing are the lessons drawn.
pmc-13294761:
Juan Jesús Muñoz García and colleagues test a questionnaire called MOLDES in people with psychotic disorders in a 2026 study. pmc-13294961:

pmc-13295861:

On this view, keeping or removing fat and the cooking method change flavour a lot. The piece aims to guide lab tests linking cooked-meat chemistry to taste.
pmc-13295961:
Xinxin Chen and co-authors devote their 2026 review to daidzein, a plant compound from legumes noted for calming inflammation and mopping up harmful oxygen species. Earlier reviews covered related compounds broadly, so the team focus on this molecule's twin actions.

Daidzein is reported to tune immune cells, block central inflammatory pathways and switch on the body's own antioxidant defences. Lab evidence links those effects to protection in cancer, heart disease and sudden kidney injury. Because the body absorbs daidzein poorly, the review also covers tiny carrier systems designed to deliver more of it to diseased tissue.
pmc-13296861:
Zhiyuan Bian and co-authors clarify, in 2026, the job of a heat-shock-related gene in thale cress defence against a bacterial leaf pathogen. Plants missing the gene caught disease more easily, while plants with extra copies resisted better, and the gene switched on after attack or defence signals.

Gene-wide reading showed the mutant mis-set defence and hormone response genes. The protein partners with an enzyme that tunes the defence hormone salicylic acid, moving toward the nucleus during attack through tube-like extensions from chloroplasts. Plants missing both partners held less hormone and fared worst. The authors map a positive defence role.
pmc-13303361:
Two mango cultivars answer a heat wave with different chemistry, Wenju Luo and colleagues dissect in a 2026 multi-omics study from southern China.
