Levels tracked a clotting breakdown marker and showed a link to oxygen measures. Blood markers, by contrast, tied inconsistently to severity. The authors read caspase-4 as a mirror of how intense lung inflammation is, rather than a fingerprint of the germ causing it. They propose it as a candidate marker for judging disease in children.
pmc-13462761:
Yufei Huang and a large team report, in a 2026 mouse study, that an overactive brain circuit dulls mental flexibility early in Alzheimer's disease, before memory fails. Young mice bred to model the disease struggled to reverse an action for reward, even while spatial memory still held. Brain recordings showed reactivation in two linked areas, the medial prefrontal cortex and a striatal zone, and cortex neurons there fired too easily with excitatory input.

Signals from cortex to one striatal cell class ran stronger. A second class of striatal cells, which release the chemical acetylcholine, was more strongly hushed, fired less, and released less of its chemical. Quieting of the circuit with engineered switches lowered amyloid build-up in cortex, eased the excess signaling, and restored acetylcholine levels. The authors name early circuit overactivity, not cell loss alone, as a driver worth targeting while treatment can preserve thinking.
pmc-13463961:
Gudra and co-authors tested in 2026 whether superglue can clean skin well enough for sampling microbes inside hair follicles. Surface contamination is the core problem in such sampling. Roe deer legs from licensed hunts stood in for human skin. Four preparations were compared, from untreated skin to alcohol wipes to cyanoacrylate glue. Cyanoacrylate is the fast-setting adhesive used in medicine. Bacterial and fungal DNA were measured in swabs and tiny biopsies.

Surface swabs carried vastly more microbial DNA than biopsies. Contamination is a real risk in follicle studies. The glue treatment cut the microbial load in biopsies by nearly fourfold against untreated skin. Treated biopsies also yielded far fewer stray bacterial types. Just eight genera appeared, against 21 in untreated samples and 45 after alcohol wipes. Follicle microbes may contribute to human skin diseases such as patchy hair loss. A cheap glue step could make future human sampling far cleaner.
pmc-13465161:
Rose Seiberth and six co-authors genotype HPV across 213 anal cancer tumor samples from 136 patients. The rare cancer is rising, and most work stops at HPV16 in first biopsies. Their assay read twenty-eight virus types at once across first tumors, returns, and spread deposits.

Twenty-four types turned up in all, and about a quarter of patients carried several types together. Return and spread samples tested HPV-positive less often than first tumors did. Some spread deposits held only non-16 high-risk types, which first-biopsy typing would miss. Over a fifth of detections fell outside current vaccine coverage. Type maps may steer immune therapy choices in advanced disease, the authors suggest.
pmc-13465661:
Xing and co-authors tested in 2026 a step-by-step model of how mindfulness might lift sport results. The survey covered 482 contest athletes from 19 universities in China's Sichuan Province. Proven scales measured mindfulness, cognitive reappraisal, resilience, and self-rated play. Reappraisal means reframing a tough moment to change how it feels. A path model tested the links, with resampling checks for the chain effects.

Mindfulness linked with better play and with both middle steps. Reframing and resilience each foretold better play in turn. Reframing also fed resilience, completing a chain. The full sequence, mindfulness to reframing to resilience to play, was real but modest in size. That pattern fits a multi-stage self-control process rather than a single switch. The authors suggest staged training that builds reframing and bounce-back strength on a mindful base, rather than drilling sport skills alone.
pmc-13465961:
Zhang and co-authors traced bone cancer pain in 2026 to star-shaped support cells in the spinal cord that start eating the wrong synapses. The cells, astrocytes, normally prune excess connections. A surface protein called NRCAM normally brakes that pruning. The team implanted fibrosarcoma cells in mouse leg bones to model cancer pain, measuring pain behavior, bone damage, and synapse proteins. A drug that quiets astrocytes and a gene therapy restoring NRCAM were both tested.

Cancer-bearing mice hurt persistently and their leg bones crumbled away. In the spinal cord, excitatory synapse markers rose while inhibitory ones fell. Astrocytes were indeed engulfing synapses, with a clear appetite for the calming GABA type. NRCAM levels had dropped sharply in tumor-bearing mice. Quieting astrocytes eased pain and partly restored synapse balance. Restoring NRCAM cut the eating of calming synapses and eased pain, pointing to a target for new pain drugs.
pmc-13467061:
Sung Jun Kim and colleagues review a newer nerve block for pain behind the knee after knee replacement surgery, in a 2026 article. The standard channel block numbs the front of the knee while sparing leg strength, yet back-of-knee pain often breaks through. The current fix, an injection behind the knee joint, can be awkward to perform.

The candidate, the popliteal plexus block, aims at small joint branches near a canal opening while leaving the main motor trunks alone. Early randomized trials suggest pain relief comparable to the older add-on block, with an easier working position for the clinician. The review folds the option into fast-recovery surgery pathways.
pmc-13467461:
Oktay Halit Aktepe and co-authors ask in 2026 whether a simple blood index can flag which melanoma patients face higher relapse risk after surgery. The index divides vitamin B12 by C-reactive protein, a marker of inflammation, giving a single number that reflects both nutrition and inflammatory state. The study covered 136 patients whose stage II or III skin melanoma had been fully removed.

Over a median follow-up of 62 months, 49 patients, or 36 percent, saw their cancer return. Patients with a high index had clearly shorter recurrence-free survival than those with a low one. The index separated the groups only modestly well on its own, with an accuracy score of 0.66 on the standard curve measure. The authors present it as a cheap extra signal alongside staging, not a replacement for it.
pmc-13467761:
Lisi Gan and Yanling Ma present a case report, published in 2026. It describes one 85-year-old man with glioblastoma. This is an aggressive brain tumour. He was far too frail for standard surgery and chemoradiation. He also had epilepsy, heart failure, and diabetes. A past stroke and severe malnutrition added to his burden. His tumour carried a gene change that can favour chemotherapy response.

He was treated gently. Low-dose daily temozolomide was given. This is a chemotherapy drug. Valproic acid was added. It is normally an epilepsy medicine. The regimen caused no serious side effects. Scans showed stable disease at three months. His functional scores improved markedly. The authors offer this as a palliative option for similar patients. Larger studies are still pending.
pmc-13468761:
Zhou and colleagues introduce BiasFormer in this 2026 computer vision paper. The task is temporal action segmentation, splitting a video into its successive actions, such as pouring or opening. Transformer models handle long videos well, but they often produce tiny spurious fragments and fuzzy boundaries because they ignore how long actions usually last and which actions can follow others.

BiasFormer adds structural guidance at two levels: statistical estimates of likely actions steer how video features are weighted, and a segment-based decoding head enforces plausible durations and transitions. Tested on four public video collections, including Breakfast and EPIC-KITCHENS, it beat the FACT model on most segment-level measures. The gains showed up as cleaner, more coherent action segments rather than scattered short pieces.
pmc-13469061:
Olivier Perrin and a French multicenter team stretch a scarce imaging tracer further in 2026 by splitting commercial single-vial kits and double-eluting radioactive generators. Gallium-68 labeled PSMA-11 lights up prostate cancer on PET scans, and French demand rose 38 percent between 2022 and 2023. Single-vial cold kits are convenient but costly, and the generator radioactivity decays through the day, capping how many patients one vial can serve.

Working under good manufacturing practice, the team compared four strategies: full vial or two aliquots drawn hours apart, each with single or double generator elution, plus manual versus automated fractionation. Every approach passed full pharmacopoeial quality control. Economics were tallied as well. Squeezing two patient batches from one kit without quality loss is the kind of unglamorous logistics that decides how many cancer patients actually get scanned.
pmc-13469361:
Jianming Wen sets out a theory paper in 2026 on a light based sensing method that rebuilds an interference pattern from one fixed detector. In the setup, called time reversed Young interferometry, the pattern comes from how often each of two light sources fires. Wen recasts the method in Bayesian terms, treating the chosen firing rates as prior beliefs that can be engineered before the light travels.

Because the prior is set in advance, it shapes which outcomes the detector actually records. Wen shows the useful signal lies in how strongly outcomes favor one explanation over another, not in brightness alone. A two source code can turn a tiny disturbance into a clear imbalance between the sources. The paper closes with design rules and a tabletop double slit test using weak phase and loss changes.
pmc-13469461:
Jianjun Rui and colleagues present in 2026 a tracking method for maneuvering targets that a radar hopes to follow without being noticed. Such low probability of intercept operation limits how often the radar can measure. Misspecified motion models and slow switching between them add further error.

Their screened method pairs a classic multi model filter with a recurrent neural network. Its outputs are checked against a smooth path built from recent measurements, and estimates that clash with local motion are rejected. During silent periods, a classifier guesses the target motion mode and guides the next prediction round. Within the tested settings, accuracy improved while the model structure stayed readable. The radar also needed fewer active measurements to hold the same accuracy.
pmc-13469661:
Yang, Lindahl, and Robben test whether patterns in T cell receptor genes can predict type 1 diabetes. The disease is autoimmune: the body attacks its own insulin-making cells. Current prediction leans on ancestry and blood antibodies. The authors note that this approach is prone to costly diagnostic errors.

The team analyzed more than 730 T cell receptor repertoires from 321 patients. Which receptor genes a person uses carried strong signal for future disease onset. A person's genetic background shaped which features mattered most. That points toward personal risk markers rather than one universal test. The same signals could also be pulled from ordinary RNA sequencing data, a cheaper measurement. This raises the prospect of a fast, accessible blood test for children at risk.
pmc-13471461:
Kai Zhao and co-authors build in 2026 a prediction model that sorts thymus tumors by risk before surgery using only plain CT scans. Thymomas are graded into low and high risk types, but scan features overlap between them, so surgeons often learn the grade only after removal. Records of 436 patients with proven thymomas, gathered over thirteen years, were split into training and validation sets.

The team extracted hundreds of texture features from each tumor outline and narrowed them to eleven that separated the risk groups best. Two ordinary clinical imaging features joined them in a combined scoring chart. That chart outperformed every single model at telling low risk tumors from high risk ones. The authors propose the tool for planning how aggressive surgery should be before the chest is opened.
pmc-13471661:
Xueyan Liu, Zhaotai Wang, and Yingjuan Cao map in 2026 the symptom web linking depression, poor sleep, and thinking problems among older adults with type 2 diabetes living in rural areas. The three burdens cluster in this group, yet which symptoms hold the web together was unknown. Eight hundred eighty five participants completed standard scales for mood, cognition, and sleep, and a network model estimated how each symptom connects to the rest.

Abstraction and calculation trouble, together with feelings of helplessness, sat most centrally in the network. Abstraction ability, perceived memory problems, and concentration trouble acted as bridges carrying influence between the three domains. Repeat analyses supported the structure, and men and women showed no meaningful difference in connection strengths. The authors suggest that targeting bridge symptoms could loosen the whole cluster at once.
pmc-13471961:
Abby Bronson and colleagues interview in 2026 adults and adolescents living with Becker muscular dystrophy to test whether standard surveys truly capture their experience. The patient experience of this milder cousin of Duchenne dystrophy is poorly mapped, leaving outcome measures unvalidated for trials. Physical fatigue, pain, and weakness bothered participants most, alongside lost mobility and emotional strain. One pain survey item and three domains of a broad outcome system were understood well and judged relevant. An upper limb survey from another system missed the mark conceptually. The authors conclude the validated pieces can support trials, while the weak one needs replacement or rework.
pmc-13472161:
Sousa and colleagues study hybrid drug-delivery bubbles in this 2026 biophysics paper. Liposomes are tiny fat-based spheres used to carry medicines, and mixing in fragments of red blood cell membrane can make them more body-like. Earlier work judged such hybrids by biological performance, but the physical consequences of mixing were poorly explored, so the team varied the lipid-to-protein ratio and measured the membranes directly.

Adding red cell membrane made the hybrid membranes more rigid, as shown by spin resonance and heat-flow measurements. The hybrids also resisted being dissolved by a detergent, Triton X-100, better than plain liposomes. Positively charged hybrids showed stronger fusion-like interaction signals in calorimetry tests, suggesting they merge with other membranes more readily. The authors frame these measurements as design parameters for building sturdier biomimetic delivery systems.
pmc-13472961:
Giuseppe Valerio Aurucci and co-authors present a 2026 trial of virtual reality paired with nerve stimulation for arm recovery after stroke. Thirty-four people with long-term stroke effects joined a small pilot phase and a main trial phase that lasted about a month. One group used the combined system, called MultiSensy, while the other group had standard rehab care. The team tracked arm movement, hand use, and sense of body position.

Scores for arm movement and hand tasks rose more in the combined group than in the standard care group. The system also gathered motion data during each session to give firm measures of progress. Readers see how pairing a virtual world with timed stimulation may support stroke rehab. The authors treat the work as a first step that needs larger trials.
pmc-13473961:
Xu Sun and co-authors design a smart particle in 2026 that attacks tumors with heat and chemistry at once. Each step of the chain makes more of the fuel for the next, ending in harsh radicals that kill cancer cells. A near-infrared light, which passes deep into tissue, adds heat to boost the attack.

Careful measures linked each design choice to the gain in effect. The work offers a recipe for building multi-action cancer tools with intent, not trial and error.
pmc-13474161: Wang and colleagues published a correction in 2026 to their earlier study of HPV vaccination intent among medical students. That study drew on the health belief model and vaccine hesitancy theory. The notice fixes the affiliation for all authors to the School of Public Health at Xuzhou Medical University, replacing the Graduate School. It also swaps the author contributions statement for a shorter, correct version, and records that Wang and Zhao share first authorship as equal contributors.
pmc-13474661:
Rohit B Ponnada and colleagues track United States deaths tied to both pancreatic cancer and heart disease from 1999 to 2020 in a 2026 study. Federal death data held just under one hundred ninety thousand such deaths. Rates were age-adjusted and split by race, sex, and city versus rural living. Trend software measured yearly change for each group.

The joint death rate rose from about twenty-six to about thirty-one per million people over the span. Men stayed above women throughout, and both rose at a similar pace. White patients had higher raw rates, while Black patients showed a faster relative climb. Rural areas carried higher rates than metro areas across the years.
pmc-13474761:
Danqing Hu and co-authors pool studies in 2026 on whether women wait longer than men before reaching care for a heart attack. Bias checks and pooled odds gave the headline results.

Women faced higher odds of long delay on both measures, with the patient part showing the stronger gap. The pattern held across heart attack types and after adjusting for other factors. Mixed results in past single studies settle into a clear pooled answer. Faster public response for women could save heart muscle and lives.
pmc-13474961:
Lemmerer and colleagues test a new way to fix the shape of 1,3-diols. These units appear in many natural products. Their shape can be hard to set during a build. That step flipped the centre into the wanted shape.

Some matched diols gave a single mirror form with very high purity. Others gave both syn and anti forms in high purity from a mixed start. Tests on how the catalyst acts tie these results into one clear picture.
pmc-13479461:
Chia-Hung Wu and coauthors published a 2026 brain imaging study of reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome, a condition where brain vessels narrow for a time and cause sudden, crushing head pain. Resting brain scans yielded an entropy measure, a gauge of signal messiness, compared between patients with and without barrier leaks. Contrast scans measured barrier leak in hard numbers, and ultrasound added vessel data. The design links a leak measure with an activity pattern measure in the same patients. Findings aim to clarify why this passing condition sometimes leaves lasting brain effects.
pmc-13479561:
Desalegn and colleagues measured moral distress in 2026 among nurses in public hospitals in Ethiopia's West Arsi Zone. It drains staff and can lower the quality of care, yet data from Ethiopia were scarce.

Nurses unhappy with their jobs had almost eight times the odds of high distress, and those in poor work settings had about four times the odds. The authors urge hospital leaders to raise job satisfaction and build more supportive wards as the surest route to relief.
pmc-13479661:
Jekaterina Strelčenko and coauthors published a 2026 forensic study of sharp-object injuries across different suicide cases in Lithuania. The retrospective analysis covered ninety-eight cases from 2019 to 2024 with anonymized records. Injury locations, counts, and types were compared against the additional methods used in each case. The team looked for correlations that help pathologists distinguish self-inflicted patterns from inflicted ones. Findings feed directly into medico-legal practice where the manner of death must be certified.
pmc-13481561:

Current suicidal thinking was graded by a depression scale item, past attempts were recorded, blood was tested for an inflammation marker, and a card sorting test probed flexible thinking.

A different error type, rigid repeats, rose only in those with a past attempt. The pattern splits signs of present crisis from signs of lasting trait, which could sharpen risk checks in youth clinics.
pmc-13482361:
Yang and colleagues track two decades of plant growth in China's Gaoligong Mountains in 2026, asking how extreme weather has helped or hurt the region's greenery. pmc-13486761:

pmc-13487361:

The acid pushed back in a dose linked way, raising Th1 signal output and the key ratio. Mice with a higher ratio tended to carry lighter tumors. pmc-13487961:
Shizuko Angerhofer and co-authors survey married, employed, childless Japanese women in their thirties about planning for children in a 2026 questionnaire study. About a third of participants worked forty hours or more each week, and the average desired family size was under two children. The authors propose support that joins reproductive planning with career planning.
pmc-13488561:
Hui Chen and Baidi Fu survey parents of school-age children with asthma at a Chinese children's hospital in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Average scores sat just below the scale midpoint, which the authors read as moderately low overall. Support networks scored weakest of the three areas, while coping and caregiving behavior scored strongest. Parent age, education, household income, illness duration, and attack history each shaped scores in the model, which explained about half of the variation.
pmc-13489561:
Saeed Sherafatmanesh and colleagues report a cross-sectional study, published in 2026. It asks whether diet and mental health combine to shape sleep. The participants were Iranian adults. The team used baseline data from the Yazd Health Study. They related diet scores to mental health measures. The diets were modified Mediterranean and DASH patterns. The measures covered depression, anxiety, and stress. Sleep quality was the outcome.

Participants with the strongest adherence and severe depression stood out. They had significantly lower odds of poor sleep quality. The comparison group had higher odds. The authors suggest this diet may aid sleep in severe depression. Prospective confirmation is still pending.
pmc-13490261:
Suelen Maria Parizotto Furlan and colleagues test progesterone blood levels as a predictor of embryo transfer success in a 2026 study in Brazil. The values barely differed between women who became pregnant and women who did not, and no useful cutoff level emerged in the reported figures. The work adds a caution against one-number rules in fertility care.
pmc-13490361:
Wang and co-authors used provincial health surveillance data from Henan, China, to test whether smoking lowers vitamin D in adults, and whether blood fats change that relationship. Their 2026 cross-sectional analysis compared smokers and non-smokers on vitamin D blood levels and deficiency categories, using weighted models that respect the survey design, and then split men by cholesterol profile.

Deficiency affected about seventeen percent of male smokers against about fourteen percent of non-smokers in the weighted estimates. Adjusted models tied smoking to higher deficiency and insufficiency risk in men, while women showed no comparable pattern. The smoking penalty grew dramatically in men with low good cholesterol and high bad cholesterol. Wang suggests targeted screening in that group.
pmc-13490561:
Crispo and colleagues dissected wild black-headed gulls found dead or dying during France's H5N1 bird flu outbreaks, asking where in the body the virus concentrated. The pattern resembled domestic ducks more than the blood-vessel pattern seen in chickens, with no evidence of vessel-lining targeting. pmc-13491061:
Li and a national team of co-authors reviewed a decade of heart early action in China, taking stock of what policy achieved and where it stalled. Their 2026 review weighs investments in public health services, outdoor hazard reductions, and primary care reach against stubborn habit trends and underused preventive drugs.

Healthy habit adherence, however, moved in mixed directions across behaviors, and at-risk groups underused proven follow-up drugs. Care quality also varied unevenly despite wider access. pmc-13491661:
Zhao and team surveyed Chinese anesthesia doctors on whether they know and follow the 2021 Surviving Sepsis Campaign advice on fluid revival care, the first-line treatment for sepsis. Their 2026 online survey ran for one month through a national messaging platform and retained 1,051 valid respondents after exclusions. It compared know-how, self-reported adherence, and answers to specific knowledge questions across hospital tiers.

Only about seven percent called themselves very familiar with the fluid advice, though about twenty-eight percent said somewhat familiar in the responses analyzed. Despite the shaky know-how, about seventy-two percent reported following the guidelines when managing septic patients around surgery. Knowledge of specific 2021 updates lagged the general claims, and junior doctors showed the largest gaps. Single traits predicted know-how more than hospital traits did. Zhao urges targeted schooling rather than blanket campaigns.
pmc-13491861:
V De Masson d'Autume leads a twenty-two-author team exploring in 2026 whether tweaking cell metabolism can wake the sleeping HIV copies that hide from treatment inside resting immune cells. Those quiet reservoirs are the main barrier to a cure, and earlier wake-and-kill attempts have underdelivered. The drug zaprinast blocks a gateway that feeds fuel into mitochondria, forcing cells to change how they burn energy.

Across several laboratory models of hidden infection, including cells taken from treated patients, zaprinast modestly but reliably raised viral gene activity and particle production. Metabolism first dipped, then shifted from oxygen-based burning toward sugar-based burning, without killing cells, sparking stray activation, or raising damaging oxygen byproducts. The effect reversed once the drug was removed. The authors propose metabolic rewiring as a companion to existing cure strategies.
pmc-13493961:
Rui An leads a fifteen-author team exposing in 2026 a blood vessel growth circuit that makes the nastiest subtype of colorectal cancer so aggressive. The mesenchymal subtype shrugs off standard vessel-blocking drugs, so the team hunted for an alternative vascular engine and landed on NOTCH3, a signaling protein enriched in these tumors. Patient samples, cell cultures, and mouse tumors traced what it switches on.

The activated protein partners with a transcription factor to order production of TGFBI, a secreted factor that drives endothelial cells to build tubes and migrate. Tumor vessel density in stage four patients tracked the protein's levels, confirming clinical relevance. Screening then found hesperidin, a citrus flavonoid, binding the secreted factor tightly enough to cancel the vessel growth and slow tumors in animals, a candidate precision therapy.
pmc-13494361:
Otsuka and colleagues examined what happens to the deep fascia when a leg nerve is cut, in a 2026 mouse study. The fascia is the dense connective sheet wrapping muscles and transmitting their force. Muscle wasting after denervation is documented, but the fascia's response was unknown. Five to six mice had the sciatic nerve severed on one side or sham surgery, and muscle and fascia were examined fourteen days later.

Otsuka found the shin muscle wasting as expected, switching on inflammatory and scarring genes while switching off a growth factor. The fascia responded differently: it thickened by about half, raised inflammatory and scarring signals, produced more of two collagen types, and shifted the balance toward the more flexible collagen form. The authors conclude denervation remodels muscle and fascia in coordinated but tissue-specific ways. Rehabilitation after nerve injury must reckon with a stiffening fascial envelope, not the shrinking muscle inside it.
pmc-13495161:
Raffaele Badolato leads a national task force reporting, in a 2026 study, how uneven the rollout of RSV protection was across Italy and what it did to infant illness. Respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, is a top cause of bronchiolitis, a chest infection of infancy, and of hospital stays. The seasons from 2023 to 2025 brought the first use of nirsevimab, a long-acting antibody shot for babies.

The team gathered data from nineteen regions on start dates, delivery models, and hospital and intensive care admissions. Northern and central regions began early with few snags and saw falls in RSV admissions, over eighty percent in one region. Southern and smaller regions started late amid shortages and red tape, and gains were smaller. Intensive care trends matched. Set beside early results from France, Spain, and Luxembourg, the lesson is plain: an early start, steady supply, and organization decide how much good the shot does.
pmc-13495261:
Karol Kruczek and colleagues introduce, in a 2026 study, a fairer way to read the braking phase of a countermovement jump in athlete testing. Peak braking velocity shows how an athlete slows the downward dip before springing up, yet deeper dips flatter the raw number. Their index scales the velocity against the free-fall speed the dip depth would allow, making scores comparable across bodies.

Seventy young male academy footballers each did three maximal jumps on force plates. The depth-scaled index proved as steady between trials as the raw measure. It also tied far more strongly to a standard jump quality score, and the tie held up when jump height was counted, where the raw tie flipped sign. Switching to the scaled index moved nearly half the athletes by ten or more ranking places. The authors say the index should sit beside, not replace, standard jump measures.
pmc-13495361:
Shidan Wang and a large team present MicNet in a 2026 article, a deep learning method that joins tissue images with spatial gene data. New tools can read gene activity across a tissue slice while keeping each spot's place, and each slice also has a stained photo rich in shape clues. Reading the two together is hard, so MicNet learns a shared code for both.

The method trains so that image and gene features from the same spot pull close, while features from unlike spots push apart, with no labels needed. In tests it beat rival approaches at finding tissue zones, spotting genes that vary by place, and drawing clear maps of tissue layout. The authors offer MicNet as a way to let photos and gene maps explain each other, which may sharpen how pathologists and biologists read tumor and organ structure.
pmc-13495461:
Tanriover and co-authors studied in 2026 how light focuses around gold nanoparticles shaped like dog bones, with knobs at both ends. Such shaped particles trap light in intense nanoscale hotspots through plasmon resonances, collective electron oscillations, and odd shapes can confine fields in ways simple rods cannot. The team paired a special electron microscope method with full-wave computer simulations to watch the fields.

The dog-bone shape gave strong tip-localized fields under both lengthwise and crosswise light polarization, an odd result. Coating the particles with silica shells shifted the resonances toward redder wavelengths and blocked charge-transfer coupling between nearby particles. Pairs showed bonding-like and antibonding-like modes that turned on their orientation and the light's polarization, while weakly coupled pairs kept mostly independent responses. Tests matched the simulations closely, giving design rules for building localized optical fields.
pmc-13496061:
Riley J Rees, Andrea D Appleton, and John J Schenk tackle in 2026 a long dispute over flower parts in the pink family, Caryophyllaceae. Some petal-like organs in these flowers might really be sterile stamens, the pollen organs, rather than true petals. Earlier work had sampled too few species and had not treated those sterile parts as a trait in their own right.

Building a dated family tree for 775 species and scoring flower traits for 613 of them, the authors traced how the organs changed over time. Their results place sterile stamens at the base of a petal-free lineage, later lost, reduced, or made petal-like in many branches. Readers gain a clear claim: these flowers lack true petals.
pmc-13497761:
Dravidsun M and co-authors compare in 2026 two ways to place reinforcing mesh during open repair of abdominal wall hernias at a large hospital in India. Mesh can sit on top of the muscle layer or beneath it, and surgeons still debate which plane gives fewer problems. The study followed both groups of patients through surgery and early recovery to weigh the trade-offs.

Sixty-two patients were split evenly between the two placements over 18 months, with similar age and health at the start. Fluid collections under the skin were far more common with the on-top placement, while infection rates differed only slightly. Surgery took notably less time with the on-top method, and pain on the first day was lower, while hospital stay was much the same.
pmc-13499361:
Lakshya Motwani, Vijay Kumar Doddapaneni, and Erin L Heuring describe in 2026 a rare blistering skin reaction linked to pembrolizumab, an immune therapy drug used against lung cancer. The drug releases immune cells to attack tumours, yet that freedom can also turn immunity against healthy tissue, most often the skin. Their patient was a 69-year-old woman who had received the drug for several years for advanced lung adenocarcinoma, a common lung cancer type.

Her condition, linear IgA bullous dermatosis, is an uncommon autoimmune blistering disease where antibodies line up along the skin's basement layer, the thin sheet anchoring outer skin. Blistering immune conditions of any kind affect only about one in a hundred patients on this drug class, and this specific type has rarely been tied to such therapy. The report adds a documented case to guide clinicians who see blistering during long-term treatment.
pmc-13500461:
Abdirizak Omar and co-authors track in 2026 whether locking carbon dioxide into basalt rock underground drags toxic trace elements into groundwater. At the Jizan pilot in an arid region, water charged with carbon dioxide was injected into basalt and recirculated. Most of the gas turned to stone within a year in earlier reports. Twenty-eight well fluid samples from before, during, and after injection were analysed for element levels, with mobility judged against sodium as a reference.

Most trace elements moved at well under a fifth of sodium's mobility in the reported averages, showing limited release from the dissolving rock. Peak concentrations for most elements also sat significantly below drinking water limits at every stage of the pilot. The authors read the pattern as evidence that groundwater pollution risk from this storage method is likely minimal, at least under Jizan conditions.
pmc-13500561:
Zhongxing Zhang and colleagues upgrade in 2026 an object detection algorithm for finding defects in solar panels from near-infrared images. Panel faults vary wildly in scale and shape, and tiny defects are easy to miss, yet they sap power output and shorten panel life. Their method builds on the YOLOv8 detector, adding dynamic convolution that adapts to each input and a lightweight module that fuses features across scales. An attention-based detection head and a reshaped loss function that adjusts its focus during training complete the design.

The combined system reached a mean average precision near the top of the reported scale while cutting computational cost to a level the authors judge fit for real-time inspection. Ablation tests, where parts are removed one at a time, and comparisons with rival detectors each supported the design choices. Field relevance spans factory quality control and maintenance scanning of installed arrays.
pmc-13501561:
Abubaker Rom Deng Ayuiel leads a nine-author team with a 2026 qualitative study of seasonal malaria chemoprevention delivery in Northern Bahr el Ghazal, South Sudan. The programme gives children monthly preventive malaria doses during the high transmission season, and the Malaria Consortium has run it in Aweil South and Aweil West counties for three years. Coverage sits at 79 percent, below target. The researchers interviewed 60 stakeholders during the 2024 round. They held 42 key informant talks and 18 in-depth talks with caregivers whose children received every dose, no doses, or doses despite being not eligible.

Enablers included government backing, community trust, workable logistics, and local Boma health workers. Barriers centred on shortages of health workers and drugs, difficult geography and transport, families moving away, late referrals, and weak messaging. The authors argue that fixing workforce, supply, and messaging gaps matters most for keeping the programme going in a conflict-affected setting.
pmc-13501661:
Hao Zhang leads a five-author team with a 2026 project to build a questionnaire measuring how dependent university students become on generative AI for programming. No validated instrument existed for this reliance, which differs from general technology use. Drawing on reliance research and learning theory, the team drafted items covering three dimensions: cognitive, affective, and behavioural reliance. Convenience sampling gathered 1,295 students who had used generative AI while learning to program.

Item analysis first screened the questions, exploratory factor analysis then uncovered the underlying structure, and confirmatory factor analysis tested how well the three-factor model fit. Correlation checks supplied evidence that the scale relates to outside criteria as expected. The three-factor structure held up with sound reliability and validity. The authors offer the scale to researchers and teachers who want to gauge AI reliance in programming courses and keep students from leaning too heavily on the tools.
pmc-13501761:
Nimei Zeng leads an eleven-author team reporting a 2026 comparison of two composite blood indices for predicting carotid artery plaque, an early sign of atherosclerosis. One index, CTI, combines C-reactive protein with the triglyceride-glucose measure; the other, RCII, combines remnant cholesterol with inflammation. The team ran both a case-control study of 2,888 age- and sex-matched pairs and a prospective cohort of 4,418 plaque-free participants followed for a median of 767 days.

Both indices tracked higher plaque risk in both designs: odds ratios of 1.45 for CTI and 1.95 for RCII in the case-control arm, with similar hazard ratios in the cohort. Added to a traditional risk model, RCII reached an area under the curve of 0.704, edging CTI at 0.681 on that metric, and reclassification statistics favoured RCII as well. The authors conclude the remnant cholesterol index may be the stronger early-warning marker, pending larger validation.
pmc-13502161:
Maryann N Krasko leads a four-author team reporting a 2026 physiology study comparing deliberate swallows with the automatic saliva swallows people make all day without thinking. Most research uses cued swallows, yet spontaneous ones dominate daily life and guard the airway. Fifty healthy adults, twenty-five of each sex, swallowed on command with two cubic centimetres of thin liquid and also swallowed saliva uncued. Meanwhile pharyngeal high-resolution manometry recorded pressures and timing along the throat.

Deliberate swallows generated far higher pressures in the velopharynx, tongue base, and the segment below the upper oesophageal sphincter after it closed. The hypopharynx alone showed no reliable difference between swallow types. Deliberate swallows also held that sphincter open longer. Pressures in the two swallow types correlated positively in the upper regions, suggesting clinic tests can proxy everyday function. Sex influenced none of the swallowing measures despite neck size differences.
pmc-13502561:
Barry Halliwell writes a 2026 review asking why iron-removing drugs keep disappointing in brain disease despite a rationale. Iron accumulates in the regions that degenerate in Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and related conditions. Free ions catalyse oxidative attack on DNA, proteins, and fats through chemistry such as the Fenton reaction. Chelators, which bind iron, should starve that damage. Yet trials of chelating agents have delivered unimpressive results, and in cases patients fared worse.

Halliwell argues the explanation sits in redox chemistry that trial design has neglected. A chelator can hold iron in a form that stays reactive, shuffle it between compartments, or strip iron from enzymes that need it, so binding is not the same as silencing. The review weighs where in the body and cell a chelator reaches, which iron pools matter, and what measurements prove engagement. Chelation is not abandoned, but it is put on probation pending chemically sound trials.
pmc-13503761:
Kakeru Matsukuma leads a chemistry team that found a controlled way to break tough carbon-halogen bonds, in a 2026 paper. Such bonds in haloarenes need extreme push from electrons, past what one flash of light can give. Two-flash methods make strong reducers, but the active forms drift off and react at random.

Their plan first pairs the partners into ordered complexes that act as tiny reaction pockets. A first flash builds a charged scaffold that grabs and holds the target in place. A second flash then fires its stored energy right at the bond. The setup blocks side paths and works even with air present. The team shows the method opens a wide range of changes for late-stage work on complex compounds.
pmc-13504961:
Minjian Kong leads a team comparing two chest openings for a combined valve and aorta operation, in a 2026 study. The Wheat procedure replaces the aortic valve and the rising aorta in one sitting. A small side cut between ribs offers a less invasive route than sawing the breastbone, but proof for this operation pairing was thin.

Of 163 patients treated over three years, 59 had the small-cut route. Matched groups of 43 each had like starting profiles. The small-cut group spent longer on the heart-lung machine yet lost less blood. No one died in hospital in either group, and no small-cut case needed rescue conversion. New rhythm trouble struck far fewer small-cut patients, who also reported less pain and left sooner.
pmc-13507061:
Heehyeon Sim and colleagues report 2026 lab work on how serpentine, a water-rich mineral in sinking ocean plates, carries water deep into Earth. Samples held about 13 percent water by weight and faced high pressure and heat along two cold sinking paths. Extra water in the setup varied widely, and X-ray and sound tools tracked new minerals as they formed.

With plenty of extra water on the coldest path, samples took up even more water and formed new water-rich phases past about 280 kilometers deep. With little extra water, change occurred without water loss. On a warmer cold path, samples instead released water. Slabs may carry far more water than once thought.
pmc-13507261:
Guo Yaqin leads a 2026 team that assesses mercury emissions unit by unit across the world's coal power fleet. Mercury builds up through food chains and harms health, and coal plants rank among its top human sources. Standard pollution gear already traps much mercury as a side benefit, yet plants differ hugely in size, efficiency, and controls.

A minority of units, dubbed super emitters, release outsized shares and clustered in emerging economies by 2020. Retiring those units first and upgrading controls elsewhere offers large, cheap near-term cuts. Deeper cuts later need mercury-specific gear such as activated carbon injection. Country-tailored, staged plans follow from the unit-level map.
pmc-13507861:
Varga and colleagues discovered that two immune signals famous for pushing macrophages in opposite directions can instead cooperate on a shared set of genes. Interferon-gamma drives macrophages toward attack mode, while interleukin-4 drives healing mode, and the two antagonize each other. The team combined gene activity mapping, chromatin profiling, and gene editing to find where synergy arises.

Varga found that co-exposure produced an intermediate cell state with a cohort of genes switched on together more than by either signal alone. The effect depended on both signals' transcription factors binding together at regulatory regions opened by the partner signal, with a cofactor protein needed. Deleting a factor or its binding sites erased the synergy, and a third factor induced by interferon proved indispensable for the program. Single-cell data from a mouse breast tumor confirmed a macrophage subset carrying this combined signature inside tumors.
pmc-13508261:
Sibin Wang and six co-authors test two ultrasound measures of the heart's upper left chamber as warnings that a rhythm disorder will return after treatment, in 2026 work. Atrial fibrillation often recurs after pulsed field ablation, a newer energy-based fix. The team reviewed 246 patients treated between 2021 and 2024. Before treatment, scans measured how much the chamber stretches as it fills, and how fast blood flows through a small side pouch. Follow-up ran a median of about 17 months.

Sixty-eight patients, just over a quarter, saw the rhythm problem return after the early healing window. Both measures ran lower in patients whose problem returned. Each held up as an independent predictor after full adjustment. Higher stretch and faster pouch flow each meant lower risk of return. The authors argue that pairing the two measures gives a fuller picture of chamber health, and could help doctors tailor follow-up intensity.
pmc-13508361:
Mengying Ma leads a ten-author team probing links among a blood compound, brain surface thickness, and working memory in hard-to-treat schizophrenia, in 2026 work. Working memory fails badly in this illness, and raised homocysteine has been tied to its progress. The study enrolled 85 patients, split between treatment-resistant and responsive forms, plus 58 healthy controls. Blood homocysteine was measured, brain scans gave cortical thickness, and memory tests scored performance. Exploratory analysis then tested whether brain thickness sits on a path between the compound and memory.

Homocysteine ran high in patients, highest in the resistant group. Within that group, more homocysteine meant worse memory by a moderate margin. Early statistical links tied thicker patches in three left-brain regions to the pattern, though the raw links faded after strict correction. The authors frame these paths as leads for new studies, not settled mechanisms, given the single-time-point design.
pmc-13514161:
Marcella Chagas-Sena and four co-authors review damage to the blood-brain barrier and brain blood vessels in COVID-19 and its long form, in 2026 work. The team searched a major medical database for peer-reviewed primary studies from 2020 to 2025 that tied the virus to the brain barrier. Of 121 records found, fifteen articles entered the final analysis.

Marker studies, tissue work, and brain imaging together point to vessel lining dysfunction, tiny clots, and barrier leakage as core routes to both sudden and lasting brain events after infection. The review follows topics such as viral receptor presence on vessel cells and downstream injury patterns. The authors argue that guarding the cerebral vessel lining should be a treatment and prevention target for post-COVID brain complications, a burden still unfolding at population scale.
pmc-13514661:
Kurose and colleagues report in 2026 on adding Gosha-jinki-gan, a traditional Japanese herbal formula, for men whose nighttime urination persisted despite desmopressin treatment. Nocturia, waking repeatedly at night to urinate, fragments sleep and raises fall risk in older adults. Desmopressin reduces urine production, yet some patients still void several times nightly, and few add-on options exist, so the team reviewed their clinic's real-world experience.

The retrospective study included forty men aged sixty or older with nocturnal polyuria, meaning most urine is made at night. After adding the herbal formula, nightly voids fell from 3.38 to 2.60 episodes per night, and hours of undisturbed sleep rose from 116 to 186 minutes at four weeks, a gain of about seventy minutes past the three-hour mark linked to meaningful benefit. Insomnia scores improved, and no serious adverse events appeared. Without a control group, the authors call the findings preliminary.
pmc-13516161:
Ying Xiang leads a ten-author team hunting a compact gut-microbe signature for necrotizing enterocolitis, a gut emergency of preterm babies, in a 2026 study. Whole-community patterns differ sharply between hospitals, so the team asked whether genus-level shifts repeat. They mined two public newborn datasets, built a four-group comparison cohort, and finally checked a fresh set of their own samples, using machine learning to rank candidate genera.

Certain shifts recurred: opportunist genera such as Enterobacter, Klebsiella, and Serratia rose, while friendly Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus fell. The distilled signature separated cases from controls better than the full profile in the discovery data. Antibiotic-treated cases stayed distinct from healthy babies, suggesting treatment bends the pattern without erasing it. In the fresh samples the signature kept its direction but discriminated only modestly.
pmc-13516261:
Pinto and colleagues evaluated whether human papillomavirus vaccination after surgical treatment of a precancerous cervical lesion lowers recurrence, in a 2026 cohort study from Italy. Women treated for grade 2 cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, abnormal cell changes that can precede cancer, face disease from lingering or fresh infections. Patients received the nine-type vaccine within a month of loop excision.

Pinto followed women who tested negative six months after surgery and compared them with unvaccinated historical controls. Recurrence of high-grade changes occurred in about two percent of vaccinated women versus about six percent of controls. That is a reduction near two thirds, though it did not reach statistical significance in this sample size. Recurrences in the vaccinated group appeared later, at eighteen months and four years, and involved both vaccine-covered and uncovered virus types. The authors call the effect clinically substantial while acknowledging the study was not powered to prove it.
pmc-13516961:
Mokrani and colleagues tested in 2026 whether grape seed flour, a winemaking by-product rich in fiber and polyphenols, can protect the gut in mice with induced colitis. Inflammatory bowel disease involves dysfunction, oxidative stress, and an unbalanced gut microbiota, and prebiotic foods may help. The team fed mice a diet with ten percent grape seed flour before and during exposure to dextran sulphate sodium, a chemical that triggers colon inflammation.

The flour contained sixty-four percent fiber and showed high antioxidant capacity. Flour-fed mice lost less weight, had lower disease activity, and kept longer colons with less tissue damage, and injury markers in colon, lymph nodes, and liver improved. The flour lowered pro-inflammatory signals while raising the anti-inflammatory marker IL-10, and it reshaped gut bacteria, enriching butyrate producers such as Muribaculaceae and Ruminococcus while blocking blooms of taxa. Caecal indole levels rose, aiding barrier health.
pmc-13517061:
Eva Greibe, Jakob N Henriksen, Niels Fristrup, and Elke Hoffmann-Lücke validate a blood test that measures six cancer drugs at once in a 2026 methods study. The drugs, all tyrosine kinase inhibitors aimed at blood-vessel growth signals, vary wildly in how patients absorb them, and blood levels predict side effects. Their mass spectrometry method also catches two breakdown products, letting clinics adjust doses to the person.

The method read straight-line results across its ranges and passed the standard checks for accuracy, precision, and carry-over. One breakdown product, sorafenib N-oxide, wobbled slightly beyond the precision limit and broke down at room temperature within a day. Everything else stayed stable for a day on the bench and at least five years frozen. Patient samples proved the method works in real care. Greibe's team offers it as a fast, sensitive tool for drug monitoring.
pmc-13518861:
Jourdan Julie and four colleagues translate and validate a French version of the PERMA-Profiler in 2026, a questionnaire measuring well-being across five pillars: positive emotion, engagement, relationships, meaning, and accomplishment. No checked French edition existed, despite wide use of the framework. Some 612 French-speaking adults completed the new version plus related measures.

Split-sample factor analysis first hinted at three factors, yet model comparisons confirmed the expected five-factor structure, plus a higher-level general well-being factor. Most scales were consistent over time and across items, though engagement scored lower, matching earlier validations abroad. Scores rose with flourishing and happiness and moved less with anxiety and depression, supporting the tool.
pmc-13518961:
Rina Tazai, Youichi Yamakawa, and Hiroshi Kontani offer a 2026 theory for the exotic superconductivity of kagome metals, a family named AV3Sb5. These materials stack several symmetry-breaking states, and their superconductivity shows both direction preference and handedness, yet a pinch of impurity restores plain s-wave behavior. Existing scenarios struggled to explain the whole pattern.

The trio show that loop-current order, a pattern of circulating charge, generates orbital magnetization that favors one handed pairing channel, yielding nematic chiral d-wave superconductivity. The mechanism works for either attractive or repulsive pairing forces. Coexisting bond order strengthens the direction preference. Their theory also predicts a doubled pair-density pattern, giving experimenters a concrete signature to hunt.
pmc-13519061:
Tetsuro Maeda leads a seven-author pilot letter in 2026 on whether insomnia, sleep apnea, or both at once worsen blood vessel function in people with COPD. Damaged vessel lining drives cardiovascular disease in COPD, and each sleep disorder alone is linked to vessel harm. The single-center study drew 24 people from a research registry.

Each person filled in sleep questionnaires and had fingertip temperature checks that yield a vessel reactivity index. Half the group scored in the low reactivity range. Worse insomnia severity and poorer sleep quality tracked with lower vessel reactivity, and insomnia past the clinical cutoff linked to a drop of about 0.94 index units. Apnea risk scores showed no such link. Maeda's team presents the pilot as early work.
pmc-13520161:
Uranbileg Ganbold leads a ten-author team sequencing in 2026 a baculovirus found in sick moth larvae in Mongolia. Baculoviruses infect only insects and serve as eco-friendly pest control agents, evolving alongside their hosts. The isolate, ManeNPV-Er, came from Eriogaster neogena caterpillars and was compared with its closest known relative from a different moth in Turkey.

Whole-genome identity between the two viruses was only 86.9 percent, a strikingly low match for members of one species. Gene-based family trees and distance measures still grouped them as the same species, while corrected distances hinted at early splitting. Host change plus geographic isolation, Ganbold and colleagues argue, is driving the pair apart.
pmc-13520361:
Himanshi Rathnasekara and Ruwan Jayathilaka analyse in 2026 two decades of data on deaths before age five across 45 African countries. Child survival tracks national progress, so the study tests which economic, health, social and environmental factors move together with mortality over time.

A fixed-effects panel model highlighted immunisation against diphtheria, tetanus and pertussis, plus total fertility rate, as the most stable regional links. Health spending, sanitation and malaria links weakened once shared year effects were added, suggesting broad trends drove them. Country-level checks complement the regional picture, helping policymakers separate durable levers from passing correlations.
pmc-13521961:
Kanako Nakano and colleagues review in 2026 breast ultrasound screening for women in their thirties in fertility care. Records came from one clinic. Dense breast tissue limits mammogram skill at this age. A cancer find can also reshape fertility plans in full.

First scans for 1,336 women from 2018 to 2025 entered the study. Dense tissue showed in nearly 96 percent of women. About one in ten women were called back for more checks. Call-back rates, hit rates and find types fill the result tables. The team also tracked if fertility care went on during workup. Clinic flow grounds the screening advice in real practice.
pmc-13522461:
Lu and colleagues report a cleaner way to make N-phenylhydroxylamine, a building block used in drug manufacturing, by reducing nitrobenzene with electricity in water during 2026 research on green chemistry. The hard part is stopping the reaction halfway, because the product easily reacts further into a different compound. The team argues that a metal surface which holds the product only weakly lets it leave before that extra step happens.

Screening metals by how strongly they bind an intermediate pointed to silver as the best candidate, and tests with infrared light confirmed the weak hold on silver. Their electrodeposited silver catalyst, called CV-Ag, then ran at ampere-level current while reaching selectivity of nearly 99.6 percent toward the desired product across the run. It also kept producing steadily at gram scale, delivering batches of 5.85 grams each without losing that selectivity.
pmc-13523261:
Jamal Hussen and colleagues survey two zoonotic infections in dromedary camels in eastern Saudi Arabia in a 2026 preliminary study. Blood from three hundred twenty camels was screened for antibodies to Brucella bacteria and to the agent of paratuberculosis, a chronic gut disease of livestock. Tests combined a rapid screen with confirmatory enzyme assays.

About one camel in eight carried Brucella antibodies and about one in seven carried antibodies to the second agent, while just over two percent showed evidence of both. Older camels faced higher Brucella risk, pregnant females showed higher rates for the second agent, and mixed evidence was commoner in males. The authors argue that overlapping exposure calls for joint surveillance and control under a One Health approach linking animal and human health.
pmc-13523461:
Ah-Hyun Yoo, Hak Seung Lee, and Kyung-Hee Kim present a 2026 case series on tracking artificial intelligence electrocardiogram scores over time during heart failure treatment. AI models can flag weak pumping or stiff filling of the left ventricle from a single tracing, yet their movement during therapy was untested. The team paired repeated scores with ultrasound measures and a blood marker of heart strain.

Four patients were followed through treatments that included reopening blocked arteries, valve replacement with resynchronization therapy, a coronary procedure, and rhythm control. Score changes generally moved in the same direction as ultrasound and blood results. Exceptions appeared, including scores that stayed high after resynchronization and shifts tied to rhythm changes. The authors call the work hypothesis-generating and urge future studies to account for rhythm and pacing effects.
pmc-13523761:
Qiu and colleagues reviewed fluorescent probes modeled on green fluorescent protein, the glowing jellyfish protein that transformed cell biology, in a 2026 perspective. Instead of the whole protein, chemists copy its small light-emitting core, a molecule called HBDI, and tune it for sensing and imaging. The authors cover how these copies are made, how their structure controls their glow, and where they are being used.

Qiu highlights probes that switch on in response to specific biomolecules, report protein clumping linked to disease, map thickness of fluids inside cell compartments, and detect metal ions. The copies are easy to modify for color and targeting, yet they remain dimmer and less durable under light than classic dyes. Selective behavior inside messy living cells is still hard. The authors call for better synthesis routes and near-infrared versions that can image deeper into tissue.
pmc-13526461:
Brown and colleagues report a 2026 case of an 88-year-old woman whose breast cancer returned as radiation-associated angiosarcoma, a rare blood vessel cancer, about 11 years after her first treatment. Because of her age and frailty, the team chose weekly paclitaxel chemotherapy with doses adjusted to her strength rather than standard multi-drug treatment.

She finished 12 cycles despite breaks caused by frailty and fall injuries, with doses raised gradually as she tolerated them. After a simple mastectomy, pathologists found no cancer left in the removed tissue, a result called a pathologic complete response. The authors argue that gentle, response-guided dosing can work for frail older patients who cannot face harsher chemotherapy regimens.
pmc-13527061:
Haniyeh Azadi and colleagues run a 2026 randomized trial testing yoga, an omega-3 rich seed powder, and their combination in women with type 2 diabetes. Camelina sativa powder supplies plant omega-3 fats, and yoga adds gentle structured activity. Whether the pairing improves blood sugar control, inflammation, and oxidative stress beyond either alone was the question.

Eighty women were randomized to placebo, powder alone, yoga alone, or both for eight weeks. The combined group improved two insulin sensitivity indices against placebo and lowered fasting sugar, insulin, hemoglobin A1c, insulin resistance, and a glycemic exposure index. Antioxidant enzymes rose across the active groups, a lipid damage marker fell with yoga-containing arms, and an inflammatory cytokine fell in all three active arms. The authors report a favorable combined effect.
pmc-13528061:
Sarah Jameel and eight colleagues study virtual health care for people with disabilities in India in a 2026 paper. The team ran twenty in-depth interviews and five group talks. Participants had vision, hearing, physical, or intellectual disabilities. Caregivers joined too. Regions across India were covered, and themes were drawn from the talks.

Video visits saved travel and felt convenient. Still, big barriers remained. Many platforms failed screen readers. Sign language interpreters were often missing. Staff rarely had disability-specific training. The public platform eSanjeevani was little known and hard to use. The authors recommend staff training, access audits of platforms, and policy that cuts costs. Awareness campaigns for public services are also needed. Inclusion must be designed in, they argue.
pmc-13528161:
Mette Møller Handrup and four colleagues pool survival data for a rare nerve sheath cancer in a 2026 review. The cancer, shortened to MPNST, is an aggressive sarcoma. It can arise alone or in people with neurofibromatosis type 1, an inherited tumor condition. The review searched to October 2024. It screened over four thousand records and kept thirty-six studies.

Eight studies fed the pooled comparison. Having NF1 raised the risk of death in that analysis. Fifteen studies reported clearly worse survival for NF1-linked tumors. Four favored the sporadic form, none firmly. Five-year survival stayed poor across the board. The authors note NF1 tumors often grow larger and harder to remove. That size gap may drive much of the survival gap. They call for studies that separate the gene effect from the size effect.
pmc-13529361:
Eleonora Gariazzo and co-authors study whether re-testing tumours at progression improves care for lung cancer patients whose EGFR-mutant disease has stopped responding to osimertinib. Their 2026 multicentre retrospective study, called Rebiopsy on Osi, uses an Italian registry of patients on this first-line targeted drug.

Of 457 patients who progressed, 206 had a rebiopsy, mostly tissue sampling. A resistance mechanism was found in 38.8 percent of those tested, with tissue testing detecting far more than blood testing, and MET amplification was the commonest actionable finding. Among patients receiving second-line therapy, those given treatment matched to their rebiopsy result lived longer without progression and overall than patients rebiopsied without adaptation or not rebiopsied at all. Median survival reached 14.1 months with adaptive therapy against 8.2 months without rebiopsy. The authors support routine rebiopsy at progression.
pmc-13529661:
Pravin Khope and seven colleagues build a learning framework that helps factories trade smartly with the power grid in a 2026 paper. Prices, weather, and machine states all shift at once. Most control algorithms flatten that richness. Their five-stage pipeline keeps it. A graph stage merges price, weather, and process data over time. A replay stage imagines counterfactual runs for safe judging.

Later stages balance cost against carbon under uncertainty. A calibrator keeps bids inside market rules. A safety layer guards live adjustments. In their tests the system cut energy bills by fifteen percent. Carbon fell twelve percent and peak demand twenty percent. Output stayed intact through the cuts. The authors pitch the design for plants joining smart grids. Real plant trials remain the proving step.
pmc-13530161:
Sijie Lou and colleagues pool evidence in 2026 on machine learning models that forecast sports injuries. Predicting who gets hurt remains hard, yet data-driven models promise earlier warnings for coaches and clinicians. Five databases yielded ten studies with ten separate models for combined analysis.

Pooled results showed moderate skill at spotting future injuries and at clearing those who stayed healthy. Wide differences in methods across studies limited how far performance could rise. The authors advise handling uneven data in small samples, using repeated cross-checks, and adding time-based signals. Larger studies must confirm whether those steps truly sharpen forecasts.
pmc-13530261:
Yinfeng Zhao and colleagues test in 2026 how plant scenery restores people under different weather and seasonal growth stages. Brain-wave recording joined with mood surveys measured recovery across blooming and fading landscapes and several plant types. Personal traits, including how tense or outgoing people are, entered the design as possible modifiers.

Blooming scenery lifted both body and mind recovery in every weather condition, while fading scenery helped or hurt depending on plant type. Traits shaped recovery most strongly, outweighing weather preference and gender. One trait showed a curved pattern, helping at moderate levels yet hindering at extremes. Planners gain evidence for healing city green space.
pmc-13531861:
Anmol Desai and colleagues lay out a 2026 trial protocol testing Stress First Aid for substance use outreach workers across the south-central United States. These frontline workers face burnout and moral strain while serving people who use drugs. About 500 workers from roughly 90 organizations in ten regions will be randomized by cluster.

The program pairs a two-hour virtual training with monthly half-hour learning sessions. Surveys at start, two months, and six months track support, burnout, coping, and turnover plans. Interviews add reach and upkeep evidence. Results will feed a national rollout plan for workforce wellbeing.
pmc-13534561:
Hajer Fraj A Alhawiti and colleagues make in 2026 zinc oxide nanoparticles using Teucrium polium plant material and test many possible uses. Plant-made particles avoid harsh chemicals and can carry several actions at once. Standard tools confirmed particle formation and shape before a battery of lab tests.

Particles scavenged harmful radicals in a dose-linked way and blocked four test bacteria, with the strongest zone against one lung pathogen. Breast cancer cells died more as dose rose, with stress signals and cell death markers present. The particles also broke down a dye under light and killed mosquito larvae.
pmc-13534861:
Sangjin Han and colleagues report in 2026 the first record of the fly genus Protopiophila in South Korea, a group tied to late-stage body decomposition. Korean skipper fly fauna lacked full form and gene data, which limits forensic work. Five male specimens were collected and identified by body traits as one known species.

Detailed drawings describe male internal parts that were poorly documented before, and a new key covers all four Korean species in the family. DNA barcodes placed the Korean specimens in a distinct, well-supported branch apart from close relatives, aiding future forensic identification.
pmc-13536861:
Luis Felipe Dias Lopes and colleagues develop a scale for why people eat out in Brazil in a 2026 validation study. Eating away from home shapes diet quality, yet Brazil lacked a full validated tool covering money, behavior, and experience together. A total of 426 adults who ate out at least weekly answered an online survey. Statistical modeling checked reliability, validity, links among dimensions, and consistency across groups.

Five dimensions held up well, covering cost, convenience, habits and tastes, social and shared experience, and perceived food quality. Cost sat at the center, lifting convenience and habits while lowering social and shared experience scores. Convenience and social experience each lifted perceived quality. Scores behaved consistently across sex, marital status, and region. The authors offer the scale for research and food policy work.
pmc-13536961:
Charles Dharmani and colleagues assess a safety program for a joint tumor drug with liver risk in a 2026 survey series from 2020 to 2024. Pexidartinib treats a rare joint lining tumor yet can seriously harm the liver, so use requires enrollment, teaching, and regular liver checks. Four voluntary survey waves asked patients and caregivers about liver risk knowledge and monitoring duties, drawing 239 completed replies in total.

Single knowledge items scored high throughout. Understanding of liver harm stayed at or above the preset success level in each wave, while understanding of monitoring improved over time and reached a perfect share in one wave. Combined understanding of both messages dipped below the level in three waves. The authors conclude that knowledge stayed broadly steady and supports program effectiveness.
pmc-13538661:
Sonja Blasche and colleagues test how common food and drug chemicals reshape gut bacteria responses to low-calorie sweeteners in a 2026 lab study. Twenty-five diverse gut strains met thirty-nine commercial sweeteners, alone and paired with four frequent co-consumed compounds including caffeine and an antidepressant. Protein, metabolite, and genetic analyses probed one strong pairing, and a synthetic gut community tested wider effects.

Three quarters of sweeteners altered growth of at least one strain, and over one hundred interactions appeared with the partner compounds. One sweetener component plus the antidepressant jointly suppressed two gut species tied to glucose control and healthy flora, apparently by altering small molecule transport. The pairing also shifted community metabolism, raising toxicity to human cell lines and changing inflammatory signals. The authors urge deeper study of such everyday mixtures.
pmc-13540861:
Tongxuan Wang and colleagues run a randomised trial in 2026. They tested whether lidocaine given into a vein cuts sedative needs. The procedure was endoscopic ultrasound. Propofol alone often depresses breathing and circulation in this setting. Lidocaine is a familiar local anaesthetic.

Eighty patients split evenly into two groups. One group got lidocaine as a bolus, then as an infusion. The other group got saline instead. Propofol rules stayed identical in both arms. The lidocaine group used less propofol in total. Oxygen drops were fewer, and blood pressure was steadier. Patients woke faster and reported less pain later. Both patients and doctors rated satisfaction higher.
pmc-13540961:
E Nicole Teal and colleagues pilot a safety bundle in a 2026 study. The bundle targets severe high blood pressure in pregnancy. It moves hospital routines into outpatient clinics. Many severe cases first appear in those clinics. Three federally qualified health centres took part. The work ran from late 2021 to mid-2022.

Nineteen care teams trained on the adapted bundle. Each team rehearsed with a patient actor. The actor showed severe hypertension at a prenatal visit. Observers scored how faithfully teams followed the steps. They also scored how respectful the care felt. Scores rose after training. Every team finished training and both simulations.
pmc-13542661:
Atere and colleagues compared blood markers in 2026 between fifty patients with type 2 diabetes and thirty matched controls at a federal medical center in Owo, Nigeria. They centered on ceruloplasmin, the blood's main copper-carrying protein and a suspected marker of metabolic dysfunction. The team measured blood sugar, the full lipid panel, ceruloplasmin, a damage marker called malondialdehyde, and total antioxidant status with standard assays.

The diabetes group differed significantly on sugar, ceruloplasmin, most lipid measures, and the damage marker, while total antioxidant status fell markedly, a pattern of stronger oxidative stress with weaker defense. Obese participants showed the worst lipid and stress profiles. Ceruloplasmin rose alongside the lipid measures, while the damage marker moved against antioxidant status. The authors propose ceruloplasmin as an early flag for the biochemical slide toward diabetes complications, worth adding to monitoring in similar clinics.
pmc-13543561:
Nir Tsur and colleagues reported in 2026 on how the COVID-19 pandemic reshaped surgery and resident training in a children's ear, nose, and throat department in Israel. Fifteen residents rotated through the department between 2019 and 2021. The team reviewed all 1,992 operations across the pre-pandemic year and the two pandemic years, comparing total volume, urgency, and case mix.

Volume swung oddly: 614 operations in 2019, a rise to 874 in 2020, then a fall to 504 in 2021. Urgent work grew steadily as a share, reaching about a fifth of cases by 2021, and foreign-body operations also increased that year. Operations per resident dropped from the sixties to about forty, though the change missed statistical significance in this small sample. Training programmes, the authors argue, need flexible designs that protect operative experience when a crisis rearranges the caseload.
pmc-13545261:
Waad A. Aljohani headed a 2026 computer-based effort to design a vaccine against Eyach virus, a tick-borne virus linked to brain inflammation for which no specific treatment exists. Working entirely in software, the team picked promising fragments from two viral proteins, checking that each fragment looked antigenic yet unlikely to trigger allergy or toxicity. The chosen pieces were stitched into a single construct of 256 amino acids with an added immune booster.

Simulations suggested the construct was stable, water-friendly, and able to dock with two immune sensors, TLR3 and TLR4. A simulated three-dose course produced strong antibody and memory cell responses. The authors stress that laboratory and animal testing must come before any claims about real protection.
pmc-13545361:
Jue Lin and colleagues examined in 2026 how two features of the aging eye, cone photoreceptor density and choroidal thickness, change together across adulthood. Sixty-eight volunteers aged 20 to 70 received full eye examinations, including adaptive optics photography, which counts individual cone cells, and OCT scans that map the choroid, the blood-rich layer beneath the retina.

Older age groups showed fewer cones at several distances from the center of vision, and their choroids were thinner than those of the youngest group. Cone density tracked choroidal thickness at every measured position. The authors read the pattern as linked aging of the eye's blood supply and its light-sensing cells, relevant to understanding age-related visual loss.
pmc-13546561:
Lunjian Xia and colleagues developed in 2026 a model that predicts which patients with newly metastatic cancer of the gastroesophageal junction will die of their cancer within six months. That early window shapes decisions about tolerating first-line treatment and starting palliative conversations. Records came from a national registry and covered 6,564 patients diagnosed between 2010 and 2021, most of them men with an average age of 64.

Six machine learning approaches were compared, and a gradient boosting model won out. Tested on patients from later years, it sorted people into low, medium, and high risk groups whose six-month death rates were about 20, 32, and 80 percent. The authors also show which factors drive each prediction, keeping the model interpretable for clinicians.
pmc-13549961:
Onur Tunca and a large Turkish study group search kidney biopsy features that foretell decline in membranous nephropathy, in a 2026 registry study. In this disease the kidney's filters thicken under immune attack, and outcomes vary widely. The team analyzed 322 patients from a national glomerular disease registry, scoring several tissue features, most notably the share of filters already scarred solid, called the global sclerotic glomeruli ratio.

Over a median five years, about one patient in eleven suffered the combined bad outcome of halved kidney function, kidney failure, dialysis, or transplant. A scarred-filter share above roughly sixteen percent marked a dramatic split, with event rates near thirty-five percent versus barely one percent below it. That ratio, inflammatory exudative changes, and response to immune-suppressing treatment each predicted outcomes independently, holding across treatment groups.
pmc-13550261:
Samuel Tschudi and colleagues compare two plates used to fix corrective bone cuts near the knee in children, in a 2026 retrospective study from Zurich. Surgeons cut the thigh bone to straighten bowed or twisted legs, then hold it with a plate while it heals. The PediLoc blade plate was designed for hip work, but surgeons used it off-label at the knee for multi-direction corrections. The team checked whether its semi-rigid build heals bone faster than a standard locking plate.

Across 111 operations, early healing signs at six weeks appeared in thirty-nine percent of blade plate cases versus six percent with the comparison plate. By three months, consolidation reached ninety-one percent against seventy percent. Complication rates did not rise. Because the gap showed in only some scoring systems, the authors call for randomized trials to test whether the faster pictures mean faster recovery.
pmc-13550661: Christopher J Borgert, for a large group of co-authors, issued a 2026 correction to a forum article on glyphosate safety. The notice is a correction only. It asks the journal to drop one cited article from three pages of text and from the reference list. The citation details were wrong, the notice says. The item also added nothing beyond other press sources already cited. The dropped item was a Retraction Watch report on the safety article's retraction. No new data or claims appear in the notice.
pmc-13551161:
